NMDA and AMPA receptors do not need on this timescale. The two classes are
kept separate rather than made to inherit from one another because their
state layouts interleave differently (P5.4's desensitized states sit between
the bound and blocked blocks), so sharing an implementation would buy
nothing but a shared indexing bug.

A test pins the distinction in the form that matters: raising ambient
glutamate monotonically reduces NBQX's block and leaves ketamine's exactly
unchanged.

### The first derivation-1 ligand in the codebase, and the error it carries

P5.1 established a three-way split for turning published affinities into
`kon`/`koff` pairs, and case 1 - both rate constants measured - had never
occurred. [Dravid2007] Table 5 supplies it: (+)MK-801 at rat NR1/NR2A,
`k_ON = 3.9e6 M^-1 s^-1` and `k_OFF = 0.12 s^-1`. Converted, that is
`kon = 0.234 nM^-1 min^-1` and `koff = 7.2 min^-1`, and their ratio is
30.8 nM against that table's own printed Kd of 33 nM (7%) and against
[Wong1986]'s independent [3H]MK-801 binding Kd of 37.2 nM in rat brain
membranes (17%). Two laboratories, two preparations, two methods, agreeing
to well under a factor of two: the tightest agreement anywhere in this
module, and all three numbers are asserted against each other by a test.

Ketamine takes MK-801's measured `kon` under derivation 3, applied within a
pool rather than within a site, because the two are the same mechanism at
the same site in the same channel lumen. The two orthosteric pools have no
measured `kon` anywhere reached and share `ILLUSTRATIVE_KON`, the same
hand-set 0.01 nM^-1 min^-1 as `acetylcholine.ILLUSTRATIVE_KON`; a test
asserts the equality so the two cannot drift.

The measured pair also carries this module's largest known error, and it is
reported rather than smoothed. [Huettner1988] measured recovery from MK-801
block during continuous agonist at ~90 minutes at -70 to -80 mV and ~2
minutes at +30 mV; [Dravid2007]'s `k_OFF` is a 5.8-second time constant. The
same molecule at the same site, 650-fold apart at physiological potentials.
Both are right about different things: [Dravid2007]'s is a relaxation rate
fitted at -40 mV in a Mg2+-free Ba2+ bath from a scheme in which the blocker
leaves an open channel, while [Huettner1988]'s is macroscopic recovery,
which for a *trapping* blocker requires the channel to reopen with the
blocker still inside and is therefore gating-limited and strongly voltage
dependent. MK-801's behavioural signature - effectively irreversible block
after one dose - is [Huettner1988]'s number, not [Dravid2007]'s. P5.5 uses
[Dravid2007]'s pair because it needs a pair from one experiment and that is
the only one reached, states that its MK-801 washout is therefore ~650-fold
too fast, and asserts the ratio in a test so the claim cannot rot. No
headline result depends on it.

### Which ketamine constant, and why not the tightest one

Three measured ketamine potencies at a GluN2A-containing receptor are in
hand and they span 16-fold:

    0.33 uM  [Kotermanski2009]  HEK293T, -66 mV, 0 Mg2+
    3.31 uM  [Dravid2007]       oocyte,  -40 mV, 0 Mg2+ (0.5 mM Ba2+)
    5.35 uM  [Kotermanski2009]  HEK293T, -66 mV, 1 mM Mg2+

The two Mg2+-free values differ 10-fold between laboratories, and the
difference runs the way the mechanism requires - open-channel block deepens
with hyperpolarization, and the tighter value is the one measured 26 mV
more negative - which is why neither is discarded.

The instantiated constant is the 1 mM Mg2+ value, because Mg2+ and ketamine
compete for the same site ([Kotermanski2009]'s whole result) and a brain has
Mg2+. The stated cost is that the model then carries one ketamine potency,
measured at one voltage in one Mg2+ concentration, while the operating
voltage is free to move: ketamine's *potency* does not track the operating
voltage, though the Mg2+ block of the *conductance* does. The approximation
runs in the conservative direction as the operating point depolarizes (real
block would weaken further), and it is not hidden behind an average.

### The circuit result, and exactly what it depends on

[Homayoun2007] gave MK-801 0.1 mg/kg i.p. to awake, freely moving rats and
recorded prefrontal single units: ~69% of fast-spiking interneurons
decreased their firing rate while 86% of regular-spiking (pyramidal) neurons
recorded in the same sessions increased theirs (chi2 = 100.42, p < 0.001),
with interneuron inhibition preceding pyramidal excitation.

P5.5 reproduces the direction, on the same two-node cortical loop P5.1, P5.3
and P5.4 use, with the weights, gain and baselines character-for-character
unchanged. Ketamine at an illustrative 50 uM bolus takes the pyramidal node
from 0.500 to a peak of 0.520 and the interneuron from 0.500 to 0.474, and
the interneuron crosses a 0.001 deviation at t = 0.25 min against the
pyramidal node's t = 0.50 min - the temporal ordering [Homayoun2007]
reported, which is not put in anywhere. Nothing here is fitted: this is a
sign test against a sign result, as it should be, because a 0.1 mg/kg
administered dose cannot be turned into a concentration without an MK-801 PK
parameter set that `drug_pk.py` does not have. That is the specific,
buildable follow-up and it is named in the module's searched-and-empty
record rather than left implicit.

**The tempting shortcut, and why it is refused.** [Homayoun2007]'s own
explanation is that NMDA receptors preferentially drive interneurons, and
the easy way to reproduce that is to give the pyramidal-to-interneuron
connection a larger NMDA share than any other. That is refused, because
[Bogart2018] measured the NMDAR:AMPAR ratio at excitatory synapses onto
prefrontal fast-spiking interneurons and onto pyramidal cells - one
laboratory, one preparation, three separate long-range inputs, mouse - and
found the interneuron ratio 8 to 10-fold **smaller**, not larger. Setting a
receptor-layer parameter to contradict a direct receptor-layer measurement
in order to reproduce a circuit-layer result is exactly the substitution
this project's rule 2 forbids. Both nodes get the same share, from the same
two measurements, and a test pins both halves of that.

**What the result actually rests on**, then, is topology: in this loop the
only glutamatergic connection is the one *onto* the interneuron, and the
return connection is GABAergic. Reduce glutamatergic transmission and the
interneuron necessarily loses drive first; the pyramidal population is
disinhibited as a consequence of the connectivity matrix rather than of a
tuned receptor parameter.

**And what that costs.** A real cortex also has recurrent
pyramidal-to-pyramidal excitation, which an NMDA antagonist would also
reduce, opposing the disinhibition. `cortical_network(recurrent_excitation=
w)` builds that variant so the question is measured rather than waved at,
and the test reports the answer: for every `w` at which P3.4's
global-uniqueness certificate still holds (`contraction_number < 1`, which
here means `w <= 0.26`) the disinhibition direction survives; the direction
reverses only at `w = 0.56`, well outside that certificate, where the
network is no longer guaranteed a unique fixed point in the first place.
So within the regime this codebase certifies, the result is unconditional,
and outside it the model stops making a single well-defined prediction
before it starts making the opposite one.

The AMPA side is the same circuit through the other receptor and is an order
of magnitude larger - NBQX at 1 uM moves the pyramidal node from 0.500 to
0.695 - because at any physiological operating potential the Mg2+ block
leaves AMPA receptors carrying ~90% of the weight. That is what makes
ketamine's small effect the expected one rather than a disappointing one,
and a test asserts the 5-fold-plus ordering.

### The one engine change, and why it is about arithmetic rather than biology

`Simulation.run` gains a `method` argument, defaulting to `"RK45"`, passed
straight to `solve_ivp`. Every pre-existing call and every pre-existing
result is unchanged.

It exists because P5.5 is the first module whose binding rate constants are
*measured* rather than illustrative, and measured ones are fast:
[Dravid2007]'s `kon` of 0.234 nM^-1 min^-1 against a micromolar dose gives
the occupancy ODE a pseudo-first-order rate around 10^4 min^-1, while the
circuit relaxes with tau = 1.5 min. Four orders of magnitude of timescale
separation in one state vector is a stiff system, and an explicit
Runge-Kutta method pays for that in step count: a 60-minute run at a 50 uM
ketamine dose takes ~125 s under RK45 and ~0.15 s under LSODA. The two
methods give the same answer, and a test compares them directly on a run
short enough for the explicit method to stay affordable, so
`method="LSODA"` remains a statement about the integrator and not about the
model.

This is worth flagging forward to Phase 9: the whole-brain numerics task
already anticipated needing a sparse Jacobian and a steady-state solver, and
P5.5 is the first concrete demonstration that stiffness, not dimension, is
what will break RK45 first.

### What P5.5 delivered, checked against the standing discipline

- **The double-counting question is answered explicitly**, in this section,
  in `glutamate.py`'s docstring, in the example script's output (the
  "effective weight" line), and as four executable identities: empty
  `coupling` on every system, a gain pinned at 1.0, shares summing to
  exactly 1.0, and a drug-free run that holds both nodes at 0.5 to 1e-9.
- **Every instantiated affinity is literature-sourced**, and one ligand has
  both rate constants measured for the first time in this codebase.
  Constants are additionally recorded, and not instantiated, for all four
  GluN2 subtypes for both channel blockers, for the second AMPA-receptor
  response component, for NBQX at kainate receptors and in intact tissue,
  and for the fast-spiking-interneuron NMDA:AMPA ratio that was used to
  refuse a shortcut.
- **The Mg2+ block is treated explicitly and its one free parameter is
  isolated and labelled.** The block function is measured; the voltage it is
  evaluated at is the module's single illustrative receptor-layer constant,
  and every result is swept across the measured range instead of being
  asserted at it.
- **This module adds no illustrative coupling gain**, which is a first for
  Phase 5, and it deletes the question rather than answering it: the
  magnitude of glutamatergic transmission belongs to `W`.
- **Two quantitative errors are reported rather than fitted away**: MK-801's
  650-fold-too-fast unblocking rate, and the NMDA:AMPA ratio's known
  direction of bias as a peak rather than charge measurement.
- **Tests must pass.** 43 new test items, all in the offline gate, none
  slow, none skipped, and no existing test deleted, weakened or modified.
  The gate now runs 810 tests, all green. The engine's `method` argument is
  additive with an unchanged default, and `ChannelBlockingReceptorSite` is a
  new class that no pre-existing site uses.

## Phase 5: histamine H1, cannabinoid CB1, adenosine A2A (P5.6)

### What the brief actually asked, and which part was the hard one

P5.6 bundles three unrelated receptor systems. Two of them, H1 and A2A, are
ordinary postsynaptic G-protein-coupled receptors and need nothing the
codebase did not already have: a competitive `ReceptorSite`, a `coupling`
gain with a sign, and cited constants. The third carries the design
question, and the brief named it precisely: *"CB1's presynaptic retrograde
signaling does not fit the postsynaptic receptor pattern: represent it as
connection modulation, as GABA-A allosterism already is."*

So the three modules are three modules -- `histamine.py`, `cannabinoid.py`,
`adenosine.py` -- following the one-transmitter-per-module convention every
Phase 5 task before this one used, rather than one `p5_6.py`. They share the
discipline and nothing else, and each is described separately below.

### CB1: why `coupling` is the wrong shape, and what the right one costs

Every receptor system in P5.1 to P5.4 adds drive to a node. That encodes a
claim -- "this receptor sits on the modelled population and changes how much
it fires" -- which is correct for a postsynaptic Gq, Gi or Gs receptor and
false for CB1, for two independent anatomical reasons:

1. **CB1 is presynaptic.** It is on the axon terminal, where it inhibits
   transmitter release. In the hippocampus it clusters on the terminals of
   cholecystokinin-positive GABAergic interneurons ([Katona1999]). The
   receptor that produces the effect modelled here is therefore not on the
   neuron whose rate changes; it is on the terminal of the neuron projecting
   onto it.
2. **The signal that activates it runs backwards.** Depolarizing a pyramidal
   neuron makes it release endocannabinoids that travel retrogradely to the
   interneuron terminal and transiently suppress GABA release ([Wilson2001],
   [OhnoShosaku2001], simultaneous and independent).

A `coupling` entry has one index, the postsynaptic node, and no notion of
which input it acts on, so it cannot express either fact.
`connection_modulation` expresses both: its key is a `(post_node, pre_node)`
PAIR, so it names a specific projection, and its effect is multiplicative on
that projection's weight,

    W_eff[post, pre] = W[post, pre] * (1 + gain * activation)

which is what presynaptic inhibition of release IS in a rate model -- the
same presynaptic firing delivering less postsynaptic effect. This is the
third occupant of a feature `engine.py` grew for diazepam and P5.5 reused
for glutamate, and the first whose reason is presynaptic LOCALIZATION rather
than allosteric potentiation (diazepam) or avoidance of a double count
(glutamate).

The consequence worth stating is what did NOT have to be built.
`receptor.py` gained a class in P5.4 and another in P5.5; P5.6 adds none.
CB1's four ligands genuinely compete for one orthosteric pool, and nothing
about the receptor's presynaptic location changes the binding arithmetic.
What changes is what is done with `activation`, and that belongs to the
receptor SYSTEM rather than to the site. The brief said CB1 does not fit the
postsynaptic receptor pattern; the answer turned out to be that the codebase
already had the pattern it does fit.

### The CB1 gain is a measurement, which is new

P5.5 was the first Phase 5 module with no illustrative coupling gain,
because algebra pinned glutamate's at 1.0. P5.6b is the second, by a
different route: **its gain is a number someone measured.**

[HoffmanLupica2000] recorded evoked GABA-A IPSCs in CA1 pyramidal neurons of
rat hippocampal slices and applied the CB1 agonist WIN 55,212-2. The IPSC
fell with an EC50 of 138 nM, and at 5 uM -- 36-fold above that EC50 -- the
reduction was **47 +/- 4%, n = 12**. The effect was blocked by SR141716A and
not by naloxone, was presynaptic (it changed the frequency of
action-potential-dependent spontaneous IPSCs without touching miniature
IPSCs), and was abolished by cadmium.

So `CB1_CONNECTION_GAIN = -CB1_MAX_SUPPRESSED_FRACTION = -0.47`. At
saturation by a full agonist the factor is 0.53 and the inhibitory weight
keeps 53% of its strength; with no drug the activation is exactly zero, the
factor is exactly 1, and no earlier result moves. Three things follow, all
tested:

- **A CB1 agonist in this model cannot silence inhibition.** It removes at
  most 47%, because that is what was measured, and the ceiling is why the
  disinhibition result is modest (pyramidal 0.500 to 0.629 at a saturating
  2-AG dose) rather than dramatic.
- **The two negative signs are different facts.** `W[PFC_Pyramidal,
  PFC_GABA] = -0.9` is negative because the synapse is inhibitory; the gain
  is negative because CB1 removes transmission. Their product is weaker
  inhibition, not a sign flip. A test sweeps activation and asserts the
  modulated weight never crosses zero, because a gain below -1 would
  silently turn an inhibitory synapse excitatory and nothing in the engine
  forbids it.
- **Where P5.5 and P5.6b differ, given both use the same feature.** P5.5 had
  to put its fraction inside the receptor SITE, because two glutamate
  systems partition ONE weight and `share_NMDA + share_AMPA == 1` is an
  identity the site must enforce. CB1 has no partition: one receptor, one
  measured maximal effect, one connection. So the fraction lives in the
  gain, exactly where GABA-A's potentiation gain lives, and `activation` is
  the ordinary positive `sum(occupancy * efficacy)`.

The two modules also modulate DISJOINT connections of the same two-node
loop: P5.5 the glutamatergic `PFC_Pyramidal -> PFC_GABA` (+0.8), P5.6b the
GABAergic `PFC_GABA -> PFC_Pyramidal` (-0.9). That is not a design
convenience; it is what the signs of the connectivity matrix already mean,
and it makes a combined glutamate + cannabinoid scenario well-posed with no
new decision. A test asserts the disjointness.

**The measurement's tissue does not match the loop's label**, and this is
the module's largest single weakness. [HoffmanLupica2000]'s 47% is rat
hippocampal CA1; the loop is labelled `PFC_Pyramidal` / `PFC_GABA` because
that is the loop P5.1, P5.3, P5.4 and P5.5 share and reusing it is what
makes the result comparable. Both readings are recorded in the module
docstring. The claim the module supports is "a saturating CB1 agonist
disinhibits a pyramidal/interneuron loop by removing the measured fraction
of its inhibitory synapse", not "THC raises prefrontal firing by X%".

### CB1's affinities: most of the orderings are NOT resolved

No single-laboratory panel measuring THC, anandamide, 2-AG and rimonabant at
CB1 was reachable ([Felder1995] and [Showalter1996], the two the IUPHAR
tables are built from, both returned HTTP 403). So all four affinities come
from ONE COMPILATION, [Pertwee2010]'s IUPHAR/BPS cannabinoid nomenclature
report (Pharmacol Rev 62:588, PMC2993256, open access), whose Table 1 prints
them as RANGES:

    (-)-Delta9-THC          5.05 - 80.3 nM
    anandamide                61 - 543  nM
    2-AG                    58.3 and 472 nM   (two values, not a range)
    rimonabant (SR141716A)   1.8 - 12.3 nM

A single scenario needs one number per ligand, so `cb1_kd(..., "midpoint")`
takes the GEOMETRIC MEAN of each pair and is labelled a DERIVED SUMMARY of
two cited numbers rather than a measurement -- no experiment reported 20.1
nM for THC. The two endpoints are selectable (`"tight"`, `"weak"`) and are
published values, and every qualitative claim is asserted under all three.

Doing that produced a finding that was not expected. Of the twelve ordered
pairs of these four ligands, **exactly two survive every combination of
published values**: rimonabant is tighter than 2-AG and tighter than
anandamide. THC's range overlaps every other ligand's, so neither
"rimonabant binds CB1 more tightly than THC" (midpoints 4.7 against 20.1 nM)
nor "THC binds more tightly than anandamide" (20.1 against 182 nM) is
settled by the compiled literature, even though both look decisive at the
midpoints. [Pertwee2010] states one of them in prose -- anandamide's
"affinity for the CB1 receptor is also similar to that of Delta9-THC" -- and
`affinity_ordering_is_resolved()` is the arithmetic version, with a test
asserting the exact resolved set. The model never states a selectivity the
compiled data does not contain.

Efficacies come from three papers, three preparations and three reference
agonists, and that is recorded rather than smoothed: 2-AG is the reference at
1.0 because [Savinainen2001] measured it a FULL efficacy agonist at rat brain
CB1 exceeding CP-55,940 under the high-GDP conditions that separate
efficacies at all; anandamide 0.61 relative to CP-55,940 ([Liu2018]); THC
0.20 relative to WIN55,212-2 ([Cheng2012], with 0.22 and 0.31 from
[Mahardhika2024] as the spread, and a parametrized test re-running every
result across all three). Rimonabant is 0.0, the fifth instance of the
inverse-agonist simplification, and it bites harder here than anywhere
before it because the constitutive activity being discarded is large:
[Landsman1997] measured SR141716A to take basal [35S]GTPgammaS binding
22.3% BELOW basal in a system where a full agonist raised it 76.3% above.

### The one place where "an antagonist alone is inert" is a correct prediction

P5.1 to P5.4 each had to record that their antagonists given alone do
nothing, because there is no endogenous transmitter tone (P6.2). P5.5 broke
the pattern: a glutamate antagonist alone is NOT inert, because `W[i,j]`
needs no dose.

P5.6b restores the pattern and, for the first time, has an experiment
agreeing with it. [HoffmanLupica2000] applied SR141716A ALONE to the same
slices and measured the evoked IPSC at 115 +/- 17% of control (n = 9), i.e.
no significant effect, because an acute slice has no ongoing postsynaptic
depolarization and therefore no tonic endocannabinoid release to block. This
model predicts inertness for exactly that reason. The limitation is not
cancelled -- an intact animal has tone and rimonabant given alone has
effects large enough to have had the drug withdrawn -- but the inertness is
now a correct prediction FOR A PREPARATION WITHOUT TONE, so the day P6.2
supplies tone, what changes is a written-down expectation.

### H1: the first use of derivation 2, and the number nothing forced

`histamine.py` is an ordinary postsynaptic module. Its interest is
arithmetic.

P5.1 wrote down a three-way split for turning published constants into
`Ligand` rate pairs: (1) both constants measured, (2) `koff` and an
equilibrium affinity measured with `kon` missing, (3) only an affinity
measured, so share the site's measured `kon`. P5.3 recorded that derivation
2 was "not needed here". P5.6a is the first task that needs it, and it uses
all three at one site:

    mepyramine       derivation 1   kon 0.200 nM^-1 min^-1, koff 0.28 min^-1
                                    both MEASURED [Bosma2017]
    diphenhydramine  derivation 2   koff = 1 / (0.41 min residence time)
                                    [Bosma2018] = 2.439 min^-1
                                    Kd = mean(11.7, 13.5) = 12.6 nM [Booth2002]
                                    => kon = koff / Kd = 0.1936
    histamine        derivation 3   shares mepyramine's kon

The derivation-2 result is a number nothing forced. Diphenhydramine's
association rate is a residence time from one paper divided into an affinity
from another laboratory, another cell line and another decade, and it lands
**3% away** from mepyramine's MEASURED association rate from a third
experiment. Nothing in the construction could have produced that agreement,
and a test asserts it.

What it means is the useful part. P5.3 took from [Sykes2022]'s 18-ligand
beta1 kinetic panel the refinement that derivation 3 is FALSE across
chemotypes and holds within one. [Bosma2017]'s ten-antihistamine panel spans
**333-fold** in `kon`, and mepyramine (an ethylenediamine) and
diphenhydramine (an ethanolamine) -- both first-generation antihistamines
built on the same protonated-amine-plus-two-aryl-rings pharmacophore --
agree to 3%. That is a second, independent confirmation of the chemotype
refinement, at a second receptor. It is also why histamine, which is not of
that chemotype, gets its shared `kon` with the warning attached.

The H1 module also carries the affinity-state problem P5.1 met at 5-HT2A
(250-fold) and P5.3 at alpha2 (10,000-fold). Here it is 33-fold: histamine's
Ki at human H1 by [3H]mepyramine displacement is 79,433 nM in COS-7 cells
([Jongejan2005]) and 2,399 nM in Sf9 cells ([Biselli2021], [Tropmann2021]),
and IUPHAR's published range (pKi 4.7-5.9) brackets both. Two sets are built,
`AFFINITY_STATES` selects, the default is the Sf9 one by P5.3's
preparation-match rule, and the tests assert every qualitative result under
both. The direction is robust; the magnitude is not (peak cortical deviation
+0.189 against +0.066), and that is reported as the error bar rather than
smoothed.

The H1 sign is not a guess. [McCormick1991] showed histamine slowly
depolarizes thalamic relay neurons with a DECREASE in membrane conductance
reversing near EK, that the depolarization is blocked by pyrilamine,
triprolidine or DIPHENHYDRAMINE -- the exact drug modelled here -- and that
the functional consequence is a switch from rhythmic burst discharge to
single-spike activity, the cellular signature of arousal. Sedation is named
as the Phase 7 endpoint it is and not claimed here.

### A2A: a receptor whose endogenous ligand has no measurable affinity

`adenosine.py` builds no circuit. [Schiffmann1991] found the striatal A2
receptor expressed exclusively by enkephalinergic medium spiny neurons and
not by substance-P or cholinergic ones, so it is a marker of the indirect
pathway; [Ferre1993] found A2 and D2 co-localized on that same GABAergic
striatopallidal neuron and acting on it in opposition, by microdialysis in
awake rats. `scenarios.basal_ganglia_indirect_pathway_network()` already has
that neuron as `Striatum_D2_MSN` and already carries a D2 system on it. So
A2A is added to that network unchanged, on that node, with the opposite
sign, and both of those are measured rather than chosen. It is the first
Phase 5 module whose receptor lands on an existing node of an existing
scenario, and the second (after P5.5, by a different route) that introduces
no new illustrative circuit-layer number.

Two results are the honest content of this module.

**The endogenous ligand has no measured binding affinity, and the reason is
a property of the ligand.** [Fredholm2011] states, in the text accompanying
the table this module's numbers come from, that "it is exceedingly difficult
to determine this affinity, because adenosine is rapidly metabolized and
rapidly formed in biological preparations, including membrane preparations",
and concludes that one must rely on functional potency instead; the table's
own footnote says the adenosine row is functional data. So every
`A2A_KD_ADENOSINE_*` in this module is a functional potency used as a Kd,
flagged in the strongest terms, and the searched-and-empty ends in a
published explanation of why the number cannot exist rather than in "not
found". This is the cleanest instance of that outcome in Phase 5.

**Caffeine is not an A2A drug.** In rat its affinity is 41,000 nM at A1 and
45,000 nM at A2A, 1.1-fold apart; in human 10,700 against 23,400, i.e.
2.2-fold A1-PREFERRING. This model has an A2A receptor and no A1 receptor, so
a caffeine dose here produces the A2A-mediated half of caffeine's action and
none of the other, and any potency statement from this module is a statement
about a hypothetical A2A-selective xanthine. The direction is nevertheless
the right one to test against, because [Ledent1997] showed in A2A-knockout
mice that caffeine does not merely lose its stimulant effect on exploratory
activity but BECOMES A DEPRESSANT, which is a causal demonstration that the
stimulant component specifically requires A2A. The A1 constants are defined
and are used by exactly one function, `caffeine_a1_a2a_selectivity()`, so the
non-selectivity is a test rather than a paragraph; no ligand is built from
them, and a test asserts that too.

Derivation 3 gets its best chemotype match in this codebase here: adenosine
shares NECA's MEASURED `kon` ([Guo2012], human A2A membranes, competition
association against [3H]ZM241385), and NECA is adenosine with one amide
substitution. The derived `koff` of 0.075 min^-1 lands within 2.5-fold of
NECA's own measured 0.03 min^-1, which is the internal check. Caffeine shares
the same `kon` across a chemotype boundary and is flagged: [Guo2012]'s panel
spans 320-fold.

Two further honest records. The A2A and D2 gains on the shared node are +1.0
and -3.0: opposite signs, which [Ferre1993] measured, and unequal
magnitudes, which is an artefact of two illustrative choices made at
different times. Giving A2A a gain of +3.0 would have LOOKED like the natural
encoding of "they oppose each other" and would have asserted that the two
receptors are equally powerful on that neuron, which nothing measured
supports; the refusal is documented on the constant and asserted by a test.
And the reused basal-ganglia network's contraction number is 2.0, not the
< 1 that P3.4's global-uniqueness certificate needs, because its weights are
+/-2.0 rather than the cortical loop's +/-0.9. That is inherited from the D2
scenario since Track A and changed by nothing here; a test asserts the
number so it is on the record. Every run in this module does converge to the
all-0.5 fixed point, which is a weaker statement than certified uniqueness
and is the one this module is entitled to make.

### Sourcing: three reachability failures, recorded as such

P5.5 recorded a primary that returned HTTP 403 and did not use its numbers.
P5.6 had to use numbers from sources it could not open directly, and the
route taken in each case is recorded on the constant rather than hidden:

- **[Booth2002]** (JPET, H1 affinities). Publisher returned 403. The values
  used are that paper's own data as deposited by the authors' laboratory in
  the NIMH PDSP Ki database and served through BindingDB entry 5364. The
  check that this is the right paper's data rather than a mis-join: the mean
  of its two diphenhydramine determinations is pKi 7.90, and IUPHAR records
  "diphenhydramine, human H1, pKi 7.9" attributed to exactly that reference.
- **[Biselli2021], [Tropmann2021], [Liu2018], [Cheng2012]** (histamine's H1
  affinity; CB1 efficacies). Paywalled; values read from ChEMBL's curation,
  with the ChEMBL document identifier recorded next to each so the
  extraction can be re-checked.
- **[Daly1991], [AboSalem2004], [Grahner1994], [Jacobson1999]** (caffeine's
  adenosine-receptor affinities). All paywalled; the values are
  [Fredholm2011]'s IUPHAR tabulation of them, with that review's own
  per-value attribution recorded so a future pass can replace any single
  entry without re-deriving the set.

None of these is as good as reading the primary. All of them are better than
inventing a number, and each is labelled at the point of use so that a
reader can see exactly how far from the bench each constant sits.

### What P5.6 delivered, checked against the standing discipline

- **Cited constants for all three receptor systems.** H1: three affinities,
  one measured rate pair, one measured residence time, three efficacies.
  CB1: four affinities (as published ranges, with the instantiation rule
  labelled), four efficacies, and a measured connection-modulation gain.
  A2A: two affinities per species plus the A1 pair that shows caffeine is
  non-selective, one measured association rate, two efficacies.
- **CB1 is handled as connection modulation with the rationale written
  down** -- presynaptic localization plus retrograde signalling, neither of
  which a single-index `coupling` entry can express -- in this section, in
  `cannabinoid.py`'s docstring, in the example script's "effective weight"
  column, and as executable identities: empty `coupling`, a gain equal to
  the measured suppression, a modulated weight that never changes sign, and
  a drug-free run reproducing the drug-free network exactly.
- **Scenarios and tests.** Three example scripts and 95 new test items, all
  in the offline gate, none slow, none skipped, and no existing test
  deleted, weakened or modified. The gate now runs 905 tests, all green;
  the full suite including the slow MCMC items runs 919, all green. `receptor.py` and `engine.py` are
  unchanged: P5.6 needed no new mechanism, which is itself the answer to the
  question the brief asked.
- **What was deliberately not built is enumerated per module**, with the
  reason and, where applicable, the missing number: H2 and H3; CB1 on
  glutamatergic terminals (missing a measured maximal EPSC suppression in a
  matched preparation, and its absence over-states a CB1 agonist's net
  excitatory effect); the retrograde loop closed as a loop (P6.1); A1, A2B,
  A3; and the A2A-D2 heteromer, whose functional consequence is reproduced
  by two opposite-signed gains on one node without asserting its molecular
  basis.

## Phase 5: opioid kappa and delta (P5.7)

### The brief's own sentence, checked rather than repeated

The task named the deliverable precisely: kappa and delta receptors with cited
constants for dynorphin, enkephalin, U50488, nor-BNI and naltrindole, "and
crucially the cross-affinities of the existing mu ligands. Fentanyl and
naloxone are not mu-selective in the limit, and naloxone's kappa and delta
affinities matter for reversal modeling."

That is checkable, and the numbers say it more sharply than the sentence does.
In one laboratory's panel on human cloned receptors:

    ligand         mu Ki    delta Ki   kappa Ki    mu-selectivity (delta/kappa)
    fentanyl        0.7      152.7       84.8            218x / 121x
    naloxone        1.4       67.5        2.5             48x /   1.8x

**Naloxone is 1.79-fold selective for mu over kappa.** Not ten-fold, not a
hundred-fold: 1.79, which is inside the spread of a single competition curve.
Any naloxone exposure large enough to reverse a mu agonist has also blocked
most of the kappa pool. `opioid.naloxone_mu_over_kappa_selectivity()` exists
so that this is a test rather than a paragraph.

Fentanyl's selectivity is large but bounded, and it has a second half a Ki
table cannot show: fentanyl is a PARTIAL AGONIST at kappa, 30 +/- 4% of U69,593 in
the same laboratory's functional panel, and a near-full agonist at delta,
86 +/- 19% of DPDPE. So above its kappa Kd, fentanyl does not merely occupy
the receptor that opposes its own mu action, it activates it.

### One paper, and why finding it was most of the task

Every affinity and every efficacy in `opioid.py` comes from [Toll1998] (Toll
L, Berzetei-Gurske IP, Polgar WE, Brandt SR, Adapa ID, Rodriguez L, Schwartz
RW, Haggart D, O'Brien A, White A, Kennedy JM, Craymer K, Farrington L, Auh
JS, NIDA Res Monogr 1998;178:440-466, PMID 9686407, SRI International under
NIDA contracts N01DA-3-8302 and N01DA-4-8307). Its Table 5 gives Ki at human
cloned mu, delta and kappa receptors expressed in CHO cells ([3H]DAMGO,
[3H]DPDPE-Cl, [3H]U69,593) and, in parallel columns, at the same three sites
in guinea-pig brain membranes. Its Table 7 gives [35S]GTPyS stimulation in
membranes from the same three cell lines, as a percentage of each site's own
reference full agonist.

Why a single-laboratory panel was worth searching for rather than assembling
seven ligands from seven papers: **a selectivity ratio built from two papers
is a comparison of two laboratories as much as of two receptors.** The whole
content of P5.7 is ratios -- naloxone's mu over its kappa, fentanyl's mu over
its delta, dynorphin's kappa over its mu -- and a ratio is only a statement
about the receptors if numerator and denominator were measured in the same
experiment. [Toll1998] measured all twenty-one cells that way.

It is also a NIDA Research Monograph, i.e. a United States government
publication in the public domain, and the full text including both tables is
readable at `archive.org/details/rms178`. So unlike P5.6's three reachability
failures, this is a primary source read directly.

The provenance check that scan needed: every one of the seven ligands was
independently verified against the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to PHARMACOLOGY's own
curation of this same paper (its human mu/delta/kappa interaction records
citing PMID 9686407), and all twenty-one available pKi values agree to the
rounding IUPHAR publishes. Trusting character recognition on a 1998 typescript
for numbers every result depends on is not good enough on its own, and the
check is recorded in `opioid.py` next to the citation.

### Eleven measured zeros: the first time `efficacy=0.0` is not a simplification

Every module from P5.1 to P5.6 had to flag a neutral-antagonist efficacy of
0.0 as a modelling simplification standing in for an unmeasured inverse
agonism. [Toll1998] Table 7 ran naloxone, nor-BNI and naltrindole in the
functional assay at all three human receptors and each was "flat" at all
three, and ran U50488 at mu and delta with the same result: eleven measured
zeros, listed in `opioid.MEASURED_FLAT`, and a test asserts that every zero in
the efficacy table is one of them rather than a default.

### Three things the numbers say that the folk summary does not

1. **Dynorphin A is only 4.53-fold kappa-selective over mu** (1.7 against
   7.7 nM) and is a full agonist at all three receptors in the same panel
   (97%, 99%, 99%). The endogenous "kappa peptide" is barely a selective
   ligand at equilibrium; its selectivity in vivo is a matter of where it is
   released, which is a Phase 6 property this model does not have.
2. **Leu-enkephalin binds mu tightly and barely activates it**: Ki 7.4 nM,
   within 3.5-fold of its delta Ki, but only 11 +/- 4% of DAMGO's maximum
   there against 104 +/- 21% of DPDPE's at delta. Affinity and efficacy point
   in different directions for one peptide at one receptor, which is exactly
   what a model carrying only Ki would get backwards. It is the reason both
   tables are used and not just Table 5.
3. **The "selective" antagonists are not very selective at equilibrium.**
   nor-BNI is 28.5-fold kappa-over-delta and naltrindole 31.5-fold
   delta-over-mu. nor-BNI's famous selectivity in vivo is a DURATION
   phenomenon -- days to weeks of kappa antagonism after one dose -- which
   `TOOL_COMPOUND_KE` and a derivation-3 `koff` cannot represent, and which is
   listed under what was deliberately not built.

### Two preparation disagreements, from the paper's own control

[Toll1998] measured the same twenty-one cells twice, in human CHO cells and in
guinea-pig brain, which is an unusually direct measurement of what a
preparation is worth. Nineteen of twenty-one agree within 3.5-fold. Two do
not: naltrindole at MU, 6.3 +/- 2.3 nM against 0.2 +/- 0.01 nM (31.5-fold,
and that one cell is the difference between "naltrindole is 32-fold
delta-selective" and "2.2-fold"), and dynorphin A at DELTA, 42.7 against
5.8 nM (7.4-fold). Worth recording alongside them: the KAPPA column is the one
the two preparations agree on best, every cell within 1.8-fold, and it is the
column this module's headline results rest on. Both columns are in
`KI_GUINEA_PIG_BRAIN`, the human-CHO one is used throughout for three stated
reasons, and a test asserts the disagreements rather than hiding them.

### Censored cells used as bounds, in the direction that makes conclusions safe

[Toll1998] prints ">10,000" rather than a number in two cells this module
needs: U50488 at delta and Leu-enkephalin at kappa. Ten thousand nanomolar is
the top of the assay, not a measurement. The rule applied, stated on the
constant and asserted by a test:

    a censored ">10,000" is instantiated AT the bound, which makes the
    modelled cross-activity an UPPER bound on the real cross-activity.

The bound is the smallest value consistent with the datum, so it maximises the
cross-talk the model can show. Every "this ligand does essentially nothing at
that receptor" conclusion drawn from those two cells is therefore
conservative, and no result depends on the difference between "10,000" and
"more than that".

### Where the three receptors go: three placements, each forced by an experiment

No new circuit was drawn. `scenarios.multi_region_mu_opioid_network()` is
reused, so a kappa result is comparable with the mu results this codebase has
had since Track C1.

- **Mu**: unchanged, P4.3's atlas-derived coupling on VTA_GABA,
  PAG_Interneuron and LC.
- **Delta on `VTA_GABA`, via `coupling`, negative.** [Devine1993] (Devine DP,
  Leone P, Pocock D, Wise RA, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1993;266:1236-1246, PMID
  7690399) microinjected DPDPE into the rat VTA and measured ventral striatal
  dopamine by microdialysis: dose-orderly increases, antagonised by intra-VTA
  naltrindole and NOT by the mu antagonist CTOP, while DAMGO's increases were
  antagonised by CTOP and not by naltrindole. The delta receptor that raises
  mesolimbic dopamine is in the VTA, is not the mu receptor, and uses the same
  Gi-on-a-GABAergic-interneuron disinhibition motif.
- **Kappa on the `VTA_DA -> NAc` CONNECTION, via `connection_modulation`.**
  Three findings force a connection rather than a node:
  [DiChiara1988] (J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1988;244:1067-1080, PMID 2855239) gave
  freely-moving rats systemic mu agonists (morphine, methadone, FENTANYL) and
  kappa agonists (U-50,488, bremazocine, tifluadom) and measured accumbal
  dopamine going up under the first and down under the second -- two of this
  module's own four drugs, so the opposite valence is not imported from a
  related compound; [Devine1993] found intra-VTA U-50,488H "failed to alter
  ventral striatal DA concentrations at any dose tested" while systemic
  injection lowered them, so the receptor carrying the effect is not on the
  VTA cell bodies; and [Svingos2001] (Synapse 2001;42:185-192, PMID 11746715)
  found by immuno-electron microscopy that kappa labelling in the rat
  accumbens is mainly PRESYNAPTIC, with 51% of 400 kappa-labelled presynaptic
  profiles also expressing the dopamine transporter. A receptor on a
  presynaptic terminal that reduces release at one identified synapse is
  P5.6b's CB1 argument, reappearing for a different receptor, and it is why
  `coupling_kappa()` returns an empty dict.

[Margolis2003] (J Neurosci 2003;23:9981-9986) is the paper that complicates
this and is not hidden: in VTA slices U69593 directly inhibits
tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive neurons via a GIRK current, blocked by nor-BNI.
A somatodendritic kappa receptor on VTA dopamine neurons exists and is
functional; [Devine1993] says it is not the one carrying the in vivo dopamine
decrease. This is a choice between two measured mechanisms, made by an
experiment, with the other named.

### The kappa gain is a measurement, and so is "the antagonist alone is inert"

[Britt2008] (Britt JP, McGehee DS, J Neurosci 2008;28:1672-1681, PMC6671549)
recorded electrically evoked dopamine overflow in rat striatal slices and bath
-applied a SATURATING concentration (1 uM) of the kappa agonist BRL52537.
Single-pulse-evoked overflow fell **to 28 +/- 5% of control**, in every
recording, throughout dorsal and ventral striatum, and unlike the mu and delta
effects in the same paper it could not be overcome by burst stimulation.
Nor-binaltorphimine (1 uM) "mostly restored the DA signal" and "alone had no
direct effect on DA overflow".

So `KOR_MAX_SUPPRESSED_FRACTION = 0.72` and `KOR_CONNECTION_GAIN = -0.72`, the
CB1 construction exactly: the engine forms `1 + gain * activation`, a
saturating full agonist drives activation to ~1, and the modulated weight
keeps 28% of its strength. This is the second measured circuit-layer gain in
this project. Two consequences, both asserted:

1. **A kappa agonist in this model cannot silence the mesolimbic projection**,
   only remove 72% of it, and the excitatory weight never inverts. A gain
   below -1 would silently flip it and nothing in the engine forbids that.
2. **Nor-BNI alone changes nothing here, and for once that is a measured
   prediction rather than an artefact.** Every module since P5.1 has had to
   say "an antagonist alone is inert because P6.2 has supplied no endogenous
   transmitter"; [Britt2008] measured that inertness in tissue that certainly
   had endogenous dynorphin in it. The model agrees with the experiment for
   the wrong reason, and the distinction is recorded rather than glossed.

The largest weakness, stated first in `opioid.py`: BRL52537 is not U50488. The
72% is treated as the maximal suppression achievable THROUGH THE RECEPTOR at
saturating occupancy by a full agonist, and both U50488 and dynorphin were
measured by [Toll1998] as full kappa agonists (93 +/- 11% and 97 +/- 5%). It
is not a claim that U50488's own maximum was measured at 0.72.

### The finding that forced a network change, which is P3.4's lesson again

This was not a stylistic preference. The kappa mechanism modulates what the
`VTA_DA -> NAc` projection transmits, and on Track C1's hand-set baselines the
drug-free fixed point of the reward block is `VTA_GABA = 0.987`,
`VTA_DA = 4.9e-6`, `NAc = 0.500`: VTA_GABA is nearly saturated ON, which pins
VTA_DA saturated OFF, which means the projection carries nothing at rest.

**A presynaptic modulator of a synapse that is transmitting nothing has,
exactly, no effect.** With U50488 at 100 nM and kappa occupancy above 99%, the
endpoint accumbal readout moves by less than 1e-4 on that network. It is a
property of the operating point, not of the pharmacology, and no gain or dose
fixes it. A test asserts both halves by running the identical receptor system
on both networks.

The intermediate option fails the other way: `balanced_baselines` alone
re-balances the baselines and leaves the weights, and with the nodes moved
into the sensitive part of their sigmoids the loop's contraction number of
2.632 makes it oscillate -- `stability.steady_state` returns residuals around
6e-2 from most initial conditions, i.e. no fixed point at all.

So the module runs on `stability.stabilize(...)`'s output: one global weight
scalar (0.342 = 0.9 / 2.632) and re-solved baselines, with relative weights,
topology, taus and gains untouched. Contraction number 0.9, and
`stability.steady_state` returns all-0.5 with a residual around 1e-9 from
every one of P3.4's default initial conditions -- the global-uniqueness
certificate neither of the other two has. What it costs is stated: this is not
literally the network the published mu results were computed on, so P5.7's
re-run reports on BOTH.

### The re-run, and what the cross-affinities actually change

`scripts/report_opioid_cross_affinity.py` writes
`results/opioid_cross_affinity.txt`: the constants as a selectivity table,
then the same ten conditions under mu-only and under mu+kappa+delta, on Track
C1's network and on the stabilized one, then the naloxone reversal comparison.
The headline rows, on the stabilized network, as the signed furthest excursion
of a dosed run from the drug-free run:

    condition            readout               mu only   mu+k+d    change
    fentanyl 10 nM       incentive_salience    0.24739   0.24372    -1.5%
    fentanyl 10 nM       analgesia_index       0.34684   0.34684     0.0%
    fentanyl 10 nM       arousal_index        -0.50000  -0.50000     0.0%
    fentanyl 100 uM      incentive_salience    0.24828   0.17662   -28.9%
    fentanyl 100 uM      accumbal_drive        0.21245   0.10699   -49.6%
    U50488 100 nM        incentive_salience        n/a  -0.13416       n/a

**At a clinical exposure the cross-affinities barely matter, and that is a
result rather than a relief**: at 10 nM, about 7x fentanyl's mu Kd and 0.07x
its kappa Kd, adding two receptors moves incentive salience by 1.5% and the
PAG and LC readouts not at all, because neither new system touches those
nodes. All three established mu results -- reward up, analgesia up, arousal
down -- survive unchanged, on both networks, and a test asserts each.

**In the limit fentanyl works against itself.** At 100 uM, four orders of
magnitude above a clinical exposure and above its 84.8 nM kappa Ki, fentanyl's
own 30% partial agonism at kappa suppresses the projection its mu action is
disinhibiting: the reward effect comes out 28.9% below what the mu-only model
predicts, and the accumbal drive 49.6% below. That is "not mu-selective in the
limit" as a number.

On Track C1's network the same comparison gives +5.6% at 10 nM and -3.7% at
100 uM on incentive salience, both smaller in magnitude, because there the
kappa half of the mechanism is inert for the saturation reason above and only
the delta half acts. Both tables are in the report.

### Naloxone reversal, which is what the brief said mattered

The circuit-level version mixes three things (naloxone's selectivity, the two
agonists' own affinities, and the shapes of two different readouts), so the
report gives the pharmacological version as well: the naloxone concentration
that halves the AGONIST's peak occupancy, with each agonist dosed at 7.5x its
own Kd so the two competitions start from the same place.

    agonist / receptor     Kd (nM)   dose (nM)   peak occ   naloxone_50
    fentanyl at mu           1.346      10.095     0.8663         10.00
    U50488 at kappa          0.200       1.500     0.8265         13.34

Ratio 1.33, against a naloxone Ki ratio of 1.79. A model treating naloxone as
a mu-selective antagonist would put those two concentrations orders of
magnitude apart; measured, they are within a small factor, because 1.4 nM and
2.5 nM are within a small factor.

What this model still cannot show is the clinically consequential half: that a
reversal dose also strips ENDOGENOUS dynorphin off kappa. P6.2 has supplied no
tone, so the kappa agonist has to be injected by hand. That is the standing
gap, and here it is the difference between a model of the receptor and a model
of the drug.

### Derivations, and the two internal checks that make derivation 3 a derivation

Neither new site has published binding kinetics for any of its seven ligands
(searched: each ligand crossed with association/dissociation rate constant,
residence time, competition association, Motulsky-Mahan, on Europe PMC and
PubMed; what exists is radioligand kinetics and biphasic characterisations
that publish no rate constants for unlabelled ligands). So derivation 3
throughout, site-wise, and each site's shared `kon` is a MEASURED constant for
that site's own radioligand with an internal check attached:

- **Kappa**: [3H]diprenorphine's kon of 1.44e8 M^-1 min^-1 from [Wang2021]
  (Front Pharmacol 2021;12:773204, PMC8635029, human KOR membranes, 25 C,
  Motulsky-Mahan). Check: that kon with the same paper's measured koff of
  0.0257 min^-1 gives a kinetic Kd of 0.178 nM, against [Toll1998]'s
  equilibrium Ki of 0.2 nM for diprenorphine at kappa-CHO. Two laboratories,
  two assay formats, 1.1-fold.
- **Delta**: [3H]pCl-DPDPE's SLOW-component kon of 0.147e8 M^-1 min^-1 from
  [Vaughn1989] (Life Sci 1989;45:1001-1008, PMID 2552241, rat brain, 25 C).
  This is the same radioligand [Toll1998] used for its delta column, which is
  why it was preferred, and the two agree independently: Vaughn's saturation
  Kd of 0.328 nM against Toll's Ki of 0.3 nM for unlabelled DPDPE-Cl, from a
  different laboratory, species and preparation. The association is biphasic,
  so a component has to be chosen and the choice is a stated rule rather than
  a preference: the slow component's kinetic Kd of 0.201 nM reproduces the
  same paper's saturation Kd to 1.6-fold, the fast component's 0.0059 nM
  misses it by 56-fold, so the slow one is used and the fast one is recorded
  unused.

The cost is P5.3's and P5.6's: the AFFINITIES are exact by construction
(`koff = kon * Kd` reproduces the Kd for any kon, and a test asserts it for
all twenty-one ligand/site pairs), the TIMESCALES are the radioligand's rather
than the ligand's, and nothing this module concludes is stated in terms of a
rate. The ten-fold gap between the two sites' `kon` is a gap between two
radioligands in two preparations and a test says so, so that it is not read as
a property of the two receptors.

### What P5.7 delivered, checked against the standing discipline

- **Cited constants at all three receptors for all seven ligands**: 21
  affinities plus 21 in a second preparation, 21 efficacies, two measured
  association rates with their measured dissociation rates and equilibrium
  cross-checks, and a measured connection-modulation gain. The mu ligand
  cross-affinities the brief asked for are four of those numbers and the two
  headline results are ratios of them.
- **The existing mu scenario re-run with cross-affinities, and the change
  reported quantitatively** on two networks, in
  `results/opioid_cross_affinity.txt` and in the tests: 1.5% at a clinical
  fentanyl exposure, 28.9% in the limit, and all three established mu results
  surviving unchanged.
- **A test showing kappa agonism producing an opposite-valence effect to mu**
  on the mu scenario's own readout, with both signs measured rather than
  chosen and with a delta-agonist control showing the result is specific to
  kappa rather than generic to adding a receptor.
- **Two illustrative numbers added, both labelled**: the delta mechanism gain
  (magnitude 1.0 by P5.1's per-receptor unit rule, sign from [Devine1993], and
  deliberately NOT matched to mu's -1.72 on the shared node, which would
  assert an unmeasured per-receptor potency comparison), and the peptide
  clearance proxy. `TOOL_COMPOUND_KE` is shared with every other P5 module and
  a test asserts the equality.
- **`receptor.py` and `engine.py` are unchanged.** The kappa mechanism reuses
  P5.6b's `connection_modulation` and the delta mechanism reuses `coupling`;
  every site this module builds is a plain `ReceptorSite`.
- **Tests.** One example script, one report script, and 38 new test items,
  all in the offline gate, none slow, none skipped, and no existing test
  deleted, weakened or modified. The gate now runs 943 tests, all green.
- **What was deliberately not built** is enumerated in `opioid.py` with the
  reason: the somatodendritic kappa receptor on VTA dopamine neurons, named
  and left to [Devine1993]'s null result; the mu and delta receptors on
  accumbal cholinergic interneurons ([Britt2008] measured them, and
  representing them needs a cholinergic node this network lacks and a
  tonic/burst distinction this abstraction cannot make -- their absence
  over-states fentanyl's net accumbal effect); nor-BNI's days-to-weeks
  duration; delta receptors outside the VTA, and with them the P4.2 density
  factorization, for which `Oprd1` and `Oprk1` ISH data are already in the
  repository and which is the obvious next step; endogenous dynorphin and
  enkephalin tone (P6.2, and here it is the whole content of the naloxone
  result); and kappa dysphoria as a named behavioural endpoint, which is
  Phase 7's job.

---

## Phase 5: monoamine transporters DAT, SERT and NET (P5.8)

### The sentence in the brief that decided the whole design

"A transporter is not a receptor: blocking it raises synaptic transmitter
concentration rather than directly producing a signal, so it needs its own
mechanism that feeds the transmitter concentration consumed by Phase 6's
projection systems."

Every target class in this codebase before P5.8 is a receptor, and all seven
of them are the same shape: ligands compete for a finite pool, occupancy is a
state, and `activation = sum(occupancy_i * efficacy_i)` is a number a circuit
node reads. A transporter breaks all three, and the temptation is to model it
as an eighth receptor whose "activation" happens to be interpreted as
blockade. That would have been wrong three times over:

1. **No efficacy, no signal.** Nothing downstream reads "DAT occupancy".
   Blocking DAT does not drive a node; it raises extracellular dopamine, and
   receptors then bind that. The output is a concentration.
2. **The substrate is the modelled thing.** A receptor's ligands are drugs. A
   transporter's principal substrate is the transmitter itself, and that
   concentration is the state variable; the drugs are inhibitors of a process
   acting on it.
3. **The published constants are enzyme constants.** What exists for a
   transporter is `Km`/`Vmax` for transport and `Ki`/`IC50` for inhibition of
   transport. Turning those into `kon`/`koff` would be a re-derivation with
   nothing measured behind it.

So `transport.py` is a new mechanism module alongside `receptor.py`, and
`engine.TransporterSystem` is a new system type alongside `ReceptorSystem`.
The distinction is structural rather than a naming convention, and a test
asserts it directly: a `MonoamineTransporter` has no `activation` method, no
`occupancy_rhs`, and its ligands have no `efficacy`, `kon` or `koff`.

### The mechanism, and the prediction that carries no illustrative number

One ODE state per transporter, the extracellular transmitter concentration in
nM, and a mass balance:

    a      = 1 + sum_i (I_i / Ki_i)                 competitive inhibition
    uptake = Vmax * C / (Km * a + C)
    efflux = release_rate * capacity * sum_j (emax_j * S_j / (EC50_j + S_j))
    dC/dt  = release_rate + efflux - uptake

Inhibitors get no occupancy state. That is the rapid-equilibrium
approximation, and it was chosen rather than defaulted to: nothing published
for any of these five drugs is a transporter association rate constant, so a
`kon`/`koff` pair would be derivation-3 invention supplying the ONLY timescale
in the mechanism; and the uptake process itself relaxes the pool with a time
constant of `Km/Vmax` = 52 ms for mouse striatal dopamine, more than three
orders of magnitude below the circuit's, so assuming inhibitor binding
equilibrates on the circuit's timescale is already implicit in using a
Michaelis-Menten rate law at all.

The payoff of that shape is a result rather than a convenience. With blockers
only and a fixed release rate, the drug-free steady state satisfies
`release = Vmax*Cb/(Km+Cb)`, and the inhibited one solves to **exactly
`C_ss = a * Cb`**, with `Km`, `Vmax` and `Cb` all cancelling. The fold-rise in
extracellular transmitter that a pure uptake blocker produces is therefore

    [transmitter]_ss / [transmitter]_basal  =  1 + [drug] / Ki

and nothing else. **The transporter layer's central quantitative prediction
depends on one measured constant per drug and on no illustrative parameter
whatever**, which is unusual in this codebase and is why this algebraic form
was preferred to any other. A test integrates the ODE and checks the law
against it rather than trusting the derivation, and a second test varies `Km`,
`Vmax` and `Cb` over two orders of magnitude and asserts the fold-rise does
not move.

The `release_rate` is a plain settable attribute, not a derived constant, and
that is the Phase 6 hand-off in its smallest form: P6.1 makes release a
function of a source nucleus's firing rate, and the only thing it has to
replace is that number.

### Substrate versus blocker, which is two terms and not an adjective

[Rothman2012] (Rothman RB, Partilla JS, Baumann MH, Lightfoot-Siordia C,
Blough BE, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 2012;341:251-262, PMC3364510) states the
operational definition and the experiment behind it: "Uptake inhibitors bind
to the transporter, are not transported into the nerve terminal, but block the
transport of endogenous substrates. Releasers are transporter substrates ...
transported into the nerve terminal and, as a result, cytoplasmic
neurotransmitters are countertransported out." The two are told apart by
SUBSTRATE REVERSAL: a releaser's effect is attenuated by a blocking
concentration of an uptake inhibitor, a blocker's is not.

In the model that is two constants on a `TransporterLigand`:

* `ki` -> the drug enters `a`, raising the apparent Km. **Every** drug has
  this, releasers included: a substrate competes for the same site.
* `release_ec50` + `release_emax` -> the drug ALSO adds an efflux term. Only
  a substrate has this, and `is_substrate` is exactly `release_ec50 is not
  None`.

`release_drive()` is therefore identically zero for any combination of pure
blockers at any concentration, which makes "a blocker cannot release
transmitter" a property of the code rather than of the parameter values, and a
test asserts it at 1 nM, 1 uM, 1 mM and 1 M.

**The measurement that makes this matter is large.** Amphetamine releases
dopamine with an EC50 of 6.4 +/- 1 nM ([Rothman2012], rat synaptosomes) and
inhibits dopamine uptake with a Ki of 560 +/- 110 nM ([HanGu2006], mouse DAT):
its releasing action is **87.5-fold more potent than its blocking action** at
the same transporter. At NET the ratio is 16.2 and at SERT 12.2. Run at 100 nM
with the release mechanism on and off:

    100 nM amphetamine        dopamine   serotonin   noradrenaline
    substrate + blocker         2.39x      1.06x        3.54x
    blocker only (wrong)        1.18x      1.00x        1.82x

The second row is what the brief says must not happen, and the gap between the
rows is what "the distinction needs to be represented" is worth.

### Where the constants came from, and why this panel rather than another

The quantity the mechanism consumes is an UPTAKE-INHIBITION constant, not a
radioligand binding affinity, and the project's species is mouse. One paper
supplies both for the three psychostimulants:

- **[HanGu2006]** (Han DD, Gu HH, BMC Pharmacol 2006;6:6, PMC1448202, open
  access). Intestine 407 cells transfected with human or mouse DAT, SERT or
  NET; uptake of 50 nM [3H]substrate, 10 min, 20 C; `KI = IC50/(1+[S]/KM)`.
  Mouse column: cocaine 490/730/460 nM, methylphenidate 260/114370/170 nM,
  amphetamine 560/23820/120 nM at DAT/SERT/NET. One laboratory, one assay, so
  a selectivity ratio built from it compares two transporters rather than two
  laboratories -- P5.7's argument for [Toll1998], made again.

  The paper does not state the KM used in its Cheng-Prusoff correction. With
  [S] = 50 nM and this module's substrate Km values the factor is 1.3, so the
  correction is bounded at well under two-fold. Recorded because it is a real
  unresolvable detail of numbers every result here depends on.

- **[JohnJones2007]** (John CE, Jones SR, Neuropharmacology
  2007;52:1596-1605, PMC2041899). C57BL/6 MICE, brain slices, 32 C, fast-scan
  cyclic voltammetry on ENDOGENOUSLY released transmitter. Dopamine in
  caudate-putamen Km 0.16 uM, Vmax 3.1 +/- 0.20 uM/s; serotonin in substantia
  nigra Km 0.17 uM, Vmax 0.080 +/- 0.006 uM/s. The uptake kinetics the
  mechanism needs, in mouse, plus its own apparent-Ki table for four of the
  five drugs -- a second, wholly different preparation to check [HanGu2006]
  against.

- **[Bosse2011]** (J Neurochem 2011;120:385-395, PMC3385875). Mouse basal
  extracellular dopamine by ZERO NET FLUX microdialysis, 5.0 +/- 0.2 nM, and
  a voltammetric Vmax of 4.1 +/- 0.1 uM/s with Km fixed at 0.16 uM "based on
  an average literature value" -- an independent confirmation of
  [JohnJones2007]'s Km and a 1.32-fold check on its Vmax.

- **[Mathews2004]** (J Neurosci Methods 2004;140:169-181). Mouse basal
  extracellular 5-HT by zero net flux, 2.8 +/- 1 nM in striatum.

- **[Bymaster2002]** (Neuropsychopharmacology 2002;27:699-711) for
  atomoxetine at human NET/SERT/DAT, Ki 5/77/1451 nM; **[Carlier1998]**
  (Bioorg Med Chem Lett 1998;8:487-492) as the second laboratory, Kd
  2.03/8.9/1080 nM; **[Tatsumi1997]** (Eur J Pharmacol 1997;340:249-258) for
  fluoxetine at human SERT, Ki 3 nM.

- **[Rothman2012]** for amphetamine's release EC50 and Emax, and for the
  substrate/blocker definition; **[Zhu2008]** (CNS Neurol Disord Drug Targets
  2008;7:393-409, PMC3133725) for the mechanism statements about cocaine and
  methylphenidate, from which no number is taken.

### Three provenance checks, and the two that fail

Because two of the five drugs come from a different species and a different
kind of assay, the mixing had to be priced rather than waved through. Three
comparisons are computed and asserted:

**Two mouse preparations.** [HanGu2006]'s cloned transporters against
[JohnJones2007]'s brain slices. At DAT they agree within 1.4-fold on all three
psychostimulants -- cocaine 490 against 350 nM, methylphenidate 260 against
210, amphetamine 560 against 420 -- which is a striking result on its own: a
cloned mouse transporter in a gut-derived cell line and a mouse striatal
terminal in a slice give the same number. At SERT they do not: cocaine
disagrees 13.7-fold and methylphenidate 6.0-fold, while amphetamine agrees to
1.04. [JohnJones2007] states the caveat itself ("direct comparisons of
apparent Km values or Ki values between the DA and 5-HT systems may not be
valid").

**Two species, from one paper's own two columns.** Eight of [HanGu2006]'s nine
mouse/human cells agree within 2.4-fold; the ninth, methylphenidate at DAT, is
4.3-fold. So substituting a human constant for a mouse one costs a factor of
two to four here.

**Two laboratories on atomoxetine.** NET 2.5-fold, DAT 1.3-fold, SERT
8.6-fold. The SERT cell is the difference between "atomoxetine is 15.4-fold
NET-selective over SERT" and "4.4-fold". **The useful ordering is that the
between-laboratory spread exceeds the between-species spread**, which is what
licenses using human constants for the two antidepressants, and a test asserts
that ordering rather than the conclusion.

### Fluoxetine: two measurements twenty thousand fold apart

This is the largest disagreement in the module and it is not hidden.
[JohnJones2007]'s apparent Ki for fluoxetine at serotonin uptake in mouse
slices is **59 uM**; the human SERT binding constant is **3 nM**. One says
fluoxetine is a subnanomolar drug, the other that it is nearly inert. The
binding constant is used, for three stated reasons: it is the same KIND of
quantity every receptor module in this codebase is built from; [JohnJones2007]'s
own DAT column agrees with an independent mouse panel to 1.4-fold while its
fluoxetine cell misses the published affinity by four orders of magnitude, so
the outlier is one cell and not the method; and the authors name the mechanism
themselves, listing "drug sequestration" among the reasons their values
"differ greatly from those reported in other studies", with fluoxetine by far
the most lipophilic drug in their panel.

What that choice costs is stated as a number rather than admitted in prose.
With Ki = 3 nM the exact steady-state law says **1 uM fluoxetine raises
extracellular 5-HT 334-fold**, which is not what SSRIs do in a living animal.
Atomoxetine at NET gives 201-fold, the same way. Both are what an OPEN-LOOP
mass balance gives when nothing lets a rising transmitter cut its own release,
and real 5-HT1A and alpha2 autoreceptors do exactly that.
`fluoxetine_fold_rise()` exists so this over-prediction is asserted by a test,
and it is the sharpest statement in this codebase so far of what P6.1's
projection-system abstraction is for.

### The gaps, recorded as gaps

`MISSING_KI` holds two cells and their reasons, and a test asserts that a
missing cell means the drug is ABSENT from that transporter's ligand list
rather than present with an implied infinite Ki:

* **fluoxetine at DAT** -- no equilibrium constant obtained.
  BOUNDED omission: [JohnJones2007] measured an apparent Ki of 270 uM against
  mouse dopamine uptake, so the omitted action is one there is independent
  evidence is negligible.
* **fluoxetine at NET** -- no equilibrium constant obtained.
  UNBOUNDED omission: fluoxetine's noradrenergic action is absent and nothing
  here bounds its size.

[Tatsumi1997] measured both. Its table was not reachable (subscription, and no
open reproduction of the fluoxetine row was found), IUPHAR curates only the
SERT cell of that paper, and ChEMBL's REST API returned HTTP 500 throughout.
The provenance of the one fluoxetine number that IS used is stated plainly:
it is IUPHAR interaction 13001's curation of PMID 9537821, not the paper. P5.7
used IUPHAR curation as a CHECK on a primary source; here it is the source,
and that difference is named rather than glossed.

Also searched and empty: Michaelis-Menten `Km` and `Vmax` for noradrenaline
uptake in any rodent preparation (what exists is clearance half-lives), and a
basal extracellular noradrenaline concentration by any quantitative
microdialysis method. And found but deliberately not used: [Rothman2001]
(Synapse 2001;39:32-41), the most-cited source for amphetamine's release
potencies, which is subscription-only; secondary quotations of its numbers
were found and NOT used, because a number read from a citing dissertation is
not a citation. [Rothman2012] is the same laboratory's open-access measurement
of the same quantities and is used instead.

### NET's first-order form, and a unit that is not a measurement

Those two gaps produced two decisions worth recording.

**NET is built in the first-order limit.** [Park2012] measured a noradrenaline
clearance half-life of 1.36 +/- 0.07 s in rat ventral BNST by voltammetry in
vivo. That fixes `Vmax/Km` = 30.6 min^-1 and says nothing about either alone.
`MonoamineTransporter.first_order()` uses the measured ratio; splitting it into
two numbers would be inventing one. The steady-state law is exact in this form
too (it is the `Km >> C` case of the same cancellation), and a test shows the
two forms agree to 3% at the concentrations these constants imply.

**`NORADRENALINE_BASAL_UNIT_SCALE = 1.0` is a unit, not a number about
noradrenaline.** With no basal measurement available, and with the fold-rise
provably independent of the basal level, setting it to 1.0 makes NET's state
numerically equal to its own fold-of-basal. A test integrates the NET pool at
three wildly different basal values and asserts the fold-changes are identical
to 1e-9, so this constant cannot quietly acquire meaning.

The module's other illustrative constant is `RELEASE_CAPACITY`, the absolute
efflux a saturating substrate drives, as a multiple of the basal release rate.
[Rothman2012]'s Emax is a percentage of its own assay's maximum and carries no
absolute rate; the in vivo measurement that would calibrate it is dose-based
and runs into the same Phase 1 bridge Track E documented for every circuit gain
in this project. A test asserts that the substrate-beats-blocker ordering holds
for every positive value of it, so the conclusion it could contaminate does not
depend on it.

### The engine change, and what it deliberately does not disturb

`Simulation` gains `transporter_systems=[...]`. The state vector becomes

    y = [PK states | receptor states | TRANSMITTER states | rates]

with the transmitter block empty when no transporter is declared, so every
pre-P5.8 layout is bit-for-bit the one it was. Transporter ligands sit AFTER
every receptor ligand in the flat `doses` order, so adding a transporter system
cannot renumber an existing receptor system's doses. `result["transmitter"]` is
a (m, n_times) array in nM and `Simulation.transmitter_index` maps a system name
to its row; those two together are the documented Phase 6 interface. A
transporter-only `Simulation` is legitimate, because a transmitter pool is a
complete model on its own.

The one place a transporter's state does something unusual: it does not start
at zero. `initial_transmitter_state()` starts each pool at its measured basal
concentration, which is the only region of the state vector that is not
initially empty, and a test asserts that a drug-free run is therefore exactly
flat rather than a start-up transient.

### The interface, closed, and the first endogenous tone in this codebase

`ReceptorSystem` gains an optional `transmitter_sources={ligand: transporter}`.
A ligand named there binds the transporter's extracellular concentration
instead of its own PK concentration. That is the whole of the closed loop, and
it is opt-in, so nothing predating P5.8 moves.

Wired to the existing calibrated D2 system it produces the result this task
was worth doing for. Two measurements and no fitting -- [Agren2021]'s dopamine
`kon`/`koff` give the D2 site a Kd of 2.03 nM, and [Bosse2011]'s zero-net-flux
basal dopamine is 5.0 nM -- put the striatal D2 receptor at **71.1% occupancy
before any drug is given**. On the P3.4-stabilized indirect pathway:

    condition              DA (nM)   D2 occ   locomotor readout
    no drug                  5.00    0.711     0.5000
    cocaine 1 uM            10.10    0.833     0.6650  (+0.165)
    methylphenidate 1 uM    14.62    0.878     0.6811  (+0.181)
    amphetamine 100 nM      10.73    0.841     0.6652  (+0.165)
    atomoxetine 1 uM         6.72    0.768     0.6089  (+0.109)
    haloperidol 100 nM       5.00    0.008     0.3000  (-0.200)

Three readings, and the third is new:

1. The psychostimulants raise the readout by raising extracellular dopamine at
   a receptor that was given no dose of dopamine. The chain is
   PK -> transporter blockade -> transmitter concentration -> occupancy ->
   node drive -> circuit -> readout, in one coupled state vector.
2. Haloperidol lowers it, which is the direction the D2 scenario has claimed
   since v0.
3. **Haloperidol given ALONE does anything at all.** Every module from P5.1 to
   P5.7 had to write "an antagonist given alone is inert here, because P6.2
   has supplied no endogenous transmitter to displace". That sentence is false
   for the first time in this codebase. A test asserts both halves: the
   transporter-fed configuration moves by more than 0.1 in rate, and the
   identical receptor system with no transporter behind it moves by less than
   1e-9.

The tone is LOCAL -- one transporter maintaining one pool -- not
projection-derived, so this closes the gap for one transmitter at one site and
not the general case, which is still P6.2's.

### P3.4's saturation lesson, for the third time

Attaching the transporter-fed D2 system to the stabilized network without
further thought pins `Striatum_D2_MSN` at a rate of 2e-4, saturated OFF: 71.1%
tonic occupancy times a coupling gain of -3.0 is a standing -2.13 on that
node's drive, and P3.4's certificate is a certificate for the DRUG-FREE
network, which tonic transmitter is not.

`tonic_compensated_network()` folds that standing drive into the node's
`baseline_input`, which is what the biology already implies: a real striatum's
resting firing rate is what it is WITH tonic dopamine present, so the tonic
inhibition belongs in the baseline the node is balanced around rather than on
top of it. It changes one node's baseline and no weight, tau or gain, and a
test asserts both that the compensated network's drug-free run is flat at 0.5
and that removing the compensation reproduces the saturation. Note what it does
NOT do: it does not decide how much of the striatum's resting drive is
dopaminergic; it asserts that the network's own calibration point already
includes whatever that is, which is the weakest statement that makes the
question askable.

This is the third time the same lesson has arrived (P3.4 found it, P5.7 hit it
with the presynaptic kappa modulator, P5.8 hits it with tonic transmitter), and
it generalizes: **any mechanism that adds a standing term to a node's drive
invalidates a stability certificate computed without it.**

### What P5.8 delivered, checked against the standing discipline

- **A transporter mechanism structurally distinct from receptor occupancy**:
  a new `transport.py` beside `receptor.py`, a new `engine.TransporterSystem`
  beside `ReceptorSystem`, one ODE state that is a concentration rather than an
  occupancy, no efficacy anywhere, and tests that assert the absence rather
  than the naming.
- **Substrate versus blocker represented and tested**: two constants rather
  than an adjective, `release_drive()` identically zero for any set of pure
  blockers at any concentration, and the 87.5-fold release-over-block ratio
  that says what leaving the distinction out would cost.
- **Cited constants for all five drugs the brief names**: 13 uptake-inhibition
  constants across three transporters, three release EC50s with their Emax
  values, a second mouse preparation's 8 cells, a second species' 9 cells and a
  second laboratory's 3, plus 5 uptake-kinetic constants (two Km, two Vmax and one
  clearance rate), a second laboratory's Vmax, and 2 measured basal
  concentrations. Two cells are recorded as gaps with their reasons and their
  bounds.
- **A documented interface to the Phase 6 transmitter concentration**:
  `result["transmitter"]` plus `Simulation.transmitter_index` as the read, and
  `ReceptorSystem.transmitter_sources` as the closed loop, with
  `MonoamineTransporter.release_rate` as the settable hook P6.1 replaces. The
  contract is stated in `engine.Simulation`'s docstring and demonstrated end to
  end.
- **Three illustrative numbers, all labelled**: `RELEASE_CAPACITY`,
  `NORADRENALINE_BASAL_UNIT_SCALE` and the shared `TOOL_COMPOUND_KE`, with
  tests asserting that no reported conclusion depends on the first two and that
  the third equals every other P5 module's.
- **Tests.** 47 new test items, all in the offline gate, none slow, none
  skipped, and no existing test deleted, weakened or modified. The gate runs
  990 tests, all green.
- **Outputs**: `examples/monoamine_transporter_psychostimulants.py` and
  `scripts/report_transporter_constants.py` -> `results/transporter_constants.txt`.
- **What was deliberately not built** is enumerated in
  `monoamine_transporters.py`: VMAT2 and the vesicular half of amphetamine's
  two-pronged efflux (which is why `RELEASE_CAPACITY` is one lumped constant);
  transporter-mediated currents, TAAR1 signalling and trafficking;
  region-wise transporter density, for which `Slc6a2/3/4` ISH data are already
  in the repository and which is the obvious next step once P6.3 supplies
  projection densities; cross-clearance (NET clearing dopamine in cortex,
  which is [Bymaster2002]'s own finding about atomoxetine); and any behavioural
  endpoint, which is Phase 7's.

## Phase 6: neuromodulatory projection systems (P6.1)

### The sentence in the brief, and the shape it forces

"Implement the abstraction that makes this a brain model rather than a large
graph: source nucleus firing rate drives transmitter release, which produces a
region-wise transmitter concentration weighted by projection density, which
drives receptor occupancy at every target region. Replace the current pattern
in which a receptor sits on one designated node."

Every receptor system in this codebase before P6.1 is the same shape:

    drive[node] += gain * activation(occupancy)

one occupancy, one activation number, one node. That is right for a locally
released transmitter and wrong for a neuromodulator, because the quantity that
couples a midbrain nucleus to a forebrain receptor is not an occupancy, it is a
CONCENTRATION FIELD. For three of the five transmitters the ultrastructure
settles which of the two the anatomy supports: [Ozcete2024] (Ozcete OD,
Banerjee A, Kaeser PS, Mol Psychiatry 2024, PMC11540752), reviewing the
quantitative EM literature, reports that for dopamine "only ~1% of the
dopamine varicosities have them [synaptic appositions]", that for serotonin
"synaptic appositions are overall rare", and that for noradrenaline they "are
largely absent". A model driven by a region-wise extracellular concentration
is not a coarse stand-in for a synaptic model there; it is closer to the
anatomy than a synaptic model would be.

For acetylcholine the same question is open and is recorded as open.
[Sarter2009] reviews studies concluding "the great majority of cholinergic
terminals in the cortex of rats and humans form synaptic contacts" alongside
studies contradicting it, and states plainly that "the reasons for the
discrepancy between these studies remain unclear". So the acetylcholine field
here is built on the same abstraction as the others because a uniform
mechanism was worth more than a per-transmitter special case, and NOT because
the anatomy was found to demand it.

So P6.1 adds two objects and replaces none:

* `projection.ProjectionSystem` is the SOURCE side. One ODE state per target
  region, that region's extracellular transmitter concentration, and a mass
  balance whose release term reads a circuit node's firing rate. It produces
  no activation and touches no node's drive, exactly like P5.8's
  `TransporterSystem`, of which it is the firing-rate-driven generalization.
* `projection.RegionalReceptorSystem` is the TARGET side: one receptor type,
  one occupancy state block PER REGION, each driven by its own region's
  concentration and contributing to its own region's node.
