`results/human_edge_provenance.txt` (generated by
`scripts/report_edge_provenance.py` from the verified caches, pinned by
tests in `tests/test_human_provenance.py`):

- F-TRACT probability, HCP-MMP1: 129,600 ordered pairs - **27,066
  measured (20.9%), 0 inferred, 102,534 absent (79.1%)**. Four parcels
  have NO measured coverage in either direction: L_V6A, L_PIT, R_V6A,
  R_7Am - visual/superior-parietal areas far from the temporal/frontal
  epileptogenic cortex the electrodes were placed for. The clinical
  placement bias stated in P13.1 is visible in the data as exactly these
  absences.
- ENIGMA/HCP dMRI, DK+subcortex: 6,724 ordered pairs - 0 measured,
  **2,380 inferred (35.4%)**, 4,344 absent. Every nonzero weight is
  inferred in BOTH directions; the direction is a convention, not a
  measurement.
- The built signed network predictions actually consume: 0 measured,
  **2,317 inferred (34.5%)**, 4,407 absent (65.5%) - the amygdala
  columns excluded by the default policy become ABSENT rather than
  inferred. The headline: **nothing in the network a prediction can be
  built on today is measured direction.** That number is what P13.3
  (macaque prior) exists to raise, and it can only be raised by edges
  still flagged inferred.

These fractions are a first-class result in the P13.2 brief's sense: any
figure, result or prediction consuming the connectome can report the
provenance mix behind it, and any drift between the code's mapping and
the committed numbers fails a test.

## Phase 19, part two: the human haloperidol parameter set (P19.2)

Phase 19 asks the repository to predict a measured human number for the
first time: haloperidol dose to striatal D2 occupancy. P19.2 is the first
link, dose to plasma concentration, and it is where the phase discovered
that the parameter set it wanted does not exist in readable form.

### The search result, which is itself the deliverable

`docs/p19-2-human-haloperidol-pk.md` records the full trail. The short
version: exactly three human haloperidol studies fitted a compartmental
model to intravenous data, and none of them yields micro-parameters.
Holley 1983 (PMID 6831826) fitted two- and three-compartment models but
its abstract prints only CL and Vss, and the full text is behind a
Cloudflare-gated Wiley paywall that a real Chrome session on this host
could not clear. Chang 1992 (PMID 1579624) states that a three-compartment
model won and then never prints the parameters of that model. Li 2022
(PMID 35335925) is readable in full but settled on one compartment,
in ICU patients whose clearance is roughly 2.4x Chang's.

Two of the four leads in the task brief turned out to be reviews, and one
much-cited pair of values (Vd ~18 L/kg, CL ~12 mL/min/kg) is attributed to
a 1976 paper that is not digitised anywhere reachable and whose numbers
are near-identical to Holley's, which is what a copied-forward citation
error looks like. Those numbers are not used here under either name.

### What was reachable, and why it is stored as apparent

Pilla Reddy 2013 (PMID 24113674) publishes a complete bootstrap-validated
two-compartment set, transcribed from Table 2 of the open-access author
copy: CL/F 88 L/h, Q/F 233 L/h, Vc/F 669 L, Vp/F 2500 L, Ka 0.236 /h.
Every arm of every pooled study was oral, so F was never estimated and
each value is an X/F.

This is not a defect for what P19.5 needs. F cancels out of an oral
plasma-concentration prediction, so an apparent set predicts the
concentration-time course exactly; what it cannot do is name an absolute
volume or clearance. Dividing through by a bioavailability borrowed from
Holley or Cheng would produce plausible absolute numbers and a two-study
composite that the acceptance criteria forbid assembling silently. Since
nothing downstream needs it, the record does not assert it, and
`HumanPKRecord` now raises if a record marked `apparent_over_F` also
carries an `F`.

### Four distinctions the schema could not previously express

The P14.2 record type had per-kg disposition fields only, and a
`complete_for_model` flag that demanded all three compartments of every
record. Pilla Reddy's values fit none of that honestly, so the type grew
four distinctions, each of which is a guard that raises rather than a
comment that asks:

- **Inapplicable is not missing.** `n_compartments` says how many
  compartments the source supported, and `required_fields` asks only for
  the slots that count supports. A two-compartment record no longer
  reports V3 and Q13 as gaps. A record that does not state a count is
  judged against three compartments, so nothing looks complete merely
  because nobody recorded what the literature supports.
- **A per-kg value needs a stated weight.** `source_reports_per_kg`
  distinguishes a value the paper printed per kilogram from one somebody
  divided, and a divided value must name the `reference_weight_kg` it was
  divided by.
- **An absolute value still belongs to a reference subject.** 669 L is
  the central volume of Pilla Reddy's 70 kg reference individual, not of
  the patient in front of you, and the record says so.
- **Apparent is not absolute.** `apparent_over_F` marks a set whose
  volumes and clearances are X/F, and blocks the borrowed-F composite.

`units` selects one of two families, per-kg or absolute, and populating
both raises. The two families exist because the sources report in both,
and silently converting between them was the failure mode this phase was
most likely to commit.

### Why the allometric exponent is stored rather than assumed

Pilla Reddy's methods state, verbatim, "a fixed allometric relationship
with individual body weight and CL/F was assumed: CL/F = TVCL * [weight /
70]0.75". Clearance therefore scales with exponent 0.75, and the volumes
carry no weight-scaling rule at all. The obvious shortcut, dividing 88 L/h
by 70 kg into a per-kg value and multiplying it back out, silently applies
exponent 1 and over-predicts a 90 kg subject's clearance by about 14%.
`cl_allometric_exponent` stores the source's own exponent and
`CL_L_per_h_at_weight` applies it, so no consumer downstream has to guess;
a record with an absolute clearance and no exponent raises rather than
extrapolating.

### The validation record was wrong and is corrected

`pk_validation.py` had haloperidol at
`blocked-missing-readable-human-two-compartment-set`, on the stated
grounds that Pilla Reddy 2013 was "not available for verified
transcription". That was false: an open-access copy was reachable. The
status is now `partial-oral-apparent-set-transcribed`, and it names what
is still blocked rather than only what landed: no readable human IV
micro-parameter set, F unidentified, no depot model, and no prediction yet
compared to a measured human observation.

That last one is the point. P19.2 produced a parameter set, and a
parameter set that has never been checked against an observation cannot be
wrong yet. P19.6 is the step that can make it wrong.

## Phase 19, part three: the human D2 PET occupancy set (P19.3)

P19.4 fits a dose-to-occupancy chain and P19.6 checks it against held-out
human measurements. P19.3 is the step that goes and gets those
measurements. The result of the search matters more than the code it
produced, so it is stated first.

### No per-subject oral dose-to-occupancy table was reachable

The canonical series (Farde 1988, Farde 1992, Nordstrom 1992, Kapur 1996,
Kapur 1997, Kapur 2000) is paywalled at every point where the per-subject
rows live. Their abstracts print group ranges, one fitted relation, and no
means. Pirate mirrors were excluded by instruction, so paywalled here
means unavailable with no workaround attempted. Fifteen observations were
registered from seven sources; eight of them carry a central occupancy
value that a prediction can be differenced against.

### Three quantities that look alike and are not the same thing

The schema in `pet_validation.py` gained a `quantity` field with three
members, because the search turned up all three wearing similar labels.

- **Occupancy**, the fraction of receptors bound by drug. Differenceable.
- **Binding index**, Xiberas 2001's term for a tracer-binding reduction
  that the authors themselves decline to call occupancy. Registered as
  what it is; `compare_pet_occupancy` refuses it.
- **Availability ratio**, Vallabhajosula 1997's basal-ganglia-to-cerebellum
  ratio, which runs 1.05 to 1.61 and moves in the *opposite* direction to
  occupancy. Registering it as occupancy would have inverted the dose
  response of the whole chain. The enum member exists so that attempt
  fails at construction rather than at interpretation.

A fourth distinction sits alongside them: total versus free plasma.
Videbaek 2001 reports free haloperidol, everyone else reports total, and
the free fraction is about 9%. `plasma_concentration_basis` is mandatory
whenever a concentration is present, so mixing the two takes a deliberate
act.

### Range-only observations are first-class

Kapur 1996 prints "53%-74%" and no mean anywhere in the reachable text.
Rather than invent a midpoint, `observed_occupancy` became optional and
`observed_range_low` / `observed_range_high` became a supported pairing.
Such a point supports exactly one test, `contains()`, and
`compare_pet_occupancy` raises on it. Three of the fifteen points are of
this kind.

### The transcription digest and what it proves

Every fixture CSV carries a SHA-256 recorded in `pet_observations.py`.
Loading a fixture whose bytes have changed raises rather than returning
data. This catches the specific failure of a later phase quietly editing an
observation so that a prediction lands.

The digest locks our reading against drift. It says nothing about fidelity
to the paper, and `HumanDatasetManifest.checksum_proves` spells that out in
words, because a green checksum reads like verification to anyone who does
not know what was hashed. `derivation` on the manifest now distinguishes
`downloaded`, `transcribed` and `digitised` for the same reason.

### Two reported relations, held apart from the observations

Kapur 1997 prints EC50 0.51 ng/ml (r-squared 0.84, n=12). Fitzgerald 2000
restates a "previously derived" ED50 of 0.40 ng/ml (n=21, striatum). They
disagree by 28%. Both are recorded in
`HALOPERIDOL_D2_REPORTED_RELATIONS`, kept in a separate type from the
observations, because comparing a fitted curve of ours against a fitted
curve of theirs would be a model-to-model comparison dressed as a
validation. Neither is averaged into the other.

Kapur's abstract also prints 80% occupancy at 2.0 ng/ml, and its own stated
EC50 implies 80% at 2.04. That internal consistency is the only check
available on a paper whose full text could not be reached, and it passes.

### The tracer disagreement P19.6 will have to report

Videbaek's four subjects each identify their own hyperbola constant, and
the paper prints a Kd column. Reconstructing it from the registered values,
Kd = C(1-Occ)/Occ, reproduces the printed 0.16, 0.24, 0.19 and 0.39 nM to
two decimals for all four. Converted to total plasma at the 9% free
fraction from P19.2, the mean sits near 1.04 ng/ml, against Kapur's 0.51
and Fitzgerald's 0.40.

A factor of two to two and a half separates the IBZM-derived constant from
the raclopride-derived ones. That is what the tracer non-interchangeability
rule predicts, and it sets the floor on how closely any single-parameter
chain can be expected to track the literature. P19.6 reports the spread
rather than fitting through the middle of it.

### What this leaves for the chain

`occupancy_observations()` returns eight differenceable points: four depot
group means on total plasma, four Videbaek subjects on free plasma. Region
is absent on eleven of fifteen points because the abstracts carrying them
name no region. Four points name no tracer at all, and each of those states
that gap in its own notes rather than by cross-reference.

The held-out test the brief imagined, per-subject oral dose against
striatal occupancy, has no data behind it in this repository. P19.6 tests
what exists: interval containment against the three Kapur ranges, and a
comparison against the two reported relations with their disagreement
stated. The full search trail is in `docs/p19-3-human-d2-pet-occupancy.md`.

## Phase 19, part five: the dose-to-occupancy chain (P19.5)

`neurocascade.human.dose_to_occupancy.predict_occupancy` is the first
end-to-end human chain in the repository. Dose, route, body weight and a
time grid go in; a striatal D2 occupancy-time curve comes out, carrying the
provenance of every layer that produced it. The full write-up is in
`docs/p19-5-dose-to-occupancy-chain.md`; three decisions are worth stating
here because each one is a departure from the obvious construction.

### Two compartments, where the brief asked for three

The brief specified `DosedThreeCompartmentPK`. P19.2 had already established
that no human three-compartment haloperidol set exists: Holley 1983 prints
only CL and Vss, Chang 1992 names a three-compartment model and never prints
its micro-constants, and both are paywalled. Satisfying the brief would have
meant inventing V3 and Q13, so the chain dispatches on the compartment count
the sourced record declares and raises for anything else. The deviation is
the finding.

### The brain-partition step is absent on purpose

The haloperidol Kp,uu record is `absent` and `not-required`, with the note
that occupancy data should identify the effective brain exposure. That note
is load-bearing here. The P19.4 EC50 was fitted against plasma measured in
living people whose striatal occupancy was measured at the same time, so
brain penetration, protein binding and competition with endogenous dopamine
are already inside it; a Kp,uu multiplication would apply them twice. The
chain re-reads the record on every call and raises if a value has since
appeared, rather than trusting that the design still holds.

### Body weight is accepted and then refused

Pilla Reddy 2013 states an allometric exponent for clearance and for nothing
else. `DosedTwoCompartmentPK` takes per-kg parameters, so the naive
conversion lets body weight cancel out of the kinetics entirely, silently
asserting an exponent of 1 where the source printed 0.75. The chain instead
raises at any weight other than the source's 70 kg reference unless the
caller supplies a `WeightScaling` naming the volume and Q exponents and
where they came from; clearance keeps the source's own exponent throughout.

### What the object carries

Five layers, each with its own status, detail, citation and provenance:
`pk` (measured), `weight-scaling` (structural, or caller-supplied),
`exposure` (structural), `occupancy` (fitted-in-repo) and `transduction`
(structural). The prediction's own provenance is the weakest claim any layer
makes. The P19.1 gate is applied to the set: an `illustrative` layer stops
the chain unless `allow_illustrative=True`, with the same `ILLUSTRATIVE`
token every other gate in the package raises. No layer is illustrative
today, so the gate is tested directly rather than through a real prediction.

`require_human_parameter("D2")` succeeds for real, which it could not before
P19.4. Nothing in the chain bypasses it.

The transduction layer applies `d2_effect` with Emax 1 and baseline
occupancy 0, neither of which has been fitted in a human, so `abs(effect)`
equals occupancy exactly. It is the occupancy curve on the transducer's sign
convention and is not a behavioural claim; a test asserts the identity so
that the claim is checkable.

A single 5 mg oral dose in a 70 kg subject peaks at 5.21 nM total plasma at
195 min and 0.734 striatal occupancy, falling to 0.483 at 24 h. Whether
those numbers are right is P19.6's question, and the EC50 behind them was
fitted on depot intramuscular steady-state observations, a mismatch carried
forward from P19.4 and stated in the `occupancy` layer's own text.

## Phase 19, part six: held-out validation of the chain (P19.6)

`neurocascade.human.occupancy_validation` is the first falsifiable human
prediction in the repository, so it is also the first place the honesty
discipline can be checked from outside. Four splits are declared in
`PRE_REGISTERED_SPLITS` before any fit runs, and `build_folds` raises if a
held-out point ever appears in its own fold's basis. The full write-up is in
`docs/p19-6-heldout-occupancy-validation.md`.

### The dose-to-plasma arm was not tested, because it cannot be

`chain_testable_observations()` returns nothing. No observation in the P19.3
set pairs an oral dose with a differenceable occupancy, so every split below
tests the plasma-to-occupancy hyperbola alone. The chain's first arm is
untested rather than failed, and the distinction is stated in the report's
own headline rather than left for a reader to infer.

### What the four splits found

| split | what is held out | MAE | bias | max abs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A leave-one-out | one of four total-basis points, refit on the other three | 0.0459 | +0.0020 | 0.0612 |
| B leave-one-study-out | one whole depot study, the patient-disjoint version of A | 0.0351 | +0.0042 | 0.0488 |
| C free-plasma basis | four Videbaek subjects, total fit converted by the free fraction | 0.0620 | +0.0601 | 0.1409 |
| D external parameter | the depot points against two published EC50s, no in-repo fit | 0.0939 | +0.0939 | 0.1637 |

The ordering is the finding. Error grows exactly as the parameter moves away
from the data being predicted, and splits C and D are one-signed: every one
of split D's eight errors is positive, because both published constants
(Kapur 1997 at 1.3569 nM, Fitzgerald 2000 at 1.0642 nM) fall below this
repository's lower profile bound. Split C's +0.0601 bias is accounted for by
a single number: the total fit converted by the 0.09 free fraction gives
0.1696 nM where a direct free-basis fit gives 0.2298 nM, a factor of 1.355.
That was recorded rather than repaired, since refitting after seeing the
held-out result would destroy the property being tested.

### Standardised error is reported as unavailable, not approximated

No source in the P19.3 set printed an SD, so `standardized_error` is `None`
on all twenty predictions and `standardized_errors_available` is `False`.
Points scored against a parameter that was never fitted in repo carry
`error_in_training_rmse_units=None` rather than borrowing another fold's
residual scale.

### The whole-chain check is a miss

Against Kapur 1996's 2 mg group range of 0.53 to 0.74, the single-dose peak
is 0.5253, which is 0.0047 below the lower bound. `ContainmentResult`
carries `contained=False` and three caveats that a reader cannot skip: the
comparison was not blind, since the 2 mg peak was already published in
`docs/p19-5-dose-to-occupancy-chain.md` before P19.6 ran; the
regimen-matched steady-state mean of 0.5635 that is contained was computed
after the miss was seen, and explains it rather than passing a second test;
and a range across seven patients says only that the prediction sits
somewhere among them.

Containment is in general the weaker instrument here. Split D is 8 of 8
contained at the worst MAE in the task, because the depot ranges are wide
enough that nothing can fail them, and split C's "0 of 0" is an absence of
test rather than a pass.

### The clinical window, in numbers

`CLINICAL_OCCUPANCY_THRESHOLDS` carries the sourced thresholds and the dose
the chain reaches each one at: clinical response at 65 percent needs
2.89 mg/day at steady state, hyperprolactinemia at 72 percent needs
4.02 mg/day, and extrapyramidal side effects at 78 percent need 5.56 mg/day.
`OCCUPANCY_IS_NOT_THE_OUTCOME` states the standing caveat that an occupancy
threshold associated with a clinical outcome is not a prediction of that
outcome.

## Phase 19, part seven: scope and failure analysis (P19.7)

`docs/p19-7-scope-and-failure-analysis.md` is written to the P8.3 standard:
attribute each gap to a layer rather than to the model, and say what data
would close it. Three things in it change how the rest of Phase 19 should be
read.

### The striatal label is inherited, not recorded

The chain is called striatal D2 throughout, and the P19.3 registry does hold
striatal observations, but the four group means the EC50 was actually fitted
on carry `region=None` alongside `tracer=None`, and eleven of the fifteen
registered observations have no region at all. The label comes from the
context of the source papers, not from a field either paper printed that
this repository could record. Since the tracer spread across
[11C]raclopride, [123I]IBZM and [76Br]FLB 457 sets a 2 to 2.5x floor that is
larger than every held-out error above, this is a gap in provenance rather
than a cosmetic one. Extrastriatal D2 is not weakly supported; it is not
supported at all.

### The fitting and driving regimens do not match

The EC50 was fitted on depot intramuscular steady-state observations and the
chain is driven orally, a mismatch carried forward unrepaired from P19.4 and
stated in the `occupancy` layer's own text. The four points are also not
independent: each study measured the same eight patients at weeks 1 and 4,
so the profile interval is narrower than two independent groups would
justify. Split B, which holds out a whole study, bounds what the
study-to-study spread costs at MAE 0.0351.

### Whether the two populations are comparable is not determined

The PK set is Pilla Reddy 2013, 122 subjects, 20 healthy and 102 with
schizophrenia, dosed orally. The occupancy set is two depot intramuscular
studies of eight patients each, and the whole-chain check is seven orally
dosed patients from Kapur 1996. No subject overlaps any other set, and sex,
age, ancestry, smoking status and CYP2D6 genotype are absent from the
repository entirely. The document records this as "not determined in the
repo" rather than assuming exchangeability.

### The illustrative register

Six constants sit behind the P19.1 opt-in: the four `HUMAN_KE0_RECORDS`
(0.10, 0.08, 0.05 and 0.04 per minute for cognitive performance, motor
activity, subjective sedation and anxiety state), the mu-opioid reserve
prior of 1.5 and the GABA-A operational reserve of 1.0. The document also
lists five more that are unfitted in a human without being covered by that
gate, including the default node gain of 4.0 reaching the human build
through `circuit.DEFAULT_NODE` and the operating gain of 0.9 defaulted into
`human/scenario.py`. Listing only the gated set would have understated the
exposure.

No behavioural endpoint can hang off the chain today, and the reason is
structural rather than a matter of effort: there are zero
`HumanDoseResponseObservation` instances outside test fixtures, and
`fit_human_log_linear` requires three, so the fit is unreachable rather than
merely unattempted.

## Phase 21, part two: whether a multi-drug occupancy table can be obtained at all (P21.2)

Phase 21 proposes to make the D2 chain take a drug key instead of being
hard-wired to haloperidol. That proposal rests on exactly one assumption: that a
plasma EC50 for striatal D2 occupancy can be sourced per drug. P21.2 tested the
assumption before anything was built on it, and wrote no ingestion code. The
full per-drug record is in `docs/p21-2-multi-drug-ec50-reachability.md`; what
follows is what the search changed about how the phase should be read.

### The assumption holds, and the phase proceeds

Six drugs have a plasma EC50 printed in a human PET paper that could actually be
opened: risperidone (11.06 ng/mL, active moiety), olanzapine (11.0), clozapine
(950 putamen), ziprasidone (84), aripiprazole (11.1 plasma / 8.63 effect-site)
and amisulpride (143.6 putamen / 59.9 caudate). Paliperidone is reachable only
through the manufacturer's restatement of its own registration study.
Haloperidol the repository already holds. That is comfortably above the
four-drug floor the brief set, so the outcome is not `BLOCKED_ON_DATA`.

### The brief was right about the paper and wrong about the numbers

The brief instructed that the pooled Uchida 2011 table be treated as unreachable
and that the search go per drug to the primaries. The first half was confirmed
independently: PMID 21508857 is `closed` at Unpaywall with no OA location, absent
from PMC and Europe PMC, and its abstract prints per-drug prediction errors with
no ED50 and no concentration unit anywhere.

The instruction that followed does not survive contact with the sources, and
rule 11 says to follow the sources. All five of Uchida's per-drug ED50 values are
quoted verbatim in open-access secondaries, in both of the paper's
parameterizations, including by the same first author restating his own constants
in Uchida 2014. **The paper is unreachable; its numbers are not.** What is lost
by going through a secondary is not the value but the apparatus around it: the
study list behind each pooled fit, the intervals, and the ability to check
overlap with data this repository has already used. Two of those losses turn out
to be load-bearing, below.

That route also carries a demonstrated failure mode rather than a theoretical
one. A 2022 review's table pairs Uchida's risperidone Emax of 88% with the EC50
of 8.2 ng/mL; in the source, 88.0% goes with 4.9 and 8.2 goes with Emax fixed at
100%. The row describes a curve nobody fitted. Any second-hand value P21.1
ingests has to carry the Emax from the same sentence, and be marked second-hand.

### EC50 and Emax are one measurement, and this decides P21.1's schema

This is the finding that most changes the design. Every recovered value is
conditional on whether Emax was fitted or pinned at 100%, and the conditioning is
not a refinement:

| Drug | Emax free | Emax fixed 100% |
|---|---|---|
| Haloperidol | 0.32 ng/mL | 0.70 ng/mL |
| Risperidone | 4.9 (Emax 88.0%) | 8.2 |
| Olanzapine | 7.1 (Emax 90.7%) | 10 |
| Clozapine | 105 (Emax 60%) | 483 |

Clozapine moves by 4.6x on that choice alone. A registry field named `ec50_ng_ml`
with no companion field recording the Emax it was fitted against stores an
ambiguous number, and mixing conventions across drugs biases every comparison
between them. The existing `D2Occupancy` model has no Emax term at all, which was
defensible while the only drug was haloperidol fitted in one convention and
becomes a silent cross-drug bias the moment a second drug arrives. P21.1 must
store the pair, and the chain must refuse to compare across conventions rather
than quietly doing it.

### The concentration a drug's EC50 is expressed in is not the same quantity per drug

Every reachable risperidone value is on the active moiety, parent plus
9-hydroxyrisperidone summed; no parent-only risperidone EC50 was found anywhere.
Every aripiprazole primary is parent-only, while the one active-moiety
aripiprazole figure in the literature is roughly double it. Paliperidone is the
sharpest case, because paliperidone *is* 9-hydroxyrisperidone: its 6.65 ng/mL is
a pure-parent figure only because the subjects took paliperidone ER and had no
risperidone to metabolise, so pooling it with the active-moiety 8.2 would be a
category error rather than an approximation. This is what P21.4 exists for, and
P21.2 establishes that the basis field is mandatory rather than a nicety: a
summed concentration fed to a parent-basis EC50 is a two-fold error that raises
no exception.

### "Striatal" continues to be a label rather than a measurement

The repository's own haloperidol points all carry `region=None` (P19.7). The new
sources mostly do print a region, and what they print is that the region matters:
amisulpride is 143.6 in putamen against 59.9 in caudate in the same nine subjects
with the same tracer, a 2.4-fold spread, while ziprasidone runs the other way,
174 putamen against 205 caudate. There is no consistent direction to correct for.
Adding drugs whose sources record a region to a model anchored on a drug whose
sources do not will widen the provenance gap rather than close it, and the
registry should carry the region string as printed rather than normalising
everything to "striatum".

### Quetiapine fails for a reason that is not about the literature

No primary prints a quetiapine plasma EC50 because the fits failed where they
were attempted: Vernaleken 2010 "did not furnish valid fits for EC50 values in
any brain region", Gefvert 2001 states the correlation "could not be calculated",
and both de Greef 2011 and Uchida 2011 excluded the drug from their pooled
models. The pharmacology explains it. Quetiapine's occupancy peaks modestly and
falls to single-digit trough within a dosing interval, so a one-site curve fitted
across scans taken at mixed times post-dose is fitting the scan schedule rather
than an affinity.

That is the same hysteresis Kim 2012 measured for aripiprazole and resolved with
an effect compartment, which is why that paper reports two EC50 values, 11.1 for
plasma and 8.63 for the effect site with a ke0 half-life of about an hour. The
chain has no effect-site kinetics at all and its four `HUMAN_KE0_RECORDS` are
illustrative. Quetiapine is therefore not a gap to be filled by a better search;
it is the boundary of what a direct-effect plasma-to-occupancy model can
represent, and it should be recorded as out of scope for the model's current form
rather than as a missing constant.

### The phase's "FDA-sourced" title does not survive this task

Drugs@FDA was checked for ziprasidone, aripiprazole and paliperidone. Labels
print in-vitro Ki values, not in-vivo EC50s; the older biopharmaceutics reviews
are scanned and unindexed; the Invega submission lists a clinical pharmacology
review whose every URL returns 404. No FDA-sourced occupancy-concentration
relation was found for any drug. The occupancy layer of Phase 21 is
literature-sourced, not regulator-sourced, and the FDA route has to earn its
place in P21.3's population-PK layer instead.

### A near-agreement that is deliberately not being claimed as a validation

Uchida's Emax-constrained haloperidol ED50 of 0.70 ng/mL sits about 1.2% from the
0.708 ng/mL (1.8849 nM) this repository fitted independently in P19.4. Against
the V3 rows, where two published constants disagree with the repository's fit by
enough to produce a one-signed bias of +0.0939, that agreement is conspicuous.
It is not being recorded as a replication. Uchida pooled 35 haloperidol subjects
across published PET studies and the study list is inside the paywalled paper, so
whether the pool contains the Nyberg 1995 and Regenthal 1997 subjects the
repository fitted on cannot be determined. An agreement of unknown independence
is a provenance question, and it goes in the ledger as one.

### Why no code

Rule 10 and the task's own acceptance criteria both say the same thing here, and
they would have said it even if the answer had come out the other way. The
deliverable of P21.2 is the reachability record, because the registry's shape is
decided by what the sources print and that was not known until they had been
read. What they turned out to print, an EC50 that is meaningless without its
Emax, a concentration basis that differs by drug, and a region that is not
optional, is three schema requirements that a registry written before the search
would not have had.

## Phase 21, part one: the drug-keyed D2 EC50 registry (P21.1)

Sequenced after P21.2, not before it. The brief for this task was explicit that
the registry's schema is decided by what the sources actually print, and that if
fewer than four drugs turned out to be reachable the refactor should not happen
at all. P21.2 found six drugs with a plasma EC50 in a primary human PET paper,
plus a seventh reachable only second-hand, so the precondition was met and this
task ran.

`src/neurocascade/human/d2_ec50.py` previously opened with

    HALOPERIDOL_D2_PLASMA_EC50_nM = 1.8849
    HALOPERIDOL_PLASMA_FREE_FRACTION = 0.090

as two bare module floats, and every qualifier that makes those floats mean
something, the total-plasma basis, the parent-only analyte, the depot regimen,
the pinned Emax, the profile interval and its non-independence caveat, lived in
prose scattered across three modules. That arrangement has exactly one drug's
worth of room in it. The refactor moves the qualifiers into the record.

### The schema is P21.2's three traps, made machine-checkable

P21.2's finding was not "here are six numbers". It was that a bare EC50 is not a
well-defined quantity, in three specific ways, each of which had already produced
a silent error somewhere in the literature it surveyed. Each is now a required
field rather than a paragraph.

**Emax is a required companion, not an optional extra.** An EC50 fitted with Emax
pinned at 100% and one fitted with Emax free are different parameters wearing the
same name and the same units. Uchida's own two parameterizations of the same
clozapine pool differ by 4.6×, 105 versus 483 ng/mL, and his haloperidol value
moves from 0.32 to 0.70 ng/mL. A row therefore carries both `emax` and
`emax_convention`, drawn from a closed vocabulary, and `__post_init__` refuses a
row that claims `fixed-at-1` while carrying an Emax that is not exactly 1.0. The
alternative, storing the number and hoping the convention was remembered, is the
error that already happened once in a review that paired an Emax from one source
with an EC50 from another.

**The analyte is a boolean, not a string to be pattern-matched.** Risperidone's
occupancy relations are quoted sometimes against parent risperidone and sometimes
against the summed active moiety, which is roughly a factor of two and reads
identically on the page. The row carries the analyte as printed *and* a separate
`analyte_is_summed` flag, because a consumer needs to branch on that fact and
should not do so by searching the free-text description for the word "active".
The flag is load-bearing rather than decorative: `dose_to_occupancy` now refuses
outright to run a summed-moiety EC50 through the chain, since the PK layer
integrates the parent drug alone and pairing the two would produce a plausible
curve that is wrong by about 2×. That refusal is the first consumer of the new
schema and the reason the flag exists.

**Region and tracer are stored as printed, including when nothing was printed.**
Amisulpride's own paper gives 143.6 ng/mL in putamen and 59.9 in caudate, a 2.4×
spread inside one drug and one study, so a registry that normalises everything to
"striatum" would be inventing agreement. Haloperidol's row is the sharper case:
all four points the repository fitted on carry `region=None` and `tracer=None`,
and P19.7 already recorded that the "striatal" label on the project's central
constant is inherited from surrounding context rather than printed by either
source. The row now says `None` in both fields, which makes that gap visible at
the point of use instead of only in a caveats section. `comparability_conflicts`
reports region and tracer mismatches between two rows, and `require_comparable_with`
raises on them, so a future cross-drug comparison has to state its terms.

Two further fields come from P21.2's provenance findings. `provenance` is a
closed vocabulary of `fitted-in-repo`, `primary`, `second-hand` and `sponsor`,
and the last two additionally require `read_in` to name the document the value
was actually read out of, because paliperidone's only reachable number is on a
sponsor page citing Arakawa 2008 and Uchida's ED50 table survives only in
secondaries quoting a paywalled primary. A row that came from a quoting document
must say which document. The free fraction is likewise inseparable from its
citation: `ec50_on_basis("free")` refuses when no fraction is recorded rather
than assuming one, which matters because V2 in the ledger is the row where the
total-to-free conversion **fails**, over-predicting with a one-signed bias.

### The constant stays a recorded literal

`ec50_nM=1.8849` is typed into the registry row rather than computed by calling
`fit_plasma_ec50()` at import. Deriving it would look tidier and would be worse
in three ways: it would make importing the module run a bisection fit, it would
make the project's central constant depend on the SciPy build present at import
time, and it would let a change in the fitting code silently move a number that
the ledger's V1 row, the V3 comparison and four documents all quote explicitly.
The fit is still the source of the number and is still tested against it; what
the registry holds is the recorded result of that fit, with the interval and its
caveat travelling alongside.

### How "bit-identical" was actually proved

The acceptance criterion was that haloperidol predictions are unchanged, and a
tolerance-based test would not have tested it, since a refactor that shifted an
occupancy by one ulp is still a refactor that changed the model. Before touching
anything, the pre-refactor code at commit `b6b0edc` was run and its output
recorded to `tests/fixtures/p21_1_haloperidol_pre_refactor.json`: sha256 digests
over the raw float64 bytes of the time, plasma and occupancy arrays at four
doses, plus every scalar in C99 `float.hex()` form, plus the refit, the interval,
the landscape and the reported-relation comparisons. `tests/test_human_d2_registry.py`
asserts equality against that fixture. Digests rather than full arrays because
289 timepoints times four doses times two arrays is 50 KB of hex in the repository
to prove a property a 3.5 KB file proves exactly as well.

One place needed care to keep that identity. The chain's occupancy line became
`occupancy = emax * C / (C + EC50)` so that the Emax convention is honoured
rather than assumed, which introduces a multiplication that was not there before.
It is safe because haloperidol's row pins `emax` at exactly 1.0 and IEEE-754
multiplication by 1.0 is the identity on every finite value, including
subnormals. The fixture confirms this empirically rather than the argument being
taken on trust.

### What this task is not

Rule 9 says scaffolding is not progress, and rule 10 says never build a container
for data you do not have. Both apply directly and neither is being finessed. This
registry is a one-row table with a schema. It adds no drug, produces no new
prediction, and earns no row in the validated table of the ledger; the ledger's
untested row for non-haloperidol drugs has been updated to say exactly that. What
distinguishes it from the empty-container failure mode is that the one row is
real and already drives the working chain, and that P21.2 established by search
that the remaining rows are reachable before any of this was written. There is no
`require_*` gate that always fails. `d2_plasma_ec50` on an unregistered drug
raises a message naming what is registered and pointing at
`docs/p21-2-multi-drug-ec50-reachability.md`, so the refusal tells the reader
where the missing data was looked for rather than implying it could be typed in.

## P21.3: population PK transcribed from FDA review documents

`src/neurocascade/human/fda_popk.py` holds 17 fitted parameter sets and 6
searched-and-empty records drawn from 26 Drugs@FDA review PDFs. The narrative
result, the access method and the failure analysis are in
`docs/p21-3-fda-population-pk.md`. This section is the design reasoning.

### Why a separate module rather than rows in `pk_parameters.py`

`pk_parameters.py` holds one drug's parameters in the form the chain consumes:
absolute, two-compartment, single analyte, one row. Nothing in this task fits
that shape. Reviews fit one, two and three compartments; half the sets are
apparent; several fit parent and metabolite simultaneously; two fit an oral and
a depot sub-model in the same document. Widening the chain's dataclass to absorb
all of that would have made the one working parameter set carry six optional
fields it never uses, and would have let a depot sub-model reach
`dose_to_occupancy` without anyone deciding that it should. The new module is a
transcription surface with its own vocabulary, and the chain's existing
`_require_pk_record` gate is untouched, so the two cannot be confused. Wiring is
a later task, and it is a modelling decision rather than a transcription one.

### Apparent is a field with evidence attached, not a derived property

The obvious implementation is to infer `apparent` from the symbol: `CL/F` is
apparent, `CL` is not. Two rows here break that and would break it silently.
NDA 207946 prints bare `CL` and `V` under a legend fixing relative
bioavailability, so it is apparent; NDA 022264 prints bare `CL` and `V` anchored
to an IV reference, so it is not. Both would be read the same way by a symbol
rule and one of them would be wrong by whatever `F` is.

So `apparent_parameters` is a required boolean and `apparent_evidence` is a
required quoted phrase from the document that decided it. There is no default
and no inference. The only automatic check is one-directional: an explicit `/F`
symbol may never appear in a record flagged absolute, while a bare symbol is
permitted in an apparent one. The asymmetry is deliberate, because the symbol
can be silent about apparentness but cannot lie in the other direction.

### Five barriers instead of one "unreachable" flag

Rule 1 requires a searched-and-empty record to say what was searched and why the
candidates were unusable. A single boolean cannot, and here the distinctions are
load-bearing for anyone deciding whether to try again. `redacted` (a full-page
Trade Secret pull-sheet) is permanent. `image-table` is recoverable with OCR and
in one case was recovered only partly. `not-fitted` means no analysis exists to
find, so retrying is pure waste. `estimates-not-printed` means the analysis was
performed and discussed and validated but no table was printed. `no-review-document`
means the application has nothing posted. Four of the five are exercised by a
real row, which is the test that keeps the taxonomy honest rather than
aspirational.

The distinction earned its keep immediately: P21.2 recorded the Invega oral
review as a 404, and the correct fact is that it fetches and its popPK section is
withheld across 13 pages. Those are opposite conclusions about whether to try
again, and a boolean would have preserved neither.

### Why `key` is five fields

It started as `(drug, application_number, review_date)` and every widening was
forced by a real collision, not anticipated. The review date, because one PDF
contains two reviews of the same application completed a year apart. The analyte,
because NDA 213586 fits risperidone and 9-hydroxyrisperidone as two separate
models in one review. The formulation, because NDA 210655 fits an oral and a
subcutaneous depot sub-model in one review with the same analyte and the same
date, and NDA 209510 contains both the applicant's model and the FDA reviewer's
refit of it, which disagree by 50% on clearance and by an order of magnitude on
V3.

`record()` therefore refuses ambiguity rather than returning the first match. An
application number alone is not a key in this registry, and a caller who passes
only one is asking a question with more than one answer; returning a row would
let a depot sub-model be compared against an oral label with no sign that a
choice was ever made.

### `require_units()` returns the unit and raises when there is none

Table 97 of NDA 209510, the FDA reviewer's refit, prints parameter values with no
unit anywhere on the page. The neighbouring Table 92 prints the applicant's
model in L/h and L, and copying those across is exactly the inference this
project forbids: the two fits disagree substantially, so the assumption is not
even locally safe. Assuming the units would have produced a terminal half-life
of 88.7 h against a label of 4 to 5 h and the row would have entered the
comparison as a spectacular false failure.

The row is therefore transcribed with `units=None` and `require_units()` raises
rather than defaulting. It returns the unit string rather than the value so that
a caller must handle the unit explicitly to reach the number.

### Why the closing comparison is half-life and how independent it is

Rule 9 needs a number nobody here chose. Transcribed parameters cannot supply
one, since checking a transcription against its source tests the typing. Label
terminal half-life is a different FDA surface (openFDA/DailyMed rather than the
review PDF) and is generally non-compartmental rather than model-derived.

It is usable across the apparent/absolute line for an algebraic reason:
half-life is a ratio, and `V/F` over `CL/F` cancels the unidentified `F` exactly.
A half-life computed from apparent parameters is not itself apparent. That is
the only quantity in these tables with that property, which is why the
comparison is built on it and not on clearance.

`terminal_half_life_h()` builds the rate-constant matrix and takes `ln 2` over
the smallest-magnitude hybrid eigenvalue, solving the three-compartment cubic in
closed form rather than using `0.693 V/CL`, which is correct only for one
compartment. The tests check the two-compartment case against an independently
derived closed-form beta root rather than against the function's own output.

Independence is partial and the ledger row says so. Four of the five label
sources are ANDA generics, whose labels copy the innovator's; `LabelHalfLife`
carries an `innovator` flag so this cannot be forgotten, and only amisulpride's
is one. Amisulpride is also partially circular, because the Barhemsys label
quotes clearances from the model under test, although the half-life itself is
non-compartmental.

### The terminal AUC fraction is what makes the failures interpretable

Eight of thirteen comparisons fail, and a bare fold error would leave that as a
shrug. `terminal_phase_auc_fraction()` reconstructs the exponential coefficients
from the eigenvalues and returns the share of total AUC carried by the slowest
phase, which separates a real terminal phase from an arithmetic artefact.

The two worst failures are exactly the two rows where that share collapses:
ARISTADA INITIO at 0.050 with 164-fold error, ARISTADA at 0.180 with 56-fold.
Both are depot fits that parked the prodrug release rate in a peripheral
compartment, so the slowest eigenvalue is a release constant in a distribution
compartment's clothing, carrying a twentieth of the exposure. ZYPREXA RELPREVV
is the control: also a depot, also weeks-long, and it passes at fold 1.00,
because its review modelled release explicitly as a mixed zero-order/first-order
input with its own `D3` and `F2` and left the disposition parameters meaning
what they say. The diagnostic therefore predicts which rows are checkable this
way before the answer is looked at, which is what distinguishes it from a
post-hoc excuse for the misses.

## Phase 21, part four: active metabolites that also occupy D2 (P21.4)

The brief named risperidone and aripiprazole, whose metabolites 9-hydroxyrisperidone
and dehydro-aripiprazole both bind D2, and asked for either a summed-occupancy
model with sourced parameters or an explicit refusal. It ruled out silently
ignoring the metabolite.

The outcome is `human/active_metabolites.py`: two refusals, one clearance under a
computed bound, and a gate wired into the chain ahead of the checks that would
otherwise reject the same drugs for less useful reasons. The full source
transcription is in `docs/p21-4-active-metabolites.md`; the design reasoning is
below.

### The failure is silent for an algebraic reason, and that dictates the design

Two ligands competing for one receptor give
`occupancy = (C_p/K_p + C_m/K_m)/(1 + C_p/K_p + C_m/K_m)`. If the metabolite
tracks the parent at a fixed ratio `r = C_m/C_p`, this collapses to a rectangular
hyperbola in the parent concentration alone, with apparent constant `K_p/(1+d)`
where `d = r K_p/K_m`.

So a parent-only fit to two-ligand data does not fail, does not warn, and
produces no residual structure. It returns a smaller constant and relabels the
metabolite's contribution as the parent's potency. Three consequences set the
whole design.

First, inside the regimen it was fitted in a parent-only EC50 is already correct,
because it has absorbed the metabolite. Adding a metabolite term on top would
count the metabolite twice, an error of the same size in the other direction and
equally invisible. This is why the module refuses drugs rather than correcting
them.

Second, the error appears only across a change of regimen, by however much `r`
moved. Whether `r` moved is an empirical question about two named regimens, and
the evidence for it is half-lives and Tmax values rather than anything about
receptors.

Third, the size is set by `d`, not by `r`. Equal exposure at 85-fold weaker
affinity is 1.2% of the drive; 40% exposure at equipotency is 40%. A registry
keyed on exposure ratio alone would decide nothing, so `ActiveMetabolite`
requires both ratios before it will issue a clearance.

### The bound is what makes this a gate rather than a warning

`max_occupancy_error()` returns `d/(1 + sqrt(1+d))**2`, the maximum over all
doses of `x d/((1 + (1+d)x)(1 + x))` with `x = C_p/K_p`, attained at
`x = 1/sqrt(1+d)`. Without it every active metabolite is an open worry. With it a
metabolite either moves the prediction by more than the chain's existing error or
it does not, and the comparison is arithmetic.

The tests check the closed form against a brute-force maximisation on a
log-concentration grid at six values of `d` spanning four orders of magnitude,
rather than against the function's own output, because a closed form checked
against itself tests nothing.

### Haloperidol was checked first because V1 depends on it

Rule 12 puts the load-bearing assumption ahead of the brief's own examples.
Neither risperidone nor aripiprazole is in this chain; haloperidol is, and
haloperidol has an active metabolite too. If reduced haloperidol contributed
materially, V1 would be measuring something other than what it claims and both
refusals would be beside the point.

Exposure is human and primary: Uematsu 1992 (PMID 1432610) reports an RHL:HAL
AUC ratio of 1.04 with SD 0.48 and an observed range of 0.39 to 1.99 across ten
patients on oral maintenance. Affinity is rat only: Bowen 1990 (PMID 2155804)
reports 85-fold weaker binding in rat striatal membranes, corroborated in
direction by Jaen 1993 (PMID 7902870). No human-tissue D2 affinity for reduced
haloperidol exists, and the searched-and-empty row records both query forms.

Rule 2 forbids substituting a species, so the 85-fold is stored with
`affinity_species="rat"` and every derived quantity is reported as conditional on
the transfer. What it supports is the conclusion that the effect is negligible,
which is the direction in which a cross-species assumption is least dangerous,
and `affinity_is_cross_species` puts that on the record's face and into the
printed summary.

Conditional on the transfer, `d = 0.0122` and the worst-case occupancy error over
all doses is 0.0030, which is 11.5-fold below the chain's own held-out MAE of
0.0351. At the largest single-patient ratio Uematsu observed, 1.99, it is 0.0058,
still below the MAE. The bound survives the whole observed range, which matters
because Uematsu's regimen is oral and the repository's EC50 was fitted on depot
steady state, where the ratio has not been measured. Haloperidol is therefore
`bounded` rather than waved through.

### Why the caveat is not a chain layer

`OccupancyPrediction` carries the haloperidol record in `metabolite_caveats` and
`summary()` prints it, but it is not a `ChainLayer`.

A layer's provenance is a claim about a number the prediction consumed, and the
prediction consumes nothing from this record. The parent-only EC50 has already
absorbed whatever reduced haloperidol contributed in the depot regimen it was
fitted in, per the first consequence above. Registering it as a layer with
provenance `illustrative` would additionally degrade the whole prediction's
provenance and break V1's own validation, in exchange for a metabolite that moves
the answer by 0.003.

### The two refusals are refused for structurally different reasons

Aripiprazole fails on a regimen mismatch that is in principle repairable. The
label's 40% AUC fraction is steady state; the only reachable in-vivo EC50, Kim
2012's parent-only 11.1 ng/mL, is single-dose. The label supplies the evidence
that these differ, in the 75 h against 94 h half-life pair and the 3 h against
12 h Tmax pair: a metabolite that is slower on both accumulates to a larger share
of the moiety at steady state. Kim's constant has therefore absorbed a smaller
contribution than a steady-state prediction needs, and no published
dehydro-aripiprazole EC50 exists to rebuild the two-ligand form and un-absorb it.
A dehydro-aripiprazole EC50 would close this.

Not a second parent-only fit, which is the first thing that was tried and the
first thing that failed. Gründer 2008 does supply one at steady state, 10 ng/mL
in putamen and 9 in caudate, reachable second-hand. A second parent-only constant
is still a parent-only constant: it has absorbed whatever metabolite was present
in its own subjects, so it relocates the regimen mismatch instead of removing it.

Risperidone fails on well-posedness, which no future search closes. Beyond the
absence of any parent-only risperidone EC50 established in P21.2, the label
records that the parent:metabolite split is CYP2D6-phenotype dependent while the
combined pharmacokinetics are not, with half-lives of 3 h and 21 h in extensive
metabolisers against 20 h and 30 h in poor metabolisers. Parent risperidone
concentration is therefore not a well-defined function of dose across a
population, while the moiety is. A parent axis for this drug is not merely
unsourced; it does not exist to be sourced.

The registry keeps that distinction and a test asserts the two reasons differ, so
that a later refactor cannot collapse them into a single rule and thereby lose
the fact that one of them is repairable.

The label's asserted equipotency for dehydro-aripiprazole is stored in `quotes`
and not in `affinity_ratio`, and `drive_ratio()` raises for that pair. The label
prints aripiprazole's own D2 Ki and none for the metabolite, so equipotency there
is an unnumbered assertion; keeping it out of the numeric field is what stops it
being consumed arithmetically. The record's `notes` state that taking it at face
value would give a worst-case error of 0.084, which is 2.4-fold above the chain's
MAE, and label that figure an illustration.

### Two EC50 bases from one study measure an exposure ratio, and no affinities

Gründer 2008 is the only study that publishes an aripiprazole EC50 on both the
parent basis and the summed-moiety basis for the same subjects, 10/20 in putamen
and 9/18 in caudate. Two bases are not two components and do not build the
summed-occupancy form. They do measure the exposure ratio.

At half occupancy `C_p/K_p + C_m/K_m = 1`. The parent-basis constant is `C_p*`
at that point and the moiety-basis constant is `C_p* + C_m*` at the same point,
so if the metabolite tracks the parent at ratio `r` then `M*/P* = 1 + r` exactly.
The affinities cancel: they decide where half occupancy falls, and the identity
divides two descriptions of one point.

That property is what makes the result usable here. This repository refuses to
substitute an in-vitro Ki for an in-vivo potency, so an exposure ratio that needs
no affinity at all is worth a function of its own. Hence
`exposure_ratio_from_ec50_bases()`, tested by constructing occupancy from the
two-ligand form with affinities swept over a 22-fold range in each direction and
recovering `r` to 1e-12, which is where a failure to cancel would appear. It
raises rather than returning a negative ratio when the moiety constant is not
above the parent constant, because a sum cannot reach half occupancy below one of
its own parts and such a pair is not two bases of one fit.

Applied to Gründer's regions, both give `r = 1.0`, against the ABILIFY label's
0.40. Integer rounding cannot reconcile them: the most label-favourable rounding
interval still bounds the ratio at 0.86 to 1.16 in putamen. The reporting review
is internally inconsistent on the same point, attributing "usually 20-30%" of
total occupancy to the metabolite, which is `d` of 0.25 to 0.43, two sentences
before printing an EC50 pair that implies `d = 1.0`.

So aripiprazole's exposure ratio is unsettled to 2.5-fold, and that is a third
reason for refusal rather than a bound. A bound is computed from a ratio; here
the sources disagree about which ratio. On the label's the metabolite is a
2.4x-MAE problem and on Gründer's a 4.9x one, and both exceed the threshold, so
the disposition does not turn on resolving it.

### Risperidone's refusal is priced, which is what makes it a measurement

The registry as first written could say only that risperidone's parent axis was
missing. Both ratios turned out to be obtainable, and the refusal is now a
number.

Bråten 2022 (PMID 35253216) measured the metabolite:parent serum ratio in a
therapeutic drug monitoring cohort stratified by CYP2D6 phenotype and NFIB
genotype: ten subgroups from 0.25 to 33.11, with 9.93 (95% CI 8.55 to 11.54) in
the 243-patient normal-metaboliser row. Schotte 1995 measured both ligands
against cloned human D2L in one assay, Ki 5.9 nM for risperidone and 4.8 nM for
9-OH-risperidone. A ratio of two same-assay Ki values is what sets relative
occupancy drive and is not a Ki standing in for an EC50; the haloperidol record
already rests on the same construction, and a test asserts the number came from
Schotte's table rather than from the label's unnumbered equipotency claim.

`d = 12.2`, and the worst-case occupancy error is **0.57**, sixteen times the
chain's held-out MAE. The same closed form that clears haloperidol at 0.0030
condemns risperidone at 0.57, so two of the three dispositions are now decided by
arithmetic against the chain's own error rather than by argument.

The conclusion is stressed against its weakest input rather than defended. At an
affinity ratio ten times more favourable to the parent than the measured one, the
error is still 0.197, nearly six times the MAE. The exposure ratio near 10 is
what decides this drug, and even at the bottom of Bråten's 130-fold phenotype
range, the poor-metaboliser ratio of 0.25, the error is 0.067, twice the MAE. No
phenotype makes the parent-only path safe; they differ in how badly it fails,
which is the label's phenotype dependence restated in occupancy units.

### Gate ordering is deliberate because the three messages recommend three repairs

`require_parent_only_path()` runs in `_require_receptor_record()` before the
ligand check and before the existing summed-analyte check. All three would reject
a risperidone record, so the ordering looks cosmetic and is not.

The ligand message says the chain is haloperidol's, which invites a caller to
generalise the chain, reopening the exact hole this task closes. The
summed-analyte message says the constant is on the wrong axis, which invites a
search P21.2 already ran to exhaustion and which cannot succeed. Only the
metabolite message names the metabolite and states why the drug is unusable. A
test hands in a risperidone record explicitly flagged `analyte_is_summed=False`,
so the pre-existing gate cannot be the rejecter, and asserts the message names
9-hydroxyrisperidone.

### The rule 9 comparison uses the coincidence the brief pointed at

The active-moiety problem offers one prediction against a number nobody here
chose, and it exists only because risperidone's metabolite is itself an approved
drug with its own PET study.

If the label's equipotency claim holds, then for a moiety of mass `M` with the
parent holding fraction `w`, competitive binding puts half-occupancy at the
weighted harmonic mean `1/(w/K_r + (1-w)/K_p)`, with `K_r` obtained from
paliperidone's own `K_p` by the molecular-weight ratio, because equipotency is a
molar claim while the moiety assay sums masses. Arakawa 2008's paliperidone
striatal ED50 of 6.65 ng/mL therefore predicts a risperidone active-moiety ED50
of 6.52 ng/mL, and the prediction moves only between 6.40 and 6.65 across every
possible composition, which is fortunate because the composition of neither study
population is known.

Remington 2006 measured 11.06 ng/mL on the long-acting injectable. The prediction
misses 1.70-fold, predicting more potency than was observed, and the miss is
reported rather than tuned away. `equipotency_check()` returns four caveats with
the number: Arakawa is reachable second-hand only, the Emax convention on the
Arakawa side is unestablished and P21.2 measured that this single choice moves
clozapine 4.6-fold, the measured value is depot while the same group's oral
figure of 6.08 ng/mL sits within 7% of the prediction, and equipotency on total
plasma is a different claim from equipotency on free plasma given the 90% against
77% binding difference.

The check is not blind, because P21.2 transcribed the Remington value into this
repository before P21.4 ran. The ledger row says so, on the same footing as V4.

### What was deliberately not built

No summed-moiety occupancy model, for any drug. It would need an in-vivo human
EC50 for parent and metabolite on one concentration basis under one Emax
convention. The published axes are moiety-only for risperidone, parent-only for
aripiprazole, and parent-only for haloperidol with no human metabolite affinity
at all. For no registered pair are both constants reachable, so a summation
function would be a container for data that does not exist.

`moiety_ec50_from_components()` exists as the algebra the equipotency check
needs, not as a modelling path: it takes both constants as arguments and is
reachable only by a caller who has them, which no registered drug does.

What decides each case is sourced numbers rather than the registry structure: the
0.40 AUC fraction and the 75/94 h half-life pair, the 3/21 h phenotype-dependent
pair and the combined-pharmacokinetics statement, and the 1.04 exposure ratio
against the 85-fold rat affinity ratio. A test asserts the registry is not empty
and that every record carries the numbers its disposition rests on.

## Phase 21, part five: partial agonism breaks the occupancy-limited transducer (P21.5)

The brief observed that `D2Effect` carried `emax=1.0` and `baseline=0.0`, which
makes `abs(effect)` equal occupancy identically. That is a re-expression of the
occupancy curve, not a prediction, and the brief argued it is provably wrong for
aripiprazole, a D2 partial agonist that sustains occupancy above 80% without the
extrapyramidal consequence a full antagonist carries at that occupancy. It asked
for intrinsic activity represented with a sourced value, or aripiprazole excluded
with a recorded reason, and for the occupancy-equals-effect identity to stop
holding silently for a partial agonist.

The outcome is in `human/d2_effect.py`: a sourced functional classification of
each D2 ligand and a drug-aware entry point `d2_effect_for_drug` that refuses a
partial agonist by name. `OccupancyPrediction.effects()` now runs through that
entry point. The design reasoning is below.

### The identity is honest for an antagonist and false for a partial agonist, for one reason

The transducer's effect is `direction * emax * max(0, occupancy - baseline)`. At
`emax=1, baseline=0` its magnitude is occupancy exactly. That is defensible only
for a silent D2 antagonist: every occupied receptor is a receptor removed from
dopamine signalling, so occupancy is the fractional loss of D2 tone and the
transducer is a sign-convention re-expression rather than a measurement. A
partial agonist occupies the receptor but itself produces D2 signalling, so its
occupancy overstates the functional effect by the drug's intrinsic activity.
Applying `emax=1` to aripiprazole silently asserts that 90% occupancy is 90% loss
of D2 tone, which is the claim its clinic falsifies: it holds roughly 85 to 95%
striatal D2 occupancy while remaining largely EPS-sparing, where a full
antagonist at that occupancy is not (Mamo 2007, PMID 17728427; Yokoi 2002, PMID
12093598; Gründer 2008, PMID 18381901).

### No single Emax can be sourced, so the honest move is exclusion not a fitted number

Rule 1 forbids inventing the number, and the acceptance criterion offered
exclusion with a recorded reason as an alternative to a sourced value. The
literature settles which branch applies: aripiprazole's D2 intrinsic activity has
no single defensible value because it is irreducibly system-dependent, and that
is documented inside single primary papers rather than only across labs.

Burris 2002 (PMID 12065741), in one human-D2L/CHO cAMP-accumulation assay,
reports that "the efficacy of aripiprazole relative to that of dopamine varied
from 25% in cells that lacked spare receptors for dopamine to 90% in cells with
receptor reserve": one assay and one cell line, 25% to 90% by receptor reserve
alone. Mailman and Murthy 2010 (PMID 19909227) find aripiprazole "appears to
elicit D2-mediated functional effects that encompass the whole range of classic
pharmacological intrinsic activity", a pure antagonist at GTPγS binding and GIRK
activity yet a full agonist for tyrosine hydroxylase, with the cAMP intrinsic
activity itself cell-line-dependent. Lawler 1999 (PMID 10327430) and Shapiro 2003
(PMID 12784105) describe the same D2 action qualitatively as mixed
agonist/antagonist and as cell-type-selective, consistent in direction.

The value that would set a transducer Emax is a single in-vivo human D2 intrinsic
activity, and that quantity does not exist. Intrinsic activity is an in-vitro
operational construct, an Emax relative to a reference agonist in one given
experimental system (Mailman and Murthy 2010's own definition), not a number
measured once in humans. A 2026-09-08 search of PubMed and Europe PMC returned
only in-vitro and animal functional characterizations and no human efficacy
fraction; the searched-and-empty ledger row records the query forms. So there is
nothing to fit, and the transducer excludes aripiprazole rather than assigning it
a number.

### What the code does, and why it is a dispatch rather than an always-failing gate

`D2FunctionalClass` is a frozen record of one drug's functional type, its `kind`
either `silent_antagonist` or `partial_agonist`, with a mandatory `reason` and
`source`; construction rejects a classification with no citation. The registry
holds two entries. Haloperidol is a silent antagonist, sourced to Mailman and
Murthy 2010's grouping of it among antipsychotics with no D2 agonist intrinsic
activity, and its transducer runs at `emax=1`, the identity that V1 already rests
on. Aripiprazole is a partial agonist carrying the four-citation reason above,
and `d2_effect_for_drug` raises `PartialAgonistTransductionError` for it.

This is not the empty registry with an always-failing `require_*` gate that rule
10 warns against. The gate passes for the one drug the chain actually integrates
and refuses the one drug that would corrupt the transducer, so it dispatches on a
real, sourced distinction rather than blocking everything. The raw
`d2_effect_from_occupancy` is unchanged: it is the drug-agnostic construction
where the caller supplies `emax` and takes responsibility, and the three original
tests exercise it untouched. An unclassified drug raises `KeyError` naming the
classified drugs rather than defaulting to the identity, so a future caller who
generalises the chain meets the classification requirement instead of silently
inheriting `emax=1`.

### Relation to P21.4 and where the guarantee bites

Aripiprazole is already refused upstream, at `require_parent_only_path` in
`_require_receptor_record` (P21.4), so today the occupancy curve never reaches the
transducer for it and the P21.5 refusal is defence in depth. The two refusals
answer different questions and a caller could repair one without the other: P21.4
refuses aripiprazole because parent concentration does not determine its occupancy
across a regimen change, a data problem a dehydro-aripiprazole EC50 would close;
P21.5 refuses it because occupancy does not determine its effect without an
intrinsic activity that has no single value, which no PK measurement closes. The
guarantee bites the moment either refusal is relaxed: if someone sources the
missing EC50 and generalises the chain, `effects()` still refuses to transduce a
partial agonist rather than silently returning occupancy as effect.

### Rule 9 disposition

No comparison against an externally measured number was produced, and the ledger
says so in the untested table. The task closes on the other admissible outcome: a
machine-enforced exclusion with a recorded, sourced reason, plus a
searched-and-empty record that no in-vivo human D2 intrinsic activity exists. The
regression it prevents is concrete and tested: at identical 0.9 occupancy the
silent antagonist yields `abs(effect)` of 0.9 while the partial agonist raises, so
the two functional classes no longer collapse to one silent number.

## Phase 21, part six: the chain is keyed by drug, not fixed to haloperidol (P21.6)

P19.5 wrote `predict_occupancy` for haloperidol alone, with the drug named in
constants and error messages. P21.1 then made the EC50 a drug-keyed registry and
P21.2 established which drugs are reachable, so the chain was the last place the
drug was still hard-coded. P21.6 turns `predict_occupancy`,
`steady_state_occupancy`, `dose_reaching_occupancy` and
`chain_testable_observations` into functions of a drug key that defaults to
haloperidol and resolves the PK set and the EC50 from the registries by that key.

### Three per-drug gates, not one, and the third was found by a test

The brief named two refusals to preserve, the weight-scaling refusal off the 70
kg reference and the Kp,uu double-correction guard, plus the illustrative-constant
gate. Generalizing surfaced a third that the haloperidol-only code had hidden.
`_require_no_brain_partition_step` requires two things in order: first that a
Kp,uu *record exists* for the drug, then that its value is absent. The record
must exist because the no-double-counting invariant ("the in-vivo EC50 already contains brain
penetration, so a partition step would count it twice") can only be asserted for
a drug whose brain-partition status has been recorded at all. A drug with no
Kp,uu record is refused at the exposure layer rather than run as if the invariant
held. This is why the "runs for another drug" test relabels onto fentanyl, which
carries a `kp_uu=None` record, and not onto clozapine, which carries no Kp,uu
record: clozapine is legitimately refused at that layer. The gate is correct, not
an obstacle to work around.

### Refusals name the layer, and the layer is resolved before the drug is trusted

Each gate names the drug it was asked for and the layer that is missing, so a
drug with a PK set but no EC50 is refused at the occupancy layer while a drug
with an EC50 but no PK set is refused at the PK layer. PK is resolved first, so a
drug the registries do not know at all stops at the PK layer, which is the first
thing missing. The occupancy layer's refusal is sourced from the drug-keyed EC50
registry rather than invented: when no usable receptor parameter names the drug,
`_require_receptor_record` calls `d2_plasma_ec50(drug)`, which raises for every
drug but haloperidol (P21.2), so the message points at the real registry gap
instead of a bare "no receptor record". Building a parallel EC50-only resolution
path would have been scaffolding for data that does not exist, so the existing
registry is reused as the refusal source.

### Haloperidol stays bit-identical, and that is tested

The molar mass, the Emax and the EC50 all travel with the receptor record's
`ec50_record`, so haloperidol resolves the same rich record it did before P21.6
and its predicted arrays are asserted bit-identical to the pre-refactor curve.
The one place the chain can fall back to the module-level
`HALOPERIDOL_MW_G_PER_MOL` constant is when the EC50 row is absent, and that
branch is reachable only by haloperidol itself; any other drug with no molar mass
is refused rather than borrowing haloperidol's mass.

### Why this earns no ledger row and could not today

By rule 1 a wiring change over an existing schema never earns a validated row,
and no external number was compared, so the ledger records P21.6 in the untested
table. It could not earn a row even in principle right now: haloperidol is still
the only drug with all three registry layers, so no second drug can be driven
end-to-end against a held-out occupancy series. The "runs for another drug" test
is therefore exercised by relabelling haloperidol's own sourced records onto a
second key, which proves the key threads through the whole chain without
inventing a single number for a drug that has none. What unblocks a second row is
data, not code: a drug needs a complete PK set, a total-plasma parent-only
in-vivo D2 EC50, a Kp,uu record, and a held-out occupancy series, all for the
same drug.

## Phase 22, part one: pre-registration before any Phase 22 number (P22.1)

`docs/p22-preregistration.md`, committed alone in its own commit so git
history proves it precedes every P22.2/P22.3/P22.4 result. The task exists
because P19.6 had to caveat its own best whole-chain figure as not blind: the
2 mg single-dose peak was published in the P19.5 document before the
comparison ran, and the steady-state figure was computed after the
single-dose miss was seen. Pre-registration is the repair for that class of
error, applied before rather than after.

Design decisions, and why they went the way they did:

**The denominators are fixed by reference to already-committed records, not
chosen fresh.** P22.2's eight drugs are exactly `fda_sources.TESTABLE`
(committed by P20.6); P22.3's nine are exactly the P21.2 reachability census.
Choosing a set now, by hand, would itself be a degree of freedom exercised
with the sources already surveyed; pointing at commitments that predate this
task removes it. `tests/test_p22_preregistration.py` guards the doc against
drifting from those records.

**The document claims procedural, not epistemic, blindness, and inventories
its own contamination.** Haloperidol's predicted window (2.89-5.56 mg/day) is
already published, the label dosage text already sits on disk from P20.6, and
antipsychotic dose ranges are ordinary clinical knowledge. A pre-registration
that claimed the answers were unknown would be false in three ways; what it
can honestly fix is metrics, denominators, extraction rules and pass criteria
before any comparison is computed, plus commit-ordering rules inside P22.2
(predictions committed before label transcription) that make the procedure
checkable afterwards.

**Pass thresholds were anchored to precedents already in the repository
rather than invented.** P22.2's twofold midpoint criterion reuses the bound
fixed in advance for V5; P22.3's MAE 0.10 is the "somebody else's constant"
precision measured by P19.6's split D (0.094), which is the same class of
question a leave-one-drug-out test asks; and nothing finer would be
defensible against the 2-2.5x tracer/region floor P19.7 and P21.2 recorded.

**Every tie resolves against the more interesting reading.** Window overlap
ties count as overlap (the phase is hunting for discriminating misses), a
P22.3 MAE of exactly 0.100 passes, and a clozapine D65 exactly at the label
maximum reads as Outcome B, anomaly absent. The consistent rule is that the
boundary never donates a headline.

**P22.4's interpretation is fixed as an outcome-to-reading map.** The
clozapine anomaly's expected direction is stated in the brief itself, so the
only thing left to protect is the reading: Outcome A (D65 above the label
maximum, or unreachable) is a model success and a falsification of
occupancy-as-sole-mediator; Outcome B is a disagreement with the PET
literature, not a vindication. Neither triggers tuning in either direction,
and the sensitivity across registered EC50 candidates (which span 4.6x on the
Emax convention alone) is reported in full with the striatal putamen row
designated primary in advance, because the 65/78 thresholds are themselves
striatal.

**What stays free.** Engineering choices with no ground-truth contact remain
unconstrained, subject to commitment C3: the modeling decision the P21.3
ledger row deliberately left unmade (what the chain does with apparent
`CL/F`, `V/F` parameter sets and parent-plus-metabolite fits) must be made,
coded and committed before the affected drug's ground truth is transcribed or
compared, and may not be revisited for that drug afterwards.

By ledger rule 1 this task produced no comparison against an externally
measured number and earns no validated row; its row goes in the untested
table. Its product is a constraint on every later Phase 22 row: none of them
may report an analysis this document does not specify without a recorded
deviation.

## Phase 22, part two: the label-dose test, scored (P22.2)

The prediction table (P22.2a) and the scoring function (P22.2f) were merged
before this step, with no label range in the repository as a number. This
step added the two transcriptions and the comparison, in
`neurocascade.human.label_dose_result`. The full result, with verbatim label
sentences and the deviations, is in `docs/p22-2-label-dose-test.md`. Ledger
row V8: 2 pass / 2 scored / 8.

### Only the drivable drugs' labels were transcribed

Six of the eight drugs are refused by a named layer. Their labels could have
been transcribed anyway for completeness. That would have been the one
irreversible mistake available in this task. The pre-registration's ordering
rule, prediction committed before ground truth, is what makes a P22.2 row
blind. A label transcribed today for clozapine or ziprasidone makes every
future prediction for that drug non-blind by construction. A refused drug
scores the same with or without its label, so leaving them untranscribed
costs nothing, and it keeps the option of a blind test open for the four drugs
refused only at pk and occupancy. `test_only_the_drivable_drugs_have_a_transcribed_label`
guards this. It is recorded as deviation D2 because the pre-registration is
silent on the point, not because it contradicts it. P22.4 will transcribe
VERSACLOZ under its own rules, after clozapine's D65 exists or is refused.

### The label result carries its own hash, not the P20.6 one

Haloperidol's on-disk snapshot no longer matches the SHA-256 that
`fda_sources` pinned in P20.6. A live fetch showed the drift is on openFDA's
side: same set_id, SPL version and effective_time, 37 more bytes. Rewriting
the pin would have been quicker and would have destroyed the record of what
P20.6 read. Instead each `LabelDoseRange` records `sha256_read` and a
`matches_p20_6_pin` flag. The flag is checked against `fda_sources` in the
fast gate. The digest and the verbatim quotes are checked against `data/fda/`
wherever that cache exists. The quotes carry the load: whatever the bytes'
history, the sentences that set L_low and L_high are asserted to be present,
character for character, in the file whose digest is recorded.

### Two readings, scored narrow, both reported

Haloperidol's label gives "up to 100 mg" alongside ranges that top out at
15 mg/day. Neither reading is clearly the "maximum recommended daily dose".
The pre-registration fixed the tie-break in advance: score the narrower range.
The wider reading fails the twofold criterion (e = −0.397), and it is reported
with that failure in the headline table rather than a footnote. This matters
because the anchor drug's pass depends on a reading choice, even though the
rule, not this task, made that choice.

### The power statement is not a metric

With linear PK and a fixed-Emax hyperbola, the dose at a fixed occupancy is
exactly proportional to EC50. So a pass converts directly into the range of
