EC50 values it tolerates: 0.73–2.9x for olanzapine, 0.48–1.93x for
haloperidol. This is written down so that "2 of 2 pass" is not read as more
than it is. The bands are about the width of the 2–2.5x tracer and region
floor. The test does confirm the chain reaches clinically used doses for a
drug it had not seen. It does not discriminate between EC50 candidates within
the floor. It is a statement about the test's resolution, not an added
metric, and it scores nothing.

## Phase 22, part three: leave-one-drug-out against published PET occupancy (P22.3)

Result in `docs/p22-3-leave-one-drug-out.md`, code in
`human/leave_one_drug_out.py`, ledger rows V9 and V10 plus two
searched-and-empty rows. **Two drugs scored out of nine. Aripiprazole passes
(MAE 0.024, three independent dose groups). Ziprasidone fails on its one
eligible subject (error −0.42).**

### What decided the outcome was the observation side, not the constants

The brief assumed the bottleneck was the EC50 registry: "the registry holds
only haloperidol until P22.2a ingests the P21.2 drugs". It was not. Five
parallel literature sweeps found constants for every drug except paliperidone,
which is second-hand only. The binding constraint was the pre-registered
eligibility test: a held-out observation must pair occupancy and
concentration *from the same visit*, on the same analyte and plasma basis,
in subjects shown to be disjoint from the EC50 source. Across nine drugs,
exactly two full texts that this host could open met all three conditions.
The typical failures teach more than the passes:

- **Unpaired summaries.** Ito 2009 (risperidone) prints occupancy by dose
  but plasma pooled over everyone. Ismail 2022 prints a mean concentration
  that matches neither visit of its own cohort. A model can be scored against
  neither without inventing the pairing.
- **Binding potential without a chosen reference.** Bench 1996 prints BP and
  serum per subject. Occupancy follows only once a reference BP is chosen,
  and the paper leaves three candidates open. The repository refused the
  same move for Xiberas 2001 in P19.3, and refusing it again keeps the rule
  the same for every drug.
- **A cross-paper link that the source itself makes.** The one ziprasidone
  point exists because Bench 1996 footnotes its subject (8) as Bench 1993's
  40 mg subject, and age, weight, dose and BP all match. Joining the two
  tables is the authors' own identification, not an inference. That is why
  it was accepted while the BP conversion was not.

### Why the new EC50 rows live in the P22.3 module

`D2_PLASMA_EC50` is not just a table. P22.2's result attributes each
refusal to the first layer that refuses, and the occupancy layer refuses by
looking a drug up in that registry. Registering aripiprazole or ziprasidone
there would change P22.2's published refusal list without changing any
evidence. So `HELD_OUT_EC50` holds the two rows, reusing the `D2PlasmaEC50`
schema so that every P21.1 field (Emax convention, analyte, region, tracer)
is still enforced. A test asserts the chain registry is unchanged. Wiring
either drug into the chain needs oral PK, which P21.3 found absent for both.
Clozapine is deliberately **not** ingested: no observation needs it, and
P22.4's inputs are clozapine's records "as they stand when P22.4 runs".

### Independence is counted, not assumed

Ito 2012 prints caudate and putamen for the same subjects. The
pre-registered metric is MAE over observations, so both regions enter. But
`DrugResult.n_independent_groups` counts the three dose groups, and the
anecdotal flag is keyed to that count, not to the six rows. Without this the
two-regions-per-subject structure would inflate n, the same mistake P19.6
recorded for V1's four non-independent points.

### Two corrections to earlier records

- P21.2 and the pre-registration said no plasma EC50 exists for quetiapine.
  Nord 2011 (PMC3198174) prints an Emax-fixed K_i,app of 1369 nmol/l. The
  ledger row is amended, not replaced. P21.2's hysteresis argument against
  trusting such a constant still holds.
- P22.2 left the disjointness of de Greef 2011's olanzapine pool open. Its
  Table II names the pool: Kapur 1999 and Nyberg 1997. Any future olanzapine
  held-out source must avoid those two.

### What the ziprasidone miss does and does not say

The point implies an EC50 near 13 ng/mL, against Suzuki's 84. That fits the
5.5-fold spread P21.2 had already found among published ziprasidone
constants, at its low end. The miss is not repaired by switching to de Greef's
15.4: that would choose a constant after seeing the error (C1), and neither
pooled constant can be shown to exclude Bench 1993. The result stands as the
second documented case, after V3 for haloperidol, where a published constant
from one study fails to predict another study's occupancy by more than the
tracer floor. This time the tracers are the same, so tracer cannot explain it.

## Phase 22, part four: the clozapine anomaly as a falsification test (P22.4)

Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic available and is clinically
effective at striatal D2 occupancy well below the 65% response threshold this
repository sources from Kapur 2000. P22.4 asks whether the untuned chain
reproduces that real anomaly, under the outcome→reading mapping fixed in advance
in `docs/p22-preregistration.md`. It does. The result is Outcome A: anomaly
reproduced, hypothesis falsified. The module is
`neurocascade.human.clozapine_falsification`; the result is validation-ledger row
V11 and `docs/p22-4-clozapine-falsification.md`.

### The decision that shaped the task: concentration domain, not dose domain

The pre-registration's literal procedure computes D65 as a *dose* and the
occupancy at the VERSACLOZ label dose range, "by the identical procedure as
P22.2". That procedure needs a clozapine dose→plasma PK bridge, and the chain
does not have one. P21.3 recorded clozapine population-PK as searched-and-empty
(VERSACLOZ NDA203479 ran no popPK analysis; the older applications predate
electronic review posting); no clozapine PK set is hand-transcribed; and
`fda_pk_bridge` has nothing to convert. P22.2 (ledger V8) already recorded this
pk-layer refusal. So the dose-domain procedure cannot run.

This is where rule 11 (the brief may be wrong about structure) and the
pre-registration's own C1 deviation clause meet. The pre-registration was written
before P22.2 established clozapine's pk refusal, so it assumed a drivable chain —
a genuine error in the document. The correction, logged as a deviation: run the
falsification in the concentration domain. The clozapine anomaly is, and always
has been in the literature (Nordström 1995, Gründer 2006, Kapur 2000), a
statement about plasma concentration and occupancy, not about dose. Clozapine is
dosed clinically to a *plasma* target (therapeutic drug monitoring) rather than a
fixed mg/day precisely because dose→plasma varies more than 45-fold between
patients (Potkin 1994). Comparing the model's 65%-occupancy *concentration*
against the clinically-effective *concentration* range removes the one unsourced
link (dose→plasma) instead of inventing it, so the concentration domain is not a
workaround but the sharper test. The pre-registered A/B logic translates exactly:
Outcome A if C65 exceeds the top of the effective range or does not exist, B
otherwise, tie→B. The dose-domain refusal is still reported, under C2
(`dose_domain_refusal`), rather than letting that half of the test disappear.

### Why clozapine's EC50 stays out of the live registry

The pre-registration says to ingest clozapine's EC50 "under P22.2/P22.3's rules".
That is satisfied by building the records with the same schema-validated
`D2PlasmaEC50` dataclass the registry uses — carrying Emax convention, analyte,
plasma basis, region, tracer and provenance. It is **not** satisfied by inserting
them into `D2_PLASMA_EC50`, and doing so would be wrong on three counts. First,
C1: P22.2 (V8) and P22.3 both committed clozapine as refused / searched-and-empty
before this task ran, and registering the EC50 would retroactively flip clozapine
from an occupancy-layer refusal to an occupancy-layer pass in P22.2, changing a
comparison already seen. Second, the suite uses clozapine as its canonical
"unknown drug" fixture (`test_human_multidrug_occupancy`) to prove the
refusal-layer ordering, and that fixture depends on clozapine having no registered
EC50. Third, the chain cannot drive clozapine anyway (no PK), so a live-registry
row would read as a capability it does not have — exactly the empty-container
failure mode rule 10 warns against. The records therefore live in the P22.4
module, outside the chain.

### The numbers and why they are robust

Primary (Gründer 2006 putamen, EC50 950 ng/mL, Emax approached 100% recorded as
1.0): 65% striatal occupancy requires 1764 ng/mL, 78% requires 3368 ng/mL. The
AGNP consensus therapeutic reference range is 350–600 ng/mL (Hiemke 2018, sourced
independently of Gründer to avoid circularity), so C65 is 2.94× above the top of
the range at which clozapine works. Equivalently, across that range the model
predicts 27–39% striatal occupancy, matching Gründer's measured putamen 36% /
caudate 43%. Even the highest observed steady-state peak on the VERSACLOZ label
(723 ng/mL, across 100–800 mg/day) gives only 43% occupancy — the anomaly holds
against the label's own measured concentrations.

The Emax=1.0 recording for "approached 100%" is the choice least favourable to
the anomaly: a lower ceiling raises C65 or makes 65% unreachable, so Outcome A
holds a fortiori. The sensitivity sweep confirms it across the full literature
span — caudate (582→C65 1081), Uchida Emax-fixed (483→897), and most sharply
Uchida free-Emax (105 ng/mL with ceiling 0.60), under which 65% occupancy is
unreachable at any plasma concentration. Every striatal candidate is Outcome A.
The single candidate that lands near the threshold rather than far above it is the
extrastriatal inferior-temporal-cortex EC50 (333→C65 618, just over the range
top), which is Gründer's own extrastriatal-preference thesis in quantitative form;
because the 0.65/0.78 thresholds were measured striatally, it is reported as
sensitivity and never decides the headline.

### What this adds to the ledger

Row V11 is the fourth independent entry in this project (V2, V3, V5–V7, V10 being
the others) where a comparison against a number nobody here chose comes out as a
failure of a hypothesis rather than of an arbitrary tolerance — and the first
where the hypothesis failing is the central one the whole occupancy chain was
built to test. The chain predicts an occupancy correctly and, in doing so,
demonstrates that occupancy alone cannot be the sole mediator of clozapine's
clinical effect. This is consistent with `OCCUPANCY_IS_NOT_THE_OUTCOME` (Siafis
2023's equal-occupancy / unequal-EPS falsification) and sets up Phase 23's
off-target fingerprint work: the thing occupancy does not capture.

## Phase 22, part five: scope and failure analysis for the multi-drug chain (P22.5)

`docs/p22-5-multidrug-failure-analysis.md` applies the P8.3/P19.7 standard to
what Phases 21 and 22 built. It gives a per-drug grid of every layer's status
across the nine-drug census, then a failure matrix. Each row of the matrix
names a layer, the drugs affected, regenerated evidence, an attribution and a
data requirement. The module behind it is
`neurocascade.human.multidrug_failure_analysis`. It adds no constant, no drug
and no prediction.

### Why the tables are rendered by code and pasted, not written

Pre-registration commitment C4 requires every number to be regenerated rather
than copied. P19.7 met that by hand. Here the two tables are produced by
`layer_grid_markdown()` and `failure_matrix_markdown()`, each figure computed
by calling the module that produced it (`fda_popk`, `fda_pk_bridge`,
`active_metabolites`, `label_dose_result`, `leave_one_drug_out`,
`clozapine_falsification`, `occupancy_validation`). A test fails if the
document stops containing them verbatim. The reasoning is that a failure
analysis goes stale silently when an upstream registry changes, and the
earlier ledger rows show it happening: three "Untested" rows still said no
second drug could be driven, after P22.2a had wired olanzapine in. Those rows
are now marked superseded rather than rewritten, so the ledger still shows
what was true when each one was added.

The module does only three pieces of arithmetic of its own, all
rearrangements of existing outputs. First, the EC50 one ziprasidone point
implies under Emax 1. Second, the EC50 multiplier band inside which a P22.2
pass still passes, which is closed-form because dose scales exactly with
EC50, and a test checks the band edges against `label_dose_scoring.score`.
Third, aripiprazole's worst-case metabolite error at the two exposure ratios
V7 found disagreeing. That third one is conditional on the label's
equipotency assertion. P21.4 deliberately kept that assertion out of
`affinity_ratio`, and the `ActiveMetabolite` validator rightly refuses a
ratio with no species. So the module applies the same closed-form bound to
d = r directly and labels the result conditional, rather than building a
record that carries a number the source never printed. A test ties the
closed form to the record method on the two drugs that have a real drive
ratio.

### The layer set is the chain's gates plus the hypothesis, plus the ground truth kept separate

The model layers are the chain's own gates in order (analyte, pk, exposure,
occupancy constant), then what the chain lacks (regimen correction,
effect-site kinetics, a non-identity transducer), then the occupancy-to-outcome
hypothesis. Ground-truth gaps (held-out PET observations, label dose ranges)
get their own rows and are labelled as the test side. The P8.3 discipline is
to attribute a failure to a layer and not to the model. That fails just as
badly if an empty or low-power test side gets read as a model failure, so the
two kinds of row are kept apart.

### Three things it found that the earlier records did not say

- **V11 is cross-tracer.** The primary clozapine constant is [18F]fallypride
  and the thresholds are [11C]raclopride. With the same-tracer candidates
  only, the outcome is still A, but the margin is 1.50x, not 2.94x. C1 keeps
  the pre-registered primary, so the result is a caveat on the ledger row,
  not a re-run.
- **The Kp,uu gate is missing from P22.2's attribution.**
  `refusal_layers` checks three gates. The chain also refuses any drug without
  a Kp,uu record. That gate is masked today, because the drugs it would refuse
  are exactly the pk-refused ones. It was not fixed here: changing
  `refusal_layers` would rewrite P22.2's committed refusal tuples, which C1
  forbids for drugs whose comparison has been seen. The repair is listed for
  the next drug that gets PK.
- **The PK search covered FDA documents only.** P21.3's searched-and-empty
  rows describe the FDA corpus. No task here has searched the journal
  literature for oral adult population PK, and seven of nine drugs stop at
  that layer. It is recorded in the ledger as an untested route, so it cannot
  be read as an empty one. It is first in the repair order because it is the
  only repair that could add drivable drugs without new measurement.

### Rule 9 disposition

No new comparison, so no new validated row. The ledger changes are a caveat
on V11, superseded notes on three stale rows, and two "Untested" rows: the
layer attribution, and the journal popPK route that was never searched.

## Phase 23, part one: human off-target binding fingerprints (P23.1)

Phase 23 is the one remaining test of the founding thesis, and the roadmap left
it deliberately unfrozen: the data is free and public and the blocker is work,
not an unobtainable measurement. The thesis is that a drug's *binding
fingerprint* — the whole receptor profile, not D2 occupancy alone — is what maps
to a behavioural outcome. The ledger already records (V11, and the
occupancy-to-clinical-outcome row) that occupancy alone is falsified as a sole
determinant, on exactly the dataset this phase is built around: **Siafis 2023**
(PMC10618092, N=37,193), where haloperidol at 11 mg/day carries an EPS odds ratio
of 4.7 against risperidone's 3.3 at ~16 mg/day, both at ~87% striatal D2
occupancy. Equal occupancy, unequal extrapyramidal risk. If anything in the model
can explain the gap, it is the rest of the profile.

P23.1 is the input layer, not the test. It assembles per-drug **human** Ki at the
five off-targets the phase names — 5-HT2A, M1, H1, alpha-1 and D3 — for the two
drugs the Siafis contrast rests on. It makes no prediction and claims no
validated-ledger row (rule 1).

### Why PDSP here, when D2 refused it

`d2_in_vitro` (P19.4) explicitly *excluded* the PDSP Ki database, on the grounds
that it is an aggregator and that for D2 seven primaries could be pulled in full
text with their sodium, tracer and temperature. That reasoning does not transfer
to five off-targets across two drugs: no full-text assay-condition retrieval was
done here, and PDSP is the task's named source precisely because it is the one
public resource that carries **species and a primary reference on every row**.
So P23.1 uses PDSP as the primary access route and says so. The full CSV (98,678
rows) was downloaded from `kiDownload/` on 2026-10-01; the loss relative to
`d2_in_vitro` is the per-row assay conditions, and the price of that loss is
visible as the within-cell spread (up to ~17-fold across human measurements of
one drug at one target). The three load-bearing primaries carry resolved PMIDs
(Richelson & Souder 2000 = 11132243, human post-mortem brain; Schotte 1996 =
8935801; Kroeze 2003 = 12629531).

### The gate is reused, not re-implemented

PDSP mixes species in a single table, and Schotte 1996 — the canonical
risperidone binding paper — is the sharpest case: it measured 5-HT2A, D2 and D3
on cloned **human** receptors but alpha-1 on **rat** cortex and H1 on
**guinea-pig** cerebellum. A naive import would carry the rodent numbers into a
human fingerprint, which is exactly rule 2. `gate_record` routes each record's
provenance species through the *existing* `species_gate.gate` — the same function
every PK, partition and endpoint parameter already passes — so a fingerprint
value cannot enter a human comparison on a looser rule than anything else. Human
rows pass; every non-human row raises `UnsourcedParameterError`.
`NON_HUMAN_EXCLUDED` holds a representative refused set spanning rat, guinea-pig,
pig, bovine and mouse, and a test confirms Schotte's own mixed table is split
human-from-rodent by the gate rather than by hand.

### The selection rule, stated so it is not cherry-picking

Each cell has 8–30 human PDSP rows, most of them secondary re-tabulations of the
same primaries and several stored as pKi back-conversions (the long-decimal
values). Registering all of them would dress duplication as independence;
registering one would hide the spread. The registry instead holds a fixed,
outcome-independent set per cell: the human-tissue value (Richelson & Souder
2000) where one exists, the PDSP minimum **and** maximum (each with its own
reference, so `human_ki_range_nM` reports the true span), the canonical Schotte
1996 human-receptor value, Kroeze 2003 where present, and one classic human
primary for D3 and M1.

### What the fingerprints show, and the two searched-and-empty sub-gaps

All ten cells (two drugs × five targets) resolved to a human value; none is
searched-and-empty at the target level, and `missing_cells()` is empty. The
contrast the Siafis test needs is already legible in the data without a model:
risperidone's human 5-HT2A range (0.14–7 nM) sits entirely below haloperidol's
(25–435 nM) — the Meltzer serotonin-dopamine mechanism — and risperidone is also
the more potent at H1 and comparable at alpha-1, while **M1 is a floor for both**
(every human value ≥ ~1.5 µM, ceiling-dominated): neither drug is anticholinergic,
so M1 cannot be part of whatever distinguishes their EPS. Two sub-class absences
are recorded as searched-and-empty: there is no human-**tissue** D3 or M1 Ki for
either drug in PDSP, only cloned/recombinant — recorded so the D3 and M1
fingerprints are not later misread as tissue measurements.

### Rule 9 disposition

A documented data layer with two searched-and-empty records, no new prediction,
no validated row. The ledger changes are two rows in the searched-and-empty
table and a note that the off-target-fingerprint data for the Phase 23 test now
exists. The comparison that would earn a validated row — fingerprint difference
against the Siafis EPS contrast — is a later Phase 23 task.

## Phase 23, part two: off-target occupancy from the shared plasma curve (P23.2)

P23.1 assembled the per-drug human Ki fingerprints. P23.2 turns those affinities
into occupancy-time curves driven by the **same** plasma concentration-time curve
that `dose_to_occupancy` already produces for D2 —
`human/offtarget_occupancy.py`. The brief's one standing instruction is that an
in-vitro Ki is not an in-vivo EC50 (P19.4 proved this for D2), so every off-target
occupancy is a *weaker quantity* and must be labelled as such everywhere it
appears.

### The hyperbola, unchanged; the constant in it, weaker

An off-target occupancy is the same rectangular hyperbola the D2 curve uses,
`theta(t) = C(t) / (C(t) + K)`, on the same total-plasma axis. The only thing
that changes is what sits in the `K` slot: the D2 curve fills it with an in-vivo
plasma EC50 (1.885 nM, fitted on human PET occupancy, which absorbs protein
binding, brain penetration and endogenous dopamine competition); the off-target
curves fill it with an in-vitro Ki, which absorbs none of that. The functional
form being identical is exactly why the labelling matters: nothing in the shape of
the curve warns a reader that one of them is a far weaker claim than the other.

Each off-target is reported as a **band**, not a point, because the P23.1
fingerprint is a Ki *range* (human measurements of one drug at one target span up
to ~17-fold). `occ_low` uses the largest Ki and `occ_high` the smallest. Every
`OffTargetOccupancyCurve` carries `quantity_kind = "ki-derived-occupancy"` and
the full `KI_DERIVED_LABEL`, distinct from the `"in-vivo-fitted-occupancy"` tag
and `IN_VIVO_LABEL` the D2 curve would carry, and the labels differ in
`summary()` output too, so the distinction survives into any text rendering.

### The measured floor: D2 is the one place the error can be weighed

Saying "weaker" is cheap; P23.2 measures how much weaker. D2 is the only target
for these drugs where both an in-vivo EC50 and an in-vitro Ki exist, so it is the
only place the error of using a Ki where an EC50 belongs can be *measured* rather
than asserted. `d2_invivo_vs_ki_discrepancy` computes the haloperidol D2 occupancy
the honest way (EC50 1.885 nM) and the way the off-targets are forced to be
computed (the registered in-vitro Ki, Bartuzi 2022, 8.85 nM) on the same plasma
curve, and returns the gap. Over a clinical 5 mg curve the two disagree by up to
**0.368 occupancy units** — larger than any held-out error anywhere in the
ledger. That gap is not a tolerance chosen here; it is two independent
measurements (the Nyberg/Regenthal PET behind the EC50, Bartuzi 2022 behind the
Ki) disagreeing, and it is the floor on how wrong every off-target occupancy in
this module could be. The sign is instructive: the in-vivo EC50 is *below* the
in-vitro Ki, so using the Ki *under*-states occupancy here — the opposite of the
naive "total plasma overstates free drug" intuition, because brain accumulation
and the high-affinity state dominate. And because the P19.4 EC50/Ki ratio
straddles unity (0.21–14.5 across the seven sources), the sign of the gap even
flips with the choice of Ki: at the smallest in-vitro value (0.13 nM) the Ki
*over*-states occupancy. A test pins both signs.

### Scope: haloperidol only, and not by choice

"The same plasma curve that drives D2" exists only for a drug the chain can drive
end to end. That is haloperidol. Olanzapine has a plasma curve (the bridged
LYBALVI set) but no P23.1 off-target fingerprint. Risperidone — the other half of
the Siafis contrast — has a fingerprint but no plasma curve: the chain refuses it
because parent-only disposition is ill-posed across CYP2D6 phenotype (P21.4), and
there is no in-vivo risperidone D2 EC50 here. `offtarget_occupancy_from_curve`
raises for any drug with no fingerprint, which naturally catches both gaps. The
asymmetry is stated, not papered over: the full Siafis two-drug comparison is
P23.3's problem and will have to source risperidone occupancy another way.

### Directional cross-check, recorded as weak

One real-number ordering is reachable without new literature. The measured
typical-antipsychotic signature is high striatal D2 and comparatively low cortical
5-HT2 occupancy for haloperidol (Kapur & Remington 1996, high D2 at low dose;
Farde/Nyberg 1995 established the reciprocal crossover for risperidone, 5-HT2
78–88% ≥ D2 75–80% at 6 mg/day). The Ki fingerprint reproduces the **sign** of
the 5-HT2A-minus-D2 occupancy difference for haloperidol: at a clinical 5 mg curve
its Ki-derived cortical 5-HT2A occupancy peaks at 0.01–0.17 against an in-vivo D2
peak of 0.73. This is a one-drug, direction-only check — no numeric error, n=1 —
and is labelled as such. It is consistent with the measured ordering; it is not a
quantitative validation and earns no validated row.

### Rule 9 disposition

P23.2 produces no new prediction against an independently measured off-target
occupancy number — none is reachable for haloperidol paired to a plasma
concentration (the familiar paywall/absence pattern). What it does produce is a
measured quantification of the weakness the brief demanded be labelled: the
0.368-occupancy-unit floor is a comparison of two independent measurements that
were never fitted to each other. That belongs in the ledger's *untested* table as
a sharpening of the occupancy→clinical-outcome row, plus the directional
cross-check, not as a validated row — the validated comparison (fingerprint vs the
Siafis EPS contrast) is still P23.3.

## Phase 23, part three: does the fingerprint explain the EPS residual (P23.3)

The task Phase 23 was built to reach. P23.1 assembled the per-drug human Ki
fingerprints; P23.2 turned them into off-target occupancy and measured how weak a
Ki-derived occupancy is. P23.3 runs the actual pre-registered test:
`src/neurocascade/human/fingerprint_eps_regression.py`, with the hypothesis,
denominator, model and criterion fixed in `docs/p22-preregistration.md` (P23.3
section) and committed one commit earlier. The result is **indeterminate**, and
reporting it as indeterminate rather than as a finding is the deliverable.

### The eight drugs are not a choice; they are the intersection of two sources

The denominator is forced, not picked. Siafis 2023 built its own
occupancy-response curves with the Lako et al. 2013 dose→D2-occupancy formulas,
which exist for exactly eight drugs (amisulpride, aripiprazole, clozapine,
haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone). Clozapine drops
on two independent pre-existing facts: Leucht 2020 published no ED95 for it (too
few fixed-dose studies) and Siafis 2023 had "no usable data" for its EPS OR. That
leaves **n = 7**. The "roughly eight drugs" of the brief is this intersection,
and the low power the brief anticipated is a property of it.

### D2 occupancy is sourced in vivo; 5-HT2A occupancy cannot be, and that is the crux

D2 occupancy at ED95 comes straight from Lako 2013 (PET/SPECT-fitted,
`OccMax·dose/(dose+OccD50)`) at the Leucht 2020 ED95 — the same strong quantity
Siafis itself used. The 5-HT2A side has **no equivalent**: there is no
meta-analytic dose→5-HT2A-occupancy model for these drugs, only scattered
single-dose PET studies at non-matched doses (recorded searched-and-empty in the
pre-registration). So 5-HT2A occupancy is built on P23.2's device — one plasma
concentration drives every receptor — by transferring the in-vitro 5-HT2A:D2
affinity ratio (PDSP human-median Ki, the P23.1 source and date) onto the D2
dose-response: `OccD50_5HT2A = OccD50_D2·(Ki_5HT2A/Ki_D2)`, `OccMax_5HT2A = 100%`.
That makes every 5-HT2A occupancy here the **weaker Ki-derived quantity** P23.2
measured at a 0.368-occupancy-unit floor, plus the extra assumption that the
in-vitro affinity ratio transfers to the in-vivo dose-ED50 ratio. The module
carries `KI_DERIVED_LABEL` on every row so the quantity cannot be read without
its warning. This asymmetry — strong D2, weak 5-HT2A — is the honest shape of the
test and is stated, not hidden.

### Why the outcome is the maximum OR, and the anchor mismatch it carries

The outcome is Siafis's per-drug **maximum** EPS OR (the headline reported
numbers: haloperidol 7.56 down to quetiapine 1.11), on `ln` because an OR is
ratio-scale. The maxima occur at each drug's top studied dose, while occupancy is
evaluated at ED95: a real anchor mismatch, uniform across drugs, pre-declared and
not a per-drug knob. It was chosen over "OR at ED95" because the latter is only
reachable by reading per-drug spline figures, which would introduce a
figure-digitisation degree of freedom worse than the mismatch. With n = 7 the
choice does not change the verdict.

### The result, and why it is indeterminate rather than either answer

Model 0 (`lnOR ~ D2 occupancy`) gives R² = 0.314. Adding the fingerprint
(`+ log10(5-HT2A:D2 occupancy ratio)`) gives R² = 0.636 with the ratio
coefficient **negative** (−0.396) — the Meltzer direction, more 5-HT2A-selective
→ lower EPS. But the nested F(1,4) = 3.54 has **p = 0.133**, not significant at
α = 0.05. The increment is a very large effect (Cohen f² = 0.88), yet the test's
power to detect even a conventionally large effect (f² = 0.35) is **0.20**, and
~0.42 at the observed effect; n ≈ 13 would be needed for 80% power, more drugs
than the eight that have a Lako formula. By the pre-registered rule — not
significant, and power to find a large effect below 0.80 — this is
**indeterminate**: the trend is consistent with H1, the data confirm nothing and
reject nothing.

Leave-one-drug-out (pre-declared sensitivity) confirms the reading: the sign is
stable across all seven deletions but significance is fragile and never crosses
0.05 (dropping the partial agonist aripiprazole gets closest, p = 0.059; dropping
quetiapine, which sits at 28% D2, far below the EPS threshold, collapses the
D2-only R² to 0.01). A result that moves this much on one drug is, itself, an
indeterminate result. The two structural confounds — aripiprazole's partial
agonism (P21.5 refuses its transducer; Siafis notes partial agonists carry small
ORs at high occupancy) and quetiapine's sub-threshold occupancy — are named, not
trimmed.

### Rule 9 disposition

A prediction (per-drug occupancy and fingerprint ratio) compared against a
measured clinical quantity nobody in this repository chose (the Siafis 2023 EPS
odds ratios), producing a definite, pre-registered outcome: indeterminate,
underpowered, with the power stated. That closes the task and earns a ledger row
(rule 3: a result at the size it came out). It does **not** earn a "validated"
claim, because the hypothesis was neither confirmed nor rejected; the row records
the indeterminacy and its cause (n = 7, power 0.20), and the occupancy→clinical-
outcome row is updated to point at it.

## Phase 23, part four: reporting the result (P23.4)

P23.4 is the reporting half of the thesis test: "write up P23.3 whichever way it
came out." It came out indeterminate, and the write-up says so without reading the
trend as a finding. The deliverable is `docs/p23-4-fingerprint-result.md`, a
plain-language, publication-ready statement that (a) opens with the one-sentence
result, (b) gives the forced n = 7 denominator and the strong-D2 / Ki-derived-
5-HT2A asymmetry, (c) states the numbers — R² 0.314→0.636, β_ratio −0.396,
F(1,4) = 3.54, p = 0.133, power 0.20 — and (d) answers the task's specific demand
of an underpowered result: *what number could settle it.* The answer is n ≈ 13 at
the observed effect size (≈26 at a conventionally large one), beyond the eight
drugs any dose→D2 formula covers; the two data items that would change that (an
in-vivo dose→5-HT2A-occupancy model, or dose→D2 formulas for more drugs with a
Siafis OR) are both searched-and-empty. The last section denies, in terms, any
claim that the model predicts behaviour: this is a regression against published
odds ratios, not a simulated endpoint.

The write-up is also lifted into the manuscript as a human-track Results
subsection (§3.6) and a Discussion caveat (§4.2), because the manuscript skeleton
was still mouse-scoped and otherwise omitted the one human-outcome test the
receptor layer was carried forward to make. A drift-guard test,
`tests/test_fingerprint_result.py`, ties every headline number in the write-up to
the live `fit_models()` output and to ledger row V12, so prose, code and ledger
cannot diverge silently — this is the machine form of the acceptance criterion
"the validation ledger row matches the write-up."

**One number corrected.** P23.3 recorded the fingerprint coefficient as −0.397 in
V12 and in the Phase 23 part-three section above. The live value is −0.39645,
which rounds to **−0.396** at three decimals; the drift-guard test caught the
mis-round, and V12, the part-three section and the write-up now all read −0.396.
This is a rounding fix to an existing committed number, not a new calibration, and
it changes no conclusion (the verdict, F, p and power are untouched).

## Phase 24, part one: the public prediction interface (P24.1)

`neurocascade.human.prediction_interface.predict(drug, dose_mg, regimen)`, also
exported as `neurocascade.human.predict`. It returns the striatal D2
occupancy-time course for a once-daily (`steady-state-daily`, one 24 h interval
at steady state) or `single-dose` (0–72 h) oral regimen. It also returns where
the regimen's statistic sits against every row of `CLINICAL_OCCUPANCY_THRESHOLDS`.
The statistic is the steady-state mean, which is the P22.1 pre-registered statistic, or
the single-dose peak. It adds no model. The curves are `steady_state_occupancy`
and `predict_occupancy`, and the tests assert them bit-identical to those
functions. The tests also pin the ledger figures they reproduce: V4's 0.5635
steady-state mean and 0.5253 single-dose peak at 2 mg, and V8's haloperidol
window edges 2.89 and 5.56 mg/day sitting on 0.65 and 0.78.

### Refusal collects every missing layer, before anything runs

The chain's own gates stop at the first missing layer, which is right inside
the chain and wrong at the boundary. A caller asking "can this drug be
predicted?" needs the whole list, because a drug missing PK *and* EC50 *and*
a Kp,uu record is three data items from a prediction, not one.
`refusal_layers(drug)` checks the four layers independently: active-metabolite,
pk, occupancy and exposure (Kp,uu). `predict` raises `PredictionRefused`, a
`ValueError`, carrying `(layer, reason)` for each one and listing the drugs that
do clear every layer. The check runs before integration, and a test replaces both
chain functions with ones that fail if called, to prove it. Every drug in the
P22.2 denominator plus amisulpride, fentanyl and diazepam is pinned to its exact
refused-layer tuple. Changing one of those is a change in what the model can
predict, so it should fail a test until someone makes it on purpose. Today exactly two drugs clear
every layer: haloperidol and olanzapine, the same two V8 scored.

### Where a cross-drug fallback could hide, and what closes each one

- **The default drug.** `predict_occupancy`, `steady_state_occupancy` and
  `dose_reaching_occupancy` still default to haloperidol (P19.5 backward
  compatibility; many tests rely on it). `predict` has no default. Omitting the
  drug is a `TypeError`, and `predict` always passes the drug explicitly. A test
  pins the signature.
- **Name normalisation.** `active_metabolites_for` lower-cases its key while the
  PK, EC50 and Kp,uu lookups do not. `"Haloperidol"` therefore clears the
  metabolite check and is refused at the other three layers. That is the
  intended outcome: case-folding is a lookup guessing which drug was meant.
  `predict` performs no normalisation, and `"Haloperidol"`, `" haloperidol"` and
  `""` are pinned as refusals.
- **Layer removal.** Removing olanzapine's EC50 row, its PK set or its Kp,uu
  record, one at a time, produces a refusal at exactly that layer, naming
  olanzapine, with the chain never called. Removing haloperidol's registry row
  refuses haloperidol at occupancy. It does not fall through to the P19.4
  receptor record, which carries the same constant. The boundary refuses when
  any registry the chain is documented to read is missing the drug.
- **Provenance text.** The chain's `transduction` layer describes `d2_effect`
  and is written for haloperidol ("honest only because haloperidol is a silent
  D2 antagonist"). `predict` applies no transducer, so it drops that layer.
  Returning it for olanzapine would hand olanzapine a haloperidol statement as
  provenance. A test asserts that no olanzapine layer cites Pilla Reddy, Nyberg,
  Regenthal or haloperidol at all.
- **The molar-mass fallback** in `predict_occupancy` to
  `HALOPERIDOL_MW_G_PER_MOL` is reachable only with `drug == "haloperidol"`
  (P21.6), so it is not cross-drug.

### The thresholds are a haloperidol relation, and the interface says so

The 65/72/78% thresholds come from Kapur 2000 (PMID 10739409). Its abstract,
read for this task, says patients "were randomly assigned to 1.0 or 2.5 mg/day
of haloperidol. After 2 weeks of treatment, D(2) receptor occupancy was
determined", and concludes "While limited to haloperidol". Showing olanzapine's
occupancy against those numbers therefore transfers a haloperidol
occupancy-outcome relation to another drug, which is the substitution rule 2
forbids when it happens silently. P22.2 already applied these thresholds across
drugs under pre-registration. The interface keeps the comparison and labels it
rather than suppressing it. `ClinicalOccupancyThreshold` gained
`measured_in_drugs` and `measured_regimen`, set to `("haloperidol",)` and
`steady-state-daily` on the three Kapur rows and left `None` on Uchida 2011,
whose pooled drug list is in a paywalled full text. Each `ThresholdPosition`
carries the following:
`same_drug`, `same_regimen`, the margin, the fraction of the time course at or
above the threshold, `unreachable_at_any_dose` (true when the drug's own Emax
fit sits below the threshold, the P22.2 distinction), and a note in words.
Olanzapine against Kapur reads "measured in haloperidol-treated patients, not
olanzapine: a cross-drug transfer". A single-dose peak against Kapur reads as
a regimen mismatch. Every `Prediction` carries `OCCUPANCY_IS_NOT_THE_OUTCOME`
and `CLINICAL_WINDOW_PROVENANCE` as `caveats`. Sitting above 0.78 is a statement
about occupancy, not a prediction of extrapyramidal symptoms; Siafis 2023 is
the falsification already on file.

### Scope fixed by the data, not by the interface

PO only, because no drug has a sourced IV set. The body weight is the 70 kg
reference only, because no sourced set prints volume or Q exponents (P19.2) and
the interface does not offer the caller-supplied `WeightScaling` escape hatch.
A public entry point should not invite numbers the repository has no source for.
Striatal only, with no effect compartment (ke0), carried from P19.7.

### Why this earns no validated row

The interface is wiring: by rule 9 it is scaffolding, and it compared nothing
against an external number. Its outputs are the computations that already
earned V4 and V8, and the tests prove that bit-for-bit, so no new claim exists
to score. The ledger records it in the untested table. What it does deliver is
that the only public way to get a number out of the chain now refuses, by layer,
for every drug the ledger does not cover.

## Phase 24, part two: the model card (P24.2)

`docs/model-card.md` is the card for the deliverable `predict(drug, dose_mg,
regimen)`. `tests/test_model_card.py` guards it. It adds no model and no number
of its own, and it earns no validated row (rule 9). It is recorded in the
ledger's untested table, like P24.1.

### Why the limits come first, and how that is enforced

The brief requires out-of-scope uses before capabilities. That is a reading
order, so a test checks it: the five section headings must appear in the order
"do not use", "unrepaired mismatches", "populations", "intended use", "what it
can do". The first section must name every scope limit P19.7 set (region,
route, chronic, effect compartment, behaviour, other drugs, body weight). The
mismatch table must name sixteen specific mismatches. Deleting one
fails a test, and so does softening one until its key phrase is gone.

### What "traceable to a ledger row" means mechanically

Each claim carries a bracketed citation. `[V4]` points to a validated row.
`[ledger: X]` points to the untested or searched-and-empty row whose first cell
begins with `X`, and that prefix must match exactly one row. The ledger's
second and third tables have no ids. Adding ids would have meant rewriting
every row of a file that other documents quote, so the first cell serves as
the key instead. The test splits the card into claim units (paragraphs,
bullets and table rows) and fails on any unit without a citation, or on any
citation that resolves to no row or to more than one.

Enforcing this exposed four gaps. The card has to state them, but the ledger
recorded them nowhere: chronic pharmacology (P19.7 had it, the ledger did not),
between-subject variability and covariates for the two drivable drugs, the
olanzapine absorption lag that `fda_pk_bridge` drops, and the population
exchangeability assumption. Each became an untested row. That is the ledger
recording an untested layer, which is what that table is for. None of the four
claims a result, and none was written to let a citation resolve. Each is a
limitation that applies to `predict()` today and was missing from the ledger.

### P19.7 verbatim, and what no longer applies

Block quotes in the card are checked as exact substrings of the P19.7 document
after whitespace normalisation. The card quotes what still holds: striatal
only, the depot-fitted versus orally-driven mismatch, no chronic pharmacology,
no effect compartment, the four haloperidol populations with the
exchangeability sentence, and the number-versus-behaviour sentence. Three P19.7
statements are not carried over:

- "The chain's published predictions ... are single oral doses." `predict()` now
  also offers a once-daily steady-state regimen, and the card names the
  steady-state mean as the reading closest to the fitting data.
- "which is why it reports `fitted-in-repo` rather than `illustrative`." The
  code does not do this. `Prediction.provenance` returns `"illustrative"` or
  `"measured"` and nothing else, so haloperidol reads `"measured"` even though
  its occupancy layer is `fitted-in-repo`. Existing tests pin that value
  (`test_human_dose_to_occupancy.py`, `test_human_prediction_interface.py`).
  P24.2 is a documentation task, so it changes neither those tests nor the
  field. The card warns that the flag is a gate rather than a grade. A test
  asserts the warning stays true: if someone later makes the flag
  three-valued, that test fails and the card has to be updated.
- The P19.7 population section covers haloperidol only, because olanzapine
  became drivable later, in P22.2. The olanzapine populations are written
  fresh from the registry records. The LYBALVI label (NDA213378,
  `effective_time` 20260131, read via openFDA for this task) was also read for
  two facts. It states that there is no PK interaction between olanzapine and
  samidorphan, which matters because every subject in the PK set took both. Its
  population-PK statement gives the race breakdown.

### Live numbers

The card's figures from V1, V4 and V8 are recomputed in the test from
`predict`, `predict_window` and the EC50 registry. The refusal table is
checked row by row against `refusal_layers`. The other ledger figures the card
quotes are checked as present in both the card and the ledger, so the card
cannot drift away from the ledger without a test failing.

## Phase 25, part one: literature population PK for six antipsychotics (P25.1)

P22.5 attributed seven of nine census drugs' failure to the PK layer and
recorded that PK had only ever been looked for in FDA review documents. P25.1
searched the journal literature. The record is
`src/neurocascade/human/literature_popk.py`, the write-up
`docs/p25-1-literature-popk.md`, the ledger row V13.

### A separate module, reusing the FDA parameter type

The literature records reuse `fda_popk.PopPKParameter` (printed symbol, value,
printed unit or `None`) and the rule that `apparent_parameters` is decided by a
quoted sentence. They are a separate class rather than more `FDAPopPK` rows
because the provenance key is different (PMID and the raw copy read, against
application number and review date), and because the literature needed three
things the reviews did not:

- **Fixed parameters with an origin.** Five of the eight models fix ka to
  another study's value. Both quetiapine models borrow it from Zhou 2015, which
  is paywalled. Recording that a parameter was fixed, and from where, is what
  stops a borrowed constant being read as an estimate.
- **A variability scale of `unstated`.** The Xuzhou TDM papers print ω without
  a scale. Assigning variance, SD or CV would be a guess worth up to a square
  root.
- **Disposition mapped per entity, plus an optional parallel elimination rate.**
  Half the models co-fit a metabolite, and each entity's half-life has its own
  label value. Reeves 2024's parent also leaves by a metabolic rate constant
  `km` beside CL/F. The mapping was validated against the source's own printed
  reference half-life: 36.8 h computed against 36 h printed, where omitting km
  would give 50 h. A parallel rate is refused on a two-compartment entity,
  where it would need a micro-constant nobody printed.

Each drug's search is a `DrugSearch` holding every query with its hit count and
every candidate with a disposition. Absence is therefore a data structure, not
a missing row. That is what lets ziprasidone be `searched-and-empty` with nine
queries and two named closed-access papers behind it.

### Why "summariser-only" is a refusal and not a caveat

Two otherwise-acceptable open-access papers (Kim 2008, Feng 2008) were
reachable only through a fetch tool that returns a model's summary of the page.
Asked twice for Kim 2008's Table 3, it gave V/F as 192 L and as 193 L. The
project's rule is that every number is traceable to a source, and a summary is
not one. The alternative, entering the values with a warning, would have put
two drugs' worth of numbers into the registry whose provenance is a language
model. So every transcribed value was read from a raw copy: XML, PDF, PMC HTML,
or a supplementary control stream. That was checked again by re-fetching each
source, not by trusting the search agents' reports.

### The comparison and the one modelling decision in it

The closing comparison reuses V5's quantity, terminal half-life against the
label, because `/F` cancels in V/CL. It also reuses V5's twofold threshold
unchanged. The one new decision was Korell 2017. Its clearance is
`10.9·(WT/74.4)^0.727 + 0.024·CrCL` with no reference CrCL printed. A
"typical" CrCL of, say, 100 mL/min would have invented a reference subject the
source does not define. The comparison instead evaluates both ends of the
covariate range the source itself prints (0 to the 150 mL/min cap) and scores
the worse end. Both ends pass.

### What the result says about TDM-derived volumes

6 of 9 pass. All three failures (Reeves, Chen, Størset's metabolite) are fits
to sparse trough TDM samples whose volume is poorly identified, and every
dense-sampling model passes. The two clozapine models agree on CL/F (21.9
against 20.2 L/h) and disagree 2.8-fold on V/F. The two quetiapine models come
from the same group with the same method and differ 4.6-fold on V/F. That is
the expected behaviour of troughs: they pin the average concentration, which is
dose over CL/F, and say little about the curve's shape, which is V. The
consequence for the chain, when someone wires these in: **a TDM model's CL/F is
usable for a steady-state mean, and its V/F is not evidence about a time
course.**

### Not wired in, deliberately

Only Chen 2024, Zheng 2024 and Knights 2015 have the shape `fda_pk_bridge`
accepts: single entity, mamillary, apparent, with a printed reference weight.
Their drugs (quetiapine, aripiprazole) are blocked at the occupancy layer for
reasons P21.2, P21.4 and P21.5 recorded. Wiring them would add PK rows the
chain must still refuse, so it was left alone. The P22.5 pinned numbers and the
P24.1 interface are unchanged.

## Phase 25, part two: literature PK records in the occupancy chain (P25.2)

The rules are in docs/p25-2-literature-pk-in-chain.md, committed before the code.
The implementation is `human/literature_pk_bridge.py`. This section records why
those rules were chosen.

### Two gates, kept apart

**Converting a record and integrating it are separate questions.**
`literature_pk_bridge.refusals` decides whether a P25.1 record can become a
`HumanPKRecord`. `_require_pk_record` decides whether the chain can integrate a
record of that shape. Only the second needed widening, from two compartments to
one or two, because `DosedOneCompartmentPK` already integrates the one-compartment
case exactly.

**Three compartments stay refused.** No sourced human oral set needs a third
compartment, and accepting it without a record to exercise it would be
capability nobody has tested.

### The rule the FDA bridge does not have: V13 as an entry gate

P25.1 found that every model fitted to sparse TDM troughs failed the label
half-life check, and that the failure sat in V/F every time. The chain predicts
time courses, single-dose peaks included. A volume the label already
contradicts would feed straight into those.

So **a literature record enters only if its own V13 comparison passed.** That
uses a number nobody in this repository chose, at the threshold V13 already
used. It is the only thing that separates Chen 2024 (refused) from Zheng 2024
(accepted): same group, same method, same borrowed ka.

The FDA bridge was not retrofitted with the same rule. Doing so would change
olanzapine's PK layer underneath a scored result (V8), and LYBALVI passed V5
anyway.

### Covariates and variability: the reference subject, and nothing else

**Every converted record is its source's reference subject.** Variability and
covariate effects are named in the record's notes as not carried.

**`cl_allometric_exponent` is left unset even when a source prints 0.75.** P25.1
stored covariate relations as verbatim text and deliberately did not evaluate
them, and Reeves 2024 shows why: it prints its age effect two incompatible ways.
Parsing an exponent out of a string here would be the first evaluation of one,
done quietly inside a converter. The consequence is real:

- a literature record cannot be moved off its reference weight;
- so `predict_occupancy` now defaults to the source's reference weight rather
  than a literal 70 kg.

That change is inert for haloperidol and olanzapine, whose references are both
70 kg. A regression test pins their `predict()` outputs to values computed at
the base commit, at a relative tolerance of 1e-12.

**One near miss.** While refactoring the model construction into
`_build_pk_model`, I reassociated `x * 1000 / 60 / bw` into
`x * (1000 / 60 / bw)`. That moved olanzapine's steady-state mean by about
1e-11. The original evaluation order was restored, and the curves are now
bit-identical.

### Freezing P22.2 and P22.5

`label_dose_prediction` and `multidrug_failure_analysis` call
`_require_pk_record(..., include_literature=False)`. Those modules reproduce
results that were scored and committed against the PK registry as it stood in
P22 (V8, and P22.5's layer matrix). Letting the registry grow underneath them
would rewrite quetiapine's recorded refusal reason after the fact. The
interface and the model card do see the literature records. The model card says
so beside the V8 citation.

### What this bought

**The PK layer of two more drugs, and no new occupancy prediction.**

- **Quetiapine** now fails only at occupancy and exposure. It has no D2 EC50,
  being outside the direct-effect form (P21.2).
- **Aripiprazole** now fails at active-metabolite, occupancy and exposure. That
  is P21.4's refusal; the EC50 is Kim 2012, which sits in the P22.3 module and
  not in the chain registry.

Each refusal list now names only missing data.

The one external comparison this enables is the absorption phase, which V13
never tested. The chain's own integrated Tmax was compared with the innovator
labels (V14), under the reused twofold criterion fixed in the design note:

| drug | source | predicted Tmax | label Tmax | fold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| quetiapine | Zheng 2024 | 1.77 h | 1.5 h | 1.18 |
| aripiprazole | Knights 2015 | 4.55 h | 3–5 h | inside the range |

Both pass. The result is weak, for three reasons:

- n is 2;
- Knights 2015 is the sponsor's model;
- Zheng 2024's ka is borrowed from an AstraZeneca-authored paper, and
  AstraZeneca holds the SEROQUEL label.

## Phase 25, part three: dose to occupancy end to end, scored against held-out PET (P25.3)

Module `neurocascade.human.heldout_dose_occupancy`; document
`docs/p25-3-heldout-dose-occupancy.md`; ledger V15.

### The brief's two missing pieces are one layer in this chain

The brief asked for Kp,uu and D2 affinity per drug. The chain has used an
in-vivo plasma EC50 since P19.5, and that constant already contains brain
penetration and protein binding. A Kp,uu value or an in-vitro Ki would count the
same effects twice, so neither is entered.

What each new drug gets instead:
- a first-hand [11C]raclopride plasma EC50: Kim 2012 for aripiprazole, as in
  P22.3; Nord 2011's IR-only K_i,app of 1373 nM for quetiapine;
- a `not-required` Kp,uu record naming that EC50, which the double-counting
  guard checks.

That is the source-over-brief deviation, stated under rule 11.

### The new rows stay out of the live registries

They are passed explicitly, through a new `kp_uu_record` argument that mirrors
`pk_record` and `receptor_record`. Adding them to `D2_PLASMA_EC50` or
`HUMAN_KP_UU_RECORDS` would have rewritten the frozen P22.2 and P22.5
attributions and the public interface's refusal lists. That is the P22.3 D1
precedent. Whether `predict()` should drive aripiprazole and quetiapine is a
separate decision:
- for aripiprazole it should not, because the interface's regimens are repeated
  dosing;
- for quetiapine, the constant is only defensible in the once-daily
  peak-and-trough design it was fitted in.

### The active-metabolite gate is opened for one regimen, with the evidence attached

Aripiprazole's refusal (P21.4) was a regimen mismatch: a single-dose parent-only
EC50 against a steady-state metabolite share. In the test subjects' own plasma
during the scan, Ito 2012 measured dehydro-aripiprazole at about 3% of the
parent.

`ActiveMetabolite.parent_only_regimen` records the one regimen that clears a
refused record. The record must also carry the measurement that justifies it.
`predict_occupancy(regimen=)` forwards the regimen to the gate, and
`steady_state_occupancy` refuses any regimen, because it superposes doses.

Without the argument, every caller behaves exactly as before. The alternative,
re-labelling the record `bounded`, was rejected: a bound needs an affinity ratio,
and none exists for the metabolite.

### Observation selection and the threshold

**Threshold.** It is P22.3's pre-registered same-tracer MAE of 0.10, reused
unchanged. The plasma arm uses the V5/V13 twofold threshold and is reported only.

**Selection rules.** An observation qualifies only if:
- it uses the same tracer as the constant;
- dose, schedule and scan time can be read from the source;
- its subjects are disjoint from the constant's source.

**The two quetiapine sources left unscored.** Gefvert 1998 and Kapur 2000 do
not print a schedule, and the once- and twice-daily readings disagree about
pass or fail. Both readings are printed in the module rather than either one
being chosen.

The disclosure that I computed those readings before choosing
Tauscher-Wisniewski 2002 is in the P25.3 document.

### What the result says

All four drugs pass, so the result is a calibration of the layers rather than a
fault in any one of them.

- **Aripiprazole:** the whole-chain bias of −0.041, with all six errors
  negative, comes from the PK layer. Plasma is predicted at 0.77–0.93 of
  observed. Given the measured plasma, P22.3's bias was −0.005. A cause
  consistent with this, but untestable, is that Knights' 74.19 kg reference
  subject is heavier than Ito's Japanese volunteers. A bridged record cannot be
  moved off its reference weight.
- **Olanzapine:** the over-prediction comes from the occupancy constant. At
  Mamo's own measured plasma it would be +0.076. The PK under-prediction offsets
  part of that.
- **Quetiapine:** it passes only in the design its constant was fitted in.
- **Not tested:** every comparison is a group mean predicted at a mean dose, for
  a typical subject. Nothing here tests variability between individuals.

## Phase 28, part one: benchmark drug list and frozen split (P28.1)

The product roadmap (`docs/roadmap-product.md`) is judged by one test: a
retrospective benchmark of CNS drugs, each given only preclinical-type inputs
and scored against what was observed in humans. P28.1 fixes **which drugs** are
in it and **which of them are held out**, before any data for any of them is
collected. It is deliberately the first task in the phase. A split drawn after
coverage was known would let coverage steer the split.

### Where the files live, and why not `data/benchmark/`

The brief named `data/benchmark/drugs.json`. In this build `data/` is read-only
reference data, and patches that touch it are rejected. The two files therefore
live with the code at `src/neurocascade/benchmark/`, the same pattern
`human/fixtures/` follows. This is a path change only; the contents are what the
brief asked for.

### Inclusion rules

The list is not hand-picked. Where a rule could decide inclusion, a rule did.

1. **Approved drugs: every WHO ATC level-5 entry under N05A (antipsychotics),
   N05B (anxiolytics) and N06A (antidepressants)**, read from the ChEMBL REST
   API `atc_class` endpoint (ChEMBL_37, released 2026-05-01). That gives 176
   entries: N05A 69, N05B 39, N06A 68. These three level-3 classes are the brief's
   three named classes. Hypnotics (N05C), anti-dementia drugs (N06D) and
   psychostimulants (N06B) were left out because the brief did not name them,
   not because of any judgement about them. Taking the whole ATC class rather
   than picking within it is what keeps the list from being chosen by
   expectation. The cost is that obscure regional drugs come in (dimetacrine,
   pivagabine, mephenoxalone) whose preclinical packages may be thin. That is
   accepted: Phase 28's coverage tasks report per-field coverage, and a drug
   with no binding panel will show up there as a gap rather than having been
   quietly dropped here.
2. **Eight ATC entries excluded by a mechanical rule** (one small-molecule
   entity per record), each recorded with its reason in
   `drugs.json["excluded_atc_entries"]`:
   - five fixed combinations, each of whose single components is already in;
   - two herbal preparations (lavender oil, St John's wort);
   - lithium, an inorganic ion with no receptor binding panel. The benchmark's
     premise is binding panel → occupancy → effect, and lithium has nothing for
     that path to score.

   That leaves 168.
3. **ChEMBL id is the parent of the molecule ChEMBL maps to the ATC code.**
   Every code resolved to exactly one parent; the script raises if any did not.
   One override: ChEMBL maps N05AC04 to pipotiazine *palmitate* (CHEMBL2106439,
   a depot ester registered as its own parent). The active moiety pipotiazine
   (CHEMBL398880) is used instead, because binding and PK belong to the moiety.
4. **Clinical failures (stratum FAIL), 17 drugs.** The brief's "known clinical
   failures with public preclinical data" has no registry to read from, so this
   stratum is the one place judgement entered. To bound that judgement, a
   compound qualifies only if all three hold:
   - it is not approved for the psychiatric indication it was tested in;
   - a published placebo-controlled trial **printed** that its primary
     endpoint was not met. Press releases do not count;
   - ChEMBL carries it with a structure, and its synonyms include the INN and
     the trial code name.

   Every PMID, title and quoted conclusion was read from Europe PMC on
   2026-10-01 and is stored per drug (`failure.pmid`, `failure.evidence`).
   Candidates considered and **rejected**, with the reason:
   - casopitant (Ratti 2011, PMID 22020354): one of its two trials was positive
     at 80 mg, so it is not a clean failure;
   - vabicaserin (Shen 2014, PMID 24613032): the 200 mg arm met its primary
     endpoint;
   - ocinaplon (Czobor 2010, PMID 20041911): its trial was positive. Development
     stopped for liver safety, which is a different kind of failure from the one
     this stratum scores;
   - bifeprunox: the only publication is a Cochrane review (PMID 27732740) that
     finds some positive effects and says the failing data were never released;
   - emraclidine, ulotaront, encenicline, rapastinel, aticaprant: the failing
     phase 3 results reached Europe PMC only as press-release-level or
     conference-abstract records, not a trial paper with a PMID;
   - MK-0777, Lu AF35700, L-745,870: no INN, and the list is keyed by INN.

   Esmethadone and roluperidone are borderline and are kept on the stated rule.
   Esmethadone missed its primary endpoint (P=.154) but was positive post hoc in
   severe depression. Roluperidone's ITT primary endpoint was P≤.064, and
   modified-ITT was nominally significant. Aprepitant is approved, but as an
   antiemetic (A04AD12), never as an antidepressant, so it qualifies.
   `intended_atc_level3` records the class each failure was being developed
   into, so that Phase 30 can group it with its would-be peers.

Total: 168 + 17 = **185 drugs**.

### Per-field sources

Every record carries `sources` with an entry for every field: name, stratum,
ChEMBL id, preferred name, InChIKey, CAS, ATC code, all ATC codes, max phase
and withdrawn flag. `tests/test_benchmark_split.py` enforces this.

- **Name.** For ATC drugs the name is the WHO ATC/DDD name, which WHO takes from
  the INN where one exists. A few are ATC forms rather than bare INNs
  ("potassium clorazepate", "imipramine oxide"). They are kept verbatim because
  they are what the classification prints. For failures the name is the INN as
  it appears in ChEMBL's synonym list.
- **CAS** comes from PubChem PUG-View, heading "CAS". Sources are tried in a
  fixed order, and the first that lists exactly one CAS is used: CAS Common
  Chemistry (172 drugs), FDA GSRS (8), ChemIDplus (2), EPA DSSTox (3). The
  PubChem record is found by ChEMBL's standard InChIKey. When that lookup gives
  no CAS, the fallback is a name lookup, and the match quality is recorded in
  `sources.cas.match`:
  - **inchikey**: 180 drugs;
  - **connectivity**: 2 drugs (cariprazine, reboxetine), where the stereo layer
    differs;
  - **name_only**: 3 drugs, each with a note.
    - Chlordiazepoxide and tranylcypromine are representation differences:
      ChEMBL draws a different tautomer for one and writes the trans racemate
      as two components for the other.
    - **Flupentixol is genuinely unresolved.** Its ATC-mapped ChEMBL record
      (CHEMBL6066864) has no structure, and PubChem's "flupentixol" is the Z
      isomer. The stored CAS therefore identifies cis-flupentixol, not
      necessarily the marketed substance. Phase 28's binding task must settle
      the isomer before using ChEMBL activities for this drug.

  Each CAS passes its check digit, and the test asserts this.
  - *Why not stop at the InChIKey?* Five of the seven first-pass misses were
    PubChem returning a secondary CID first (aprepitant's InChIKey resolves to
    CID 6918365 before the main record, CID 135413536). Trying up to five CIDs
    and then the name fallback was enough to make the list complete.

### The split

- **Drug-level**, so no drug has rows on both sides.
- **Stratified** by the four strata (N05A, N05B, N06A, FAIL).
- **Drawn once**:
  - Within each stratum the INNs are sorted, then shuffled by a single
    `random.Random(20261001)` that is walked across the strata in sorted
    order.
  - The first round(0.3 n) of each stratum are held out.
  - The seed is the drawing date. It was fixed before the draw and was not
    tuned.
- **Result:**

  | Stratum | Train | Held out |
  |---|---|---|
  | N05A | 47 | 20 |
  | N05B | 25 | 10 |
  | N06A | 46 | 20 |
  | FAIL | 12 | 5 |
  | **Total** | **130** | **55** |

- **Frozen in three places:**
  - `neurocascade.benchmark.SPLIT_SHA256`, which `load_split()` checks on every
    load;
  - a literal in `tests/test_benchmark_split.py`;
  - `docs/validation-ledger.md`.

  Changing the split means editing all three, and that should look exactly as
  deliberate as it is. The `split` stage of the build script refuses to run if
  `split.json` exists.

**Disclosed after the draw:** four held-out drugs are not blind to this
repository. Amisulpride, quetiapine, ziprasidone and diazepam already have human
PET, PK or label values read or fitted in Phases 19-25. Alprazolam appears only
as a rodent elevated-plus-maze series in the retired mouse calibration, which
is not human data. The split was not redrawn: choosing a split after seeing what
it contains is the leak the freeze exists to stop. Instead the ledger requires
every held-out score to be reported both over all 55 drugs and over the 51
untouched ones.

### What this task did not do

It collected no preclinical or human data for any drug, so it produced no
prediction and earned no validated-claims row in the ledger. It is a
precondition for Phase 28's coverage tasks, not a result. The list is useful
only to the extent that those tasks fill it. The drugs with thin public data
will show up as coverage gaps; they were not quietly dropped here.

## Phase 28, part two: receptor binding panel per benchmark drug (P28.2)

P28.2 gives every benchmark drug the first input in its preclinical package: a
**human** receptor panel with a Ki per target and an action type where a
source prints one. It makes no prediction and earns no validated row (ledger
rule 1). Its result is a coverage table, now in the ledger:

- 118 of 185 drugs have a panel;
- 12.57 targets per covered drug, on average;
- 67 drugs are searched and empty.

### Where the files live

The brief named `data/benchmark/binding/<drug>.json`. `data/` is read-only in
this build, so the panels sit at `src/neurocascade/benchmark/binding/<inn>.json`
beside P28.1's `drugs.json`, for the reason given under P28.1. Spaces in an INN
become underscores in the filename. `coverage.json` sits beside the panels.
They are loaded through `neurocascade.benchmark.load_binding_panel` and
`load_binding_coverage`. `scripts/build_benchmark_binding.py` regenerates them:
`fetch` caches the three sources outside the repo, and `build` runs offline.

### Sources and what each one contributes

- **PDSP Ki database.** Full CSV from `kiDownload/download.php`, 98,678 rows.
  Its sha256 is in every file. Every row carries species and a reference, but
  PDSP prints no efficacy.
- **ChEMBL_37 REST API.** Every `Ki` activity on the drug's parent molecule,
  with salt forms included through `parent_molecule_chembl_id`. The script
  also pulls the assay, document and target records behind each activity, and
  the curated `mechanism` table, which carries an action type and references.
- **GtoPdb 2026.3.** Bulk `interactions.csv`, with `pKi` rows on human
  targets. Every interaction row also gives its Type/Action pair as an action
  type, including rows whose affinity is not a Ki.

### Rule-12 check: the species of a ChEMBL Ki is not the target's species

The load-bearing assumption was that a ChEMBL Ki filtered to
`target_organism = Homo sapiens` is a human measurement. **It is not.** The
first haloperidol row returned was a "human" sigma-1 Ki of 3.2 nM.

- Its assay (CHEMBL802065) is [3H](+)-pentazocine binding in **guinea-pig
  brain**.
- ChEMBL maps that assay to the human target as a homologue, with
  `confidence_score` 8.
- Filtering on the target organism would have imported rodent and guinea-pig
  tissue values wholesale. That is the rule-2 substitution P23.1's species
  gate exists to stop.

The panel therefore requires both:

- the **assay** organism to be human (`assay_tax_id == 9606`);
- a direct target assignment: confidence 9 for a single protein, 7 for a
  protein complex.

A test reproduces the guinea-pig case. PDSP rows must say `HUMAN`; the
uncertain `? HUMAN` rows and `UNDEFINED` rows are refused. GtoPdb rows must
have `Target Species == Human`.

What the rule costs is visible in the data. The classical benzodiazepine-site
literature was measured on rat or bovine brain. Lorazepam has 89 ChEMBL Ki rows. 81 are on non-human assays, and the
other 8 are human DrugMatrix screens that printed only "inhibition < 50% @
10 uM" at unrelated targets. That is most of why N05B has a panel for only 5 of 35 drugs.
Translating a rat-brain benzodiazepine-site Ki to the human receptor is the
kind of explicit, error-measured step that `roadmap-product.md` allows. It
belongs to Phase 29, which can measure that step's error, not to a data task
that would hide it inside a panel.

### Drug identity: same entity only

Each panel is for the benchmark record's own entity. It is never for a
racemate, an enantiomer, a prodrug or a metabolite standing in for it (rule 2).

- **ChEMBL**: the parent id from `drugs.json`, which ChEMBL keeps separate per
  stereoisomer (citalopram CHEMBL549, escitalopram CHEMBL1508).
- **GtoPdb**: matched by standard InChIKey, then ChEMBL id. GtoPdb's ligand 958
  is (-)-sulpiride, so it reaches levosulpiride and not racemic sulpiride.
- **PDSP**: matched by ligand name, because its CAS column is unreliable. In
  many rows it holds NSC numbers or a salt's CAS. Exact INN matches are
  accepted, plus a curated `PDSP_ALIASES` table of spelling variants,
  salts and synonyms for the same stereochemical entity. Examples:
  - "CHLORIMIPRAMINE" for clomipramine;
  - "PROPERICIAZINE" for periciazine;
  - "9-OH-risperidone" for paliperidone, which is racemic
    9-hydroxyrisperidone;
  - "cis-Clopenthixol" for zuclopenthixol;
  - "Methadone,(S)(+)" for esmethadone.

  Enantiomer rows for a racemic drug are deliberately absent: "(+)Mianserin",
  "Fluoxetine-R-(-)", "Hydroxyzine, (R)". A test asserts that the alias sets
  of racemate/single-isomer pairs never overlap. Two-site fit components
  ("Sulpiride-high,(-)") are not taken as a Ki.
- **Flupentixol** was left open by P28.1 and is settled here. Its ATC-mapped
  ChEMBL record (CHEMBL6066864) has no structure and no activities. The
  record's CAS is the cis(Z) isomer.
  - Lundbeck's FLUANXOL product monograph (Canada) states that commercial
    flupentixol dihydrochloride is about a 1:1 cis:trans mixture whose trans
    isomer is pharmacologically inactive.
  - The depot is pure cis(Z)-flupentixol decanoate.
  - The panel is therefore the active isomer's: ChEMBL CHEMBL54661, GtoPdb 948,
    PDSP "FLUPENTHIXOL, Alpha" / "cis-flupenthixol". The record's
    `entity_note` says so.
  - Phase 29 must halve oral dose to active-isomer dose. That is a fact about
    the product, not an assumption made here.
- **Clopenthixol** (the cis/trans mixture, CHEMBL3989892) is *not* given
  zuclopenthixol's data. Zuclopenthixol is its own benchmark drug, and the
  mixture's record has no structure-level stereo. Clopenthixol is searched and
  empty.
- **Prodrugs** are left empty rather than given the active moiety's numbers:
  potassium clorazepate, which acts through nordazepam; pomaglumetad
  methionil, through LY404039; and imipramine oxide. Whether a prodrug inherits
  its active moiety's panel is a PK question, and it belongs to Phase 29 with
  its own error measured. Nordazepam itself is empty too, so for the
  nordazepam-precursor benzodiazepines the substitution would not even have
  had data.

### Targets

Targets are keyed by human gene symbol. A heteromer is keyed by its sorted
subunit symbols joined with `+`, e.g. `GABRA1+GABRB3+GABRG2` or
`CHRNA4+CHRNB2`.

- **ChEMBL**: symbols come from the target components.
- **GtoPdb**: from `Target Gene Symbol`.
- **PDSP**: free-text receptor names go through `PDSP_TARGETS`, by name, not
  by its `Unigene` column, which is sometimes wrong. PDSP labels "Cholecystokinin
  A" with CCKBR, for example.
  - Generic names that do not identify one gene product are left unmapped and
    counted, not guessed. Examples: "alpha1", "5-HT2", "Cholinergic,
    muscarinic", "GABA A", "Sigma".
  - Splice and editing variants map to their gene: D2L/D2S → DRD2, D4.2/D4.4
    → DRD4, 5-HT2C-INI → HTR2C.

### How a per-target Ki is summarised

Every included measurement is stored with:

- its value;
- its relation: `=`, or `>` for censored values;
- its source and source record (ChEMBL activity/assay id, PDSP Ki ID with
  tissue and radioligand, or GtoPdb ligand/target);
- a reference key that resolves in the file's `references` block. That block
  holds a PMID wherever one exists, and the ChEMBL document id, the PDSP
  reference string or the GtoPdb row otherwise.

The summary `ki_nM` is a stated rule applied to those measurements, not a
chosen number:

1. Take the exact (`=`) values.
2. Average pKi within each reference.
3. Take the median across references.

Grouping by reference first keeps one paper's table, which may reach ChEMBL,
PDSP and GtoPdb all at once, from counting three times. ChEMBL's own
`potential_duplicate` re-tabulations and rows carrying a
`data_validity_comment` are dropped for the same reason. The median is used
because the spread is real and wide, and one outlier should not move the
summary. Haloperidol D2 spans 0.12-6,400 nM across 73 references; its median is
2.0 nM. `ki_min_nM`, `ki_max_nM`, `n_references` and `n_censored` keep that
spread visible.

Censored values are kept but never enter the summary:

- PDSP's 34,300 `>` rows, ChEMBL `>`/`>=` and GtoPdb `>` rows are stored as
  censored measurements.
- DrugMatrix "inhibition < 50% @ 10 uM" screens print no Ki. They are kept as
  their printed statement under `screened_inactive_without_ki`, and no number
  is made from them.

A test recomputes every summary from the stored measurements.

### Action type (the efficacy field)

Ki databases print no efficacy; P8.1 recorded this as a property of the assay.
Action types therefore come from two sources:

- **GtoPdb**: the Type/Action pair. For example, "Allosteric modulator /
  Positive" becomes `positive allosteric modulator`, and "Antagonist / Inverse
  agonist" becomes `inverse agonist`.
- **ChEMBL**: the curated mechanism table.

Each action carries its own reference. Disagreements are kept, not arbitrated.
Risperidone at 5-HT2A is `inverse agonist` in GtoPdb and `antagonist` in
ChEMBL's mechanism table, and both are listed.

An action recorded at family level (ChEMBL "D2-like dopamine receptor
inverse agonist", "GABA-A receptor; anion channel positive allosteric modulator")
says nothing subtype-specific. Haloperidol at D2, for instance, is `antagonist`
in GtoPdb, and ChEMBL's only D2 record for it is that family-level inverse
agonist row. It goes to `action_types_via_family` on the
member targets, kept apart from the target's own `action_types`. Action types
on targets with no Ki stay visible under `actions_without_ki`. For example,
lorazepam and brexanolone have a GABA-A PAM action but no human Ki.

Efficacy coverage is the thin field, at 3.14 action-typed targets per covered
drug against 12.57 Ki targets. Most off-target Ki values have no functional
assay behind them in these sources. Phase 29's occupancy step needs only Ki.
Phase 30, if it weighs occupancy by efficacy, will have to treat "unknown
action" as its own category rather than default it to antagonist.

### Coverage, and what the gaps are

The table is in the ledger. Some of the shape:

- **N05A** is well covered: 57 of 67 drugs, 17 targets each.
- **N06A** is reasonably covered: 47 of 66.
- **N05B** has 5 of 35 drugs. The species rule above causes most of that gap.
- **The FAIL stratum** is covered for 9 of 17, but thinly: 2.9 targets per
  drug, mostly the intended target only.

The 67 empties fall into three kinds, and each record's `searched` and
`excluded_counts` block shows which:

- **Species**: rat or bovine values exist but no human ones, e.g. lorazepam,
  iproniazide, cloxazolam, fluanisone.
- **Unit**: human pIC50 exists but no Ki (iclepertin, levomilnacipran,
  mardepodect, pexacerfont), or there is no affinity at all for a functional
  action (brexanolone, zuranolone).
- **Absence**: the regional and older drugs, which have nothing in any source.
  Examples: dimetacrine, pivagabine, mephenoxalone, oxaflozane, quinupramine,
  thiopropazate.

Fourteen of the 55 held-out drugs are empty.

### What was deliberately not done

- **No IC50 or Kd was converted to a Ki.** Cheng-Prusoff needs the radioligand
  concentration and its Kd, which these rows do not carry. Pooling IC50 as if
  it were Ki would put a different quantity in the panel under the Ki name.
  Whether Phase 29 admits other affinity types is its decision, and it must
  measure the effect on its error.
- **No non-human Ki** is in a panel, for the reason above.
- **No minimum-panel threshold.** A drug with one human Ki has a panel.
  Whether one target suffices for a prediction is a Phase 29-30 question, and
  answering it here would be deciding the score before it is run.

## Phase 28, part three: preclinical ADME/PK inputs per benchmark drug (P28.3)

P28.3 assembles the second input in each benchmark drug's preclinical package:
the ADME/PK quantities a compound would have had before an IND. The brief names
four fields — plasma fraction unbound, brain fraction unbound or Kp,uu, in-vitro
intrinsic clearance (microsomal/hepatocyte), and rodent in-vivo CL/Vss — and
four source families: Lombardo 2018 companion data, the Fridén/Loryan Kp,uu
compilations, ChEMBL ADME assays, and primary rat PK papers. Like P28.2 it makes
no prediction and earns no validated row (ledger rule 1); its result is a
coverage table, now in the ledger.

### Why ChEMBL is the aggregator, not a scrape of each named source (rule 11)

The brief lists four source families as if they were four separate ingests. Read
first: ChEMBL_37 already **contains** three of the four as curated activities,
each row carrying its own species, tissue, units and source document, and the
document resolves to a PMID. Confirmed by fetching `assay_type=A` activities on
the parent molecules and reading the documents behind them:

- **Lombardo/Obach IV-PK** — the human CL and Vss trend-analysis databases are
  in ChEMBL as documents CHEMBL1135488 (Lombardo 2002, *J Med Chem*, PMID
  12061889), CHEMBL1148291 (Lombardo 2004), CHEMBL1614630/1614632 (Obach 2008
