  670-compound set, PMID 18426954) and CHEMBL3588773 (Lombardo 2016 "Volume of
  Distribution in Drug Design", PMID 25799158).
- **Fridén brain tissue binding** — CHEMBL3526149 (Fridén 2011 porcine brain
  TRANSIL, PMID 21071520) and CHEMBL3525956 (Fridén 2011 species-independence,
  PMID 21474681).
- **Loryan unbound brain exposure** — CHEMBL3525927 (Loryan 2011, PMID 21149540)
  and CHEMBL4373730 (2019 Kp,uu set).

Scraping the published supplements directly was tried and is not available: the
Elsevier (`ars.els-cdn.com`) and ASPET (`dmd.aspetjournals.org`) supplement
URLs for Lombardo 2018 all return HTTP 403. ChEMBL is the one machine-readable
mirror that carries these compilations **with a per-row citation and the
original species/units**, which is exactly what the sourcing discipline needs.
So P28.3 ingests ChEMBL ADME activities and resolves each to its primary paper,
rather than hand-transcribing supplements behind a paywall. The fourth family,
primary rat PK papers not in ChEMBL, is a documented residual gap (below), not a
field left blank by oversight.

`scripts/build_benchmark_adme.py` has the same two-stage shape as the P28.2
build: `fetch` caches ChEMBL activities, assays and documents outside the repo;
`build` runs offline and writes `src/neurocascade/benchmark/adme/<inn>.json` and
`coverage.json`. Records load through `neurocascade.benchmark.load_adme_record`
and `load_adme_coverage`.

### The field classifier

ChEMBL's ADME layer is heterogeneous free text (the parent-molecule pull returns
~12,700 activities across ~160 `standard_type` values, most of them irrelevant:
bacterial biotransformation, hepatotoxicity indices, Caco-2 permeability). A
drug's ADME record keeps only rows `_classify` maps to one of the four fields:

- **plasma_fu** ← `Fu`/`logFu` rows whose tissue/description is plasma, serum or
  blood, and `PPB` rows (converted, below). In this corpus `logFu` rows store the
  de-logged fraction (haloperidol 0.08), so they are read as a fraction.
- **brain_fu** ← `Fu` rows whose tissue or description is brain or cortex.
- **kp_uu** ← `K(p,uu,brain)`. **kp_total** ← `Kp` (unitless) and `BPR`.
- **clint** ← `CL` rows naming an in-vitro system (microsomes, hepatocytes, S9,
  intestinal/cytosol) or carrying a per-mass/per-cell unit; the matrix is
  recorded.
- **invivo_cl / invivo_vss** ← `CL` in mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (or ml/min) and
  `Vdss`/`Vd` in L·kg⁻¹, that are **not** an in-vitro system.

Two refusals are explicit and tested: a `Kp` row whose unit is cm/s is PAMPA
permeability, not a partition coefficient, and is dropped; a `PPB` row described
as microsomal/liver covalent binding is not plasma protein binding.

### The human / non-human boundary for in-vivo PK (the P28.4 seam)

The brief scopes the in-vivo field to **rodent** CL/Vss because this is the
*preclinical* package. Human in-vivo CL, Vss and half-life are the clinical
outcomes P28.4 scores the model against; putting them in the preclinical inputs
here would be scoring against part of the input. So `_classify`'s in-vivo fields
accept only non-human species, and a human in-vivo CL/Vss row is dropped and
counted per drug under `excluded` (`human_invivo_cl`, `human_invivo_vss`). A
test asserts no in-vivo measurement is human. The headline coverage is rodent
(rat/mouse); dog and monkey in-vivo PK are kept (they are preclinical species a
real IND package would carry) but tagged by species. In-vitro plasma fu and
CLint are preclinical regardless of species, so human in-vitro values stay.

Species is read from ChEMBL's `assay_organism`, falling back to the assay
description when the organism is null — the Lombardo rows say "in man" with no
organism field, and a null-species row would otherwise be wrongly admissible to
the rodent in-vivo field. "in man" → human (excluded); "in rat/Wistar/Sprague"
→ rat. Rows whose species cannot be resolved are kept out of the in-vivo field
and counted (`species_unresolved_*`).

### Summarising without fabricating a number (rule 1, rule 5)

The first draft summarised each field per species with a single median. That is
wrong where a field's rows carry different units: a drug's clint rows mix
mL·min⁻¹·g⁻¹ (microsomal) with µL·min⁻¹·(10⁶cells)⁻¹ (hepatocyte), and a median
across the two is a number nobody measured. Several `Vdss` rows are even
mislabelled mL/min/kg (a flow unit) in ChEMBL. The summary therefore computes
one value **per (species, units, matrix) group**: mL·min⁻¹·g⁻¹ microsomes and
S9 are separate rows, the mislabelled mL/min/kg Vdss sits alone rather than
contaminating the L·kg⁻¹ figure, and a reader sees the unit on every value. A
test (`test_summaries_never_pool_incompatible_units_or_matrices`) enforces this.

Within a group the rule mirrors P28.2: exact (`=`) values only; geometric mean
within a document (fu, clearance and partition coefficients are ratios/
concentrations that span decades, so the log scale is the right average), then
the median across documents, keeping `min`/`max`/`n_measurements`/`n_documents`/
`n_censored` visible. A `PPB` percent enters plasma_fu as fu = 1 − PPB/100, is
marked unitless so it pools with the `Fu` fractions, and keeps the original
percent in `ppb_percent`. Censored (`<`/`>`) rows are stored but never summarised.

Spot checks against well-established human plasma protein binding (a test, not a
hand-entered number — the build computes these medians): diazepam fu 0.0215
(~98% bound), haloperidol 0.08 (~90%), fluoxetine 0.0514 (~95%).

### Coverage and the residual gap

80 of 185 drugs have at least one preclinical field (53 train, 27 held out), from
903 cited measurements across 117 ChEMBL documents. Per field: plasma fu 71,
brain fu/Kp,uu 40, in-vitro CLint 47, rodent in-vivo CL 22, rodent Vss 22. The
105 empties are the same population as P28.2's — the N05B benzodiazepines and the
pre-2000 regional antipsychotics/antidepressants, characterised before the
microsomal-stability and brain-binding assay era — plus a few marketed drugs
(asenapine, droperidol, penfluridol) whose ADME is only in closed primary PK
papers. The fourth brief source, primary rat PK papers not in ChEMBL, would
reach some of these, but transcribing per-drug paywalled PK was out of scope for
a reproducible single-source build; it is recorded as the known residual gap in
the searched-and-empty row rather than closed by an invented value.

## Phase 28, part four: human clinical truth per benchmark drug (P28.4)

P28.4 assembles what the benchmark is scored **against**: human PK, clinical
dose, PET occupancy, and a clinical-effect label vector per drug. Like
P28.1-28.3 it makes no prediction and earns no validated row. Its ledger
entries are a coverage table, the effect prevalences, two measurements of how
noisy the truth itself is, and three searched-and-empty rows.

### Where the files live, and how they are built

The brief named `data/benchmark/truth/<drug>.json`. `data/` is read-only in this
build, so the records sit at `src/neurocascade/benchmark/truth/<inn>.json`, for
the reason given under P28.1. `coverage.json` and `effect_labels.json` (the
matrix, its rule, and prevalence) sit beside them. They load through
`neurocascade.benchmark.load_truth_record`, `load_truth_coverage` and
`load_effect_labels`.

`scripts/build_benchmark_truth.py` has the P28.2/28.3 two-stage shape:

- `fetch` caches openFDA, SIDER 4.1, WHO ATC/DDD pages, ChEMBL and Europe PMC
  outside the repo;
- `build` runs offline.

The hand-curated inputs live in `scripts/benchmark_truth_inputs/`:

- `pet_observations.json` and `pet_searched_empty.json`;
- `label_transcriptions.json`.

The build checks each one against its cached source and refuses to write if a
check fails. Quote-level verification is the only defence against a
transcription error, so it runs on every build, not once.

### Human PK: ChEMBL's IV compilations, not the Lombardo 2018 file (rule 11)

The brief named the Lombardo 2018 1352-drug IV set. It is not reachable:

- the article PDF and the supplement return HTTP 403;
- ChEMBL has no document for PMID 30115648.

ChEMBL does carry, row by row with citations, the compilations that preceded
it: Obach 2008 (670 drugs, IV CL/Vss/t½) and Lombardo 2002-2016. P28.3 already
excluded exactly these human rows from the preclinical package and counted them
per drug (`human_invivo_cl`), so the seam between input and truth is the same
classifier read from the other side.

`classify_human_pk` keeps three kinds of row:

- **total systemic CL** (mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹). It refuses hepatic, renal, unbound and
  intrinsic clearances, any in-vitro system, and oral CL. Oral CL is CL/F, a
  different quantity, which comes from the label instead.
- **Vss** (L·kg⁻¹), excluding unbound and oral.
- **Terminal t½**. It refuses absorption half-lives, metabolite and enantiomer
  half-lives, DDI arms, and microsomal "half-lives".

Route is kept on every row and is a grouping key in the summary, so an
explicit-IV value is never pooled with an unspecified-route compilation value.
The summary rule is P28.3's: geometric mean within a document, median across
documents.

### The label: one per drug, chosen by a fixed rule, then transcribed by hand

**Why one label.** openFDA returns up to 248 labels per drug (generics,
reformulations, combinations). A truth record needs one cited document. The
selection rule:

1. **Same entity only.** The generic name must equal the INN once salt and
   formulation words are removed. This drops combinations (olanzapine and
   fluoxetine), esters (haloperidol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate,
   aripiprazole lauroxil) and supplement "tryptophan" labels.
2. **Oral or sublingual, NDA or ANDA.** amisulpride's only US label is
   Barhemsys, an IV antiemetic: a different dose and population, so amisulpride
   has no label.
3. **A psychiatric indication first.** BRISDELLE (paroxetine 7.5 mg for hot
   flushes) and SILENOR (doxepin 3-6 mg for insomnia) are otherwise the newest
   NDAs.
4. **NDA over ANDA, and among NDAs the lowest application number.**

**The first version of rule 4 was wrong, and reading the transcriptions found
it.** It preferred the latest NDA. That picked 505(b)(2) reformulations whose
dosing is product-specific:

- a sertraline capsule label recommending "150 mg or 200 mg once daily";
- a duloxetine product dosed at 80-120 mg;
- a venlafaxine tablet only for patients switching from another product.

NDA numbers are assigned in submission order, so the lowest is the innovator.
Thirteen drugs changed label and were re-transcribed. A test pins Zoloft
50-200 mg/day and Cymbalta 40-120 mg/day.

**Why transcription, not a parser.** `scripts/fetch_fda_labels.py` (P22.2)
already explains that a regular expression over DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION
produces a number that looks sourced and is not. A quick test confirmed it.
Regex candidates included:

- a flattened table ("MDD 50 mg 50-200 mg OCD 50 mg …");
- a nasal diazepam product;
- "450 mg twice daily" read as a daily dose.

So the label PK and dose ranges (196 items over 67 drugs) were transcribed by
hand, each with its verbatim sentence. `verify_transcription` then refuses:

- a transcription whose set_id is not the selected label;
- a quote that is not in that label's text;
- a value not printed in its quotes, unless a `derivation` states the arithmetic
  ("450 mg twice daily printed; 2 × 450 = 900 mg/day").

Doses are mg of the labelled salt, as printed (e.g. bupropion HCl).

**WHO DDD** is parsed as printed for every ATC code: value, unit, route and
note, so haloperidol's 8 mg oral, 8 mg parenteral and 3.3 mg depot rows all
stay. An ATC code with no DDD (lumateperone, vilazodone, every unapproved FAIL
compound) stays `ddd: []`.

### PET: abstract-quoted, checked against the abstract on every build

There are 82 group occupancies (D2 54, SERT 20, 5-HT2A 8) for 27 drugs, from 37
abstracts. Each row carries the abstract sentence that prints both the dose and
the occupancy, and the build refuses any quote that is not a verbatim substring
of the Europe PMC abstract. Rows were reviewed one by one:

- **Doses written per administration** ("300 mg b.i.d.", "100 mg three times
  daily") carry a `dose_derivation`. So does asenapine's "100 micrograms", a
  single sublingual sub-therapeutic dose that is flagged as such.
- **Bounds are not means.** "<5%" is `upper_bound`, ">80%" is `lower_bound`, and
  "up to 39%" is `peak`. A test pins these.
- **Not a dose-occupancy table.** Abstracts print group values, so this set is
  for Phase 29's occupancy-at-dose check, not for fitting an EC50. The per-
  subject PET this repo holds from Phases 19-25 stays in `human/`.

Full texts were not read, so a drug in `pet_searched_empty.json` may still have
a value in a paper's table. The ledger row says so.

### The effect-label vector, and the two places the first rule was wrong

**Sources.**

- SIDER 4.1, the frequency and side-effect tables.
- The selected label's own adverse-reaction tables, parsed into per-term
  drug-arm incidences. `parse_ar_tables` lays the HTML out on a real grid
  (colspan *and* rowspan; ABILIFY's header uses rowspan, which shifted every
  drug column onto placebo until this was handled). A column counts as the
  drug's only when its stacked header names the drug and not placebo, so a
  haloperidol comparator column in another drug's table is never attributed to
  it. Pediatric and discontinuation tables are skipped.

**Matching SIDER to the drug (rule 2).** SIDER keys rows by a STITCH "flat" id
that merges stereoisomers. Matching rules:

- **The ATC links are not usable.** SIDER's ATC table maps escitalopram's code
  to citalopram's flat id, clopenthixol's to zuclopenthixol, and esketamine's
  to racemic ketamine.
- **So matching is by SIDER drug name equal to the INN** (or a same-entity
  spelling: dothiepin, thiothixene, propericiazine).
- **Two flat ids hold two benchmark entities each.** Citalopram/escitalopram and
  milnacipran/levomilnacipran are split by SIDER's stereo-id column.
- **Clopenthixol and esketamine get no SIDER data.**
- **Fluphenazine keeps the hydrochloride record**, not the decanoate's.

**The rule** is in `effect_labels.json["rule"]` and in the ledger. The threshold
is 5%: the incidence most US labels use for "most common adverse reactions" in
Highlights. CIOMS "common" (1%) would admit almost every term in a psychiatric
label table. 5% was fixed before any prevalence was computed. Every per-term
maximum is stored, so another threshold can be applied without refetching.
**Tremor is not EPS** and plain hypotension is not orthostasis, because both are
labelled for SSRIs and TCAs through other mechanisms.

**The rule-12 check found two errors in the first negative rule:**

1. **"No term reaches 5%" was read as negative.** Haloperidol came out
   EPS-negative and amitriptyline anticholinergic-negative, because their old
   labels name these effects with no incidence at all. A first fix still made
   haloperidol anticholinergic-negative off one "very rare" urinary-retention
   row while its label names dry mouth and constipation without numbers. The
   final rule works per concept:
   - with the drug's own table parsed, absence means below the table's
     inclusion threshold;
   - without one, the effect is negative only if every concept named for the
     drug has a printed frequency below 5%;
   - otherwise it is unknown.

   Synonyms ("weight gain", "weight increased") are one concept.
2. **SIDER stores a postmarketing report as frequency 0-0.001.** A spontaneous
   report has no denominator, so that range is a placeholder, not an incidence.
   It had made thioridazine EPS-negative. Postmarketing rows now name a term
   (the `listed` vector) and are never frequency evidence.

**What was not changed after seeing the data.** The two sources agree on 202 of
224 drug-effect pairs (90.2%). The disagreements are visible:

- SIDER counts bupropion's "akinesia/bradykinesia 8%" as EPS with no placebo
  subtraction;
- SIDER includes the pediatric tables that the label parse skips.

Editing the term list to remove these would be tuning the truth toward an
expected answer, so it was left alone and the disagreement is reported instead.
The twice-placebo half of the label convention is not applied, because SIDER
placebo rows are not paired with drug rows by trial.

### What the truth can and cannot score (for Phase 29-30)

- **Seizure cannot be scored.** It is 0 of 46 under the frequency rule and 70 of
  79 under "listed". It is a rare, dose-dependent warning. Phase 30 should drop
  it or source a per-dose incidence, not lower the threshold until it
  separates.
- **Anticholinergic is near-saturated** (42 of 46). Dry mouth and constipation
  at ≥5% are common to SSRIs and SNRIs, so as defined this is a weak AUROC
  target.
- **The FAIL stratum has almost no human truth.** 16 of 17 failed compounds have
  no label, no DDD and no PK compilation. Their outcome is the failed trial
  P28.1 recorded, which is a different kind of label from an adverse-event
  vector.
- **The truth has its own noise floor.** For 16 drugs with both a ChEMBL IV t½
  and a label t½, the two sources differ by a median 1.17-fold (max 2.47:
  trazodone, label terminal t½ 18 h against 7.3 h in the IV compilation). A predicted half-life
  cannot be judged more precisely than that.
- **45 drugs have no human truth of any kind.** These are mostly the FAIL
  stratum and regional or withdrawn drugs. They can carry inputs, but no score.

## Phase 29, part one: the translation-aware species gate (P29.1)

P11.2 built the species gate on one rule: a non-human provenance species raises
`UnsourcedParameterError` at every driving position, with a single licensed
exception — a registered `CrossSpeciesAnchor`, which may be *reported* beside its
human counterpart but structurally can never *drive* a prediction
(`may_drive_predictions = False`). That rule was correct for a human-primary
model whose numbers were all meant to be human. Phase 29 is preclinical-to-human
translation, and it needs exactly the move P11.2 forbade: a rat Kp,uu or a
rat-hepatocyte intrinsic clearance driving a human prediction. The whole point of
allometric scaling, IVIVE and Kp,uu transfer is to carry a non-human measurement
across the species boundary.

### Why a tag, not a species

The failure mode to avoid is the obvious one: relaxing the gate to "rat is fine
for PK" would re-open the door P11.2 closed, because a bare rat number carries no
evidence that anyone intended it as a translation input, and nothing would
distinguish a deliberate IVIVE from a mouse Km that drifted in beside a human Ki.
So the exception is a **tag on the quantity, never a property of the species.**
`gate(species, ..., translation=TranslationTag(...))` admits the number; the same
`gate("rat", ...)` with no tag refuses it exactly as before. The two paths are
pinned against each other in `tests/test_species_gate_translation.py`
(`test_an_untagged_non_human_number_is_still_refused` and
`test_a_tagged_non_human_number_is_admitted_as_a_translated_input`).

A `TranslationTag` names three things and validates all three:

1. **A registered method.** `TRANSLATION_METHODS` holds three, each cited to the
   paper that defines it as a species bridge and each verified against Europe PMC
   on 2026-10-02: `allometric-scaling` (Boxenbaum 1982, PMID 7120049),
   `ivive` (Obach 1999, PMID 10534321, the in-vitro half-life approach with
   microsomal and blood binding), and `kp-uu-transfer` (Friden 2009, PMID
   19764786, which showed the rank order of rat and human Kp,uu,CSF is similar
   across 43 drugs). None of these papers supplies a *parameter value* — they
   supply the *method* — so registering them is not inventing a number. An
   unregistered method string is a `ValueError`.
2. **The source species**, which must normalize to a recognized non-human token.
   A tag "from human" is a `ValueError` (there is no crossing to declare), and so
   is one from an unrecognized token like `HEK293` (the crossing cannot be
   checked). The tag must also name the *same* species the parameter carries:
   a rat tag on a mouse number is refused, so a tag licenses only the one species
   it names.
3. **A citation for the measurement being translated.** Empty is a `ValueError`.
   The method citation says the bridge is real; the measurement citation says
   *this* number is real. Both are required.

### What the gate returns, and why it must be carried

The gate does not return `None` (pass) for a tagged input the way it does for a
human number. It returns a `TranslatedInput` — layer, label, species, source and
tag. This is deliberate: a translated number is not the same as a human number
and the prediction must say so. `ChainLayer` now carries a `translations` tuple,
and the invariant is enforced both ways — provenance `"translated"` requires a
non-empty tuple of `TranslatedInput` records, and a non-empty tuple requires
provenance `"translated"` (`test_a_layer_cannot_claim_translated_without_the_gate_record_or_hide_one`).
A layer cannot quietly consume a translated number under a `"measured"` label,
and cannot claim `"translated"` without naming what crossed and by what method.
`OccupancyPrediction.translated_inputs` gathers them across layers and
`.summary()` prints each, so a reader sees which of a prediction's inputs crossed
a species. `"translated"` sits between `"structural"` and `"illustrative"` in the
provenance ordering: one translated layer makes the whole prediction
`"translated"`, but one illustrative layer still outranks it
(`test_illustrative_still_outranks_translated`).

### The exposure layer and the scored check (V16)

`transfer_kp_uu` is the first consumer. Before P29.1 it accepted a rat Kp,uu and
an arbitrary transfer factor with no gate at all — a hole, since the module's
whole job is the species crossing P11.2 polices. It now routes the non-human
source through `gate(..., translation=...)`: without a tag the rat number is
refused (`UnsourcedParameterError`), with a `kp-uu-transfer` tag it is admitted
and the returned record carries the `TranslatedInput`. A tag for a different
method is refused, because a Kp,uu transfer is not an allometric scaling.

To close the task on a number nobody here chose (rule 9), `score_rat_kp_uu_transfer`
translates each drug's rat Kp,uu,brain from its P28.3 ADME record to human by the
tagged identity transfer (factor 1.0 — Friden 2009's own cross-species claim,
not a fitted coefficient, so no split is needed) and compares against the human
Kp,uu,CSF measured in the *same* Friden 2009 dataset (ChEMBL_37 document
CHEMBL1795238, human assay CHEMBL1798468). Four benchmark drugs have both:
bupropion (1.00x), diazepam (1.35x over), amitriptyline (4.06x over) and
thioridazine (3.11x under), GMFE 2.03, 2 of 4 within twofold. The surrogate is
imperfect on purpose and the ledger says so: CSF is not brain interstitial
fluid, and Friden's own rat data put Kp,uu,CSF within 3-fold of Kp,uu,brain for
33/39 drugs and over-predicting for strongly effluxed drugs, which is exactly
where amitriptyline and thioridazine miss. The number is a sanity check on a
surrogate; the *result* of P29.1 is the enforced rule and the provenance it
propagates, which is what later Phase-29 tasks (human PK from preclinical inputs,
dose-to-engagement) build on when they cross a species.

### What this is not

A translation input is not an anchor. An anchor is a matched pair kept to
*measure* transfer error and structurally never drives anything; a translation
input *drives* a prediction and *declares* that it does. Both coexist in the
module and the anchors' `may_drive_predictions = False` is untouched
(`test_anchors_still_never_drive_a_prediction`). The translation path adds a way
in for a number that announces its crossing; it does not weaken the refusal for a
number that does not.

### The leaf module, and why the types do not live in species_gate

Wiring the tag into the occupancy chain exposed a constraint. `species_gate`
imports `fingerprint` (its binding-layer check in `check_binding_target` resolves
targets through it), and `fingerprint` imports the eager `neurocascade` package,
which loads the frozen circuit/connectome/opioid tree. `test_v1_frozen_layers.py`
forbids the v1 prediction path (`human.dose_to_occupancy` and its closure) from
reaching any frozen layer. The v1 chain did *not* import `species_gate` before —
it relies on its registries already being human — so adding
`from ..species_gate import TranslatedInput` to `dose_to_occupancy`, and a gate
call to `kp_uu`, would have dragged the whole frozen tree into the v1 closure and
failed that guard.

The fix is a genuine architectural improvement rather than a workaround: the
parts of the species boundary with no fingerprint dependency —
`UnsourcedParameterError`, the species tokens, `normalize_species`, and all the
P29.1 translation types plus `check_translation` — moved to a new leaf module
`neurocascade/translation.py` that imports only `re`. `species_gate` re-imports
every name from it, so its public API (`species_gate.normalize_species`,
`species_gate.TranslationTag`, the shared `UnsourcedParameterError` identity that
`legacy.drug_pk` re-exports, …) is byte-for-byte unchanged, and `gate()`
delegates its translation handling to the leaf's `_admit_translation` so there is
one implementation of the rule. `dose_to_occupancy` and `kp_uu` import from the
leaf, keeping the v1 closure free of the fingerprint layer. `check_translation`
is the leaf's self-contained gate: human/no-claim → `None`, tagged non-human →
`TranslatedInput`, untagged non-human → `UnsourcedParameterError`, the same two
paths `gate()` enforces, available to a caller that must not import the full gate.

## Phase 29, part two: preclinical-to-human PK, scored held out (P29.2)

P29.2 was rebuilt on standard, textbook PK methods with no fitted log-log
regressions. The previous implementation fitted three regressions (a near-flat
rat-CL exponent ~0.11, an IVIVE arm that regressed CLint x fu rather than
applying the liver model, and a Vss model fitted on two drugs). It scored
held-out CL at GMFE 6.77 (n=5), worse than predicting the train geometric
mean, and its Vss result regressed human plasma Vss on rat *brain-slice*
unbound volumes, an incompatible matrix, so it was spurious.

The clearance IVIVE arm is now the well-stirred liver model
(Rowland, Benet & Graham 1973, PMID 4764426; Obach 1999, PMID 10534321):
``CL_H = Q_H * fu_b * CLint_u / (Q_H + fu_b * CLint_u)``, with
Q_H = 20.7 mL/min/kg (Davies & Morris 1993, PMID 8378254), in-vitro CLint
scaled by MPPGL ~= 40 mg/g and liver weight ~= 21.4 g/kg (Barter 2007,
PMID 17266522; hepatocyte CLint by hepatocellularity ~= 99e6 cells/g, also
Sohlenius-Sternbeck 2006, PMID 16930941), and fu_b = fu_p / Rb with Rb = 1 for
the bases/neutral set. The fu_mic microsomal-binding correction
(Austin 2002, PMID 12433825; Hallifax & Houston 2006, PMID 16552024) is
omitted because the benchmark ADME records carry no logP; this is the main
reason the raw arm under-predicts. CLint groups are keyed on
(organ, matrix, bound/unbound, units) read from the measurement descriptions,
so human liver microsomes are never pooled with intestinal microsomes or with
unbound vs total CLint (the ziprasidone pooling bug). Ziprasidone is excluded
outright because its clearance is aldehyde-oxidase dominant and AO is absent
from the microsomal assay.

The rat clearance arm is simple single-species allometry with the FIXED
exponent b = 0.75 (Boxenbaum 1982, PMID 7120049), standard rat 0.25 kg and
human 70 kg (Davies & Morris 1993, PMID 8378254). No exponent is fitted. Only
rat plasma/systemic CL (<= 100 mL/min/kg) is used; brain-ECF, hepatic,
distributional and intrinsic rows are rejected at the measurement level. IVIVE
is preferred; rat allometry is the fallback when IVIVE inputs are missing, and
on this benchmark it adds no drug IVIVE does not already cover.

The Vss arm is the Oie-Tozer fu-ratio method (Oie & Tozer 1979, PMID 501558),
Vss_h = Vss_rat * fu_h / fu_rat, scored only on clean rat *plasma* Vss.

The only empirical quantity is one optional TRAIN geometric-mean bias factor
(2.85), reported separately, never tuned on held-out. Human truth is selected
by a fixed rule: IV summary first, then unspecified route, never oral/depot.

`neurocascade.benchmark.human_pk_translation` records the method citation,
input references and each prediction, plus the train drugs used for the bias
factor. Development used TRAIN only; the held-out split was scored exactly once
after the method was frozen, then a second time after the CLint aggregation
fix described below (declared; both results are kept).

The primary (no-fit / leave-one-drug-out over train) and held-out results:

| parameter | split | scored drugs | GMFE | within 2-fold | within 3-fold |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CL | train (no-fit) | 15 | 2.855 | 7/15 (0.47) | 9/15 (0.60) |
| CL | held-out | 5 | 3.420 | 1/5 (0.20) | 3/5 (0.60) |
| CL (bias-corrected) | held-out | 5 | 2.733 | 2/5 (0.40) | 3/5 (0.60) |
| CL, train-mean baseline | same 15 train drugs | 15 | 2.751 | | |
| CL, train-mean baseline | held-out | 5 | 4.983 | 0/5 | 1/5 |

Baselines (leave-one-out train geometric-mean predictor): CL GMFE 3.082 (n=32),
Vss GMFE 3.889 (n=32). On the same 15 train drugs the mechanistic CL arm is
level with the train-mean floor (2.855 vs 2.751); on the 5 held-out drugs it is
better (3.42 vs 4.98), which n=5 cannot establish. The error is a systematic
under-prediction of lipophilic bases (haloperidol 18-fold, desipramine 8.7,
chlorpromazine 7.5), the signature of the omitted microsomal binding (fu_mic).

CLint aggregation fix (2026-10-12, after the first held-out score). The first
held-out score was GMFE 5.489 with imipramine 86-fold low. Its CLint was a
geometric mean over rows that included one ChEMBL document (CHEMBL3526124) at
0.04-0.05, mL/min/mg stored under the uL/min/mg-equivalent unit. CLint is now
reduced per reference, references more than 30-fold from the others' median are
dropped as unit-suspect, and the median is taken. The fix applies to every drug;
it moved train from 2.735 to 2.855 (worse) and held-out from 5.489 to 3.420.
Because a held-out result prompted it, the 3.420 is a second look, logged in
the conductor's held-out evaluation log.
The superseded fitted method's held-out CL was GMFE 6.77.

Vss is reported as **n=0, data-limited**: no benchmark drug pairs clean rat
plasma Vss with human Vss truth. The drugs that have human Vss truth carry only
rat brain-slice unbound volumes, not plasma Vss, so the Oie-Tozer arm has no
compatible input to score. This is an honest limitation, not a failure to
implement the method.

### Oral exposure is searched-and-empty, not a fabricated endpoint

The frozen human truth has no matched oral AUC, absolute F, or CL/F. Its
records contain IV CL/Vss compilations plus labels for dose and sometimes
half-life, but no quantity from which oral exposure can be scored. The
repository-wide search covered every P28.4 truth record, its ChEMBL human-PK
inputs, and the selected openFDA label transcriptions. The external PhRMA
CPCDC dataset described by Ring et al. 2011 (PMID 21541938) does contain oral
AUC for 107 blinded compounds, but the compound identities are intentionally
hidden and cannot be matched to these benchmark INNs. It is therefore not a
usable held-out source here. Because ``AUC_po = F * dose / CL`` requires F (or
CL/F), assuming F=1 or borrowing a value from another drug would violate rules
1 and 2. P29.2 adds no oral-exposure container or score until a same-entity,
route-matched truth is obtained; the searched-and-empty result is recorded in
the ledger.

## Phase 29, part three: target-engagement dose, scored held out (P29.3)

P29.3 was stopped at the load-bearing assumption check. The requested
prediction is not determined by P29.2's output alone. For a competitive target,
the intended steady-state mean-dose calculation is

```
Cbrain,u = Kp,uu * fu,p * Cplasma,total
Ctarget,u = Ki * p / (1 - p)
Dtarget/kg/day = Ctarget,u / (Kp,uu * fu,p) * CL/kg * 1.44 / F
```

where `p` is the target occupancy. Converting this per-kg result to the
clinical `mg/day` label scale additionally requires a source-defined human
reference weight. The benchmark has no route-matched oral absolute F, oral
CL/F, or oral AUC in any of its 55 held-out truth records. P29.2 deliberately
returns per-kg CL because its preclinical records contain no animal body
weights; multiplying it by an unreferenced 70 kg would undo that refusal.
Setting `F=1` or borrowing F from another drug would violate the sourcing and
entity rules. A label dose range also does not define a unique pointwise
clinical dose without a predeclared interval scoring rule.

The second load-bearing check is the endpoint itself. The 70% striatal D2
threshold is admitted only for N05A antipsychotics, supported by the published
65–70% efficacy discussion (Kapur and Seeman 2001, PMID 11729039) and the
70–80% therapeutic window review (Kapur et al. 2009, PMID 21143431). No
equivalent class-level human target-engagement threshold was found for N05B,
N06A, or FAIL, so the threshold is not transferred to those strata.

The repository census and the full refusal table are in
`docs/p29-3-dose-engagement.md`. It covers all 55 held-out drugs and records
the binding-target, rat Kp,uu, P29.2 CL, human plasma-fu, PET, and oral-exposure
layers separately. The closest row is ziprasidone: D2 Ki, rat Kp,uu, human fu,
and a P29.2 CL prediction exist, but the benchmark still has no same-entity
oral F/CL/F and no source-defined reference weight for a clinical mg/day
comparison. Diazepam has the P29.2 CL, rat Kp,uu, and human fu layers but no
N05B threshold. No row therefore reaches a defensible prediction.

The external-source check did not change that result. de Greef et al. (2011,
PMID 21184291; PMC3032087) and the FDA GEODON label (NDA 020825) provide
ziprasidone oral-PK fields, but not a complete benchmark-wide input set or a
reference-weighted held-out comparison. Fridén et al. (2009, PMID 19764786)
supports the P29.1 rat-to-human Kp,uu method but has human CSF overlap for only
four benchmark drugs and no human ziprasidone Kp,uu. Lako et al. (2013, PMID
23948784) and Suzuki et al. (2013, PMID 23417515) provide PET dose/occupancy
observations; using those dose/occupancy relations as the prediction would
collapse the requested PET comparison into its input. They remain future
anchors, not substitutes for the missing oral bridge.

P29.3 consequently produces no score: clinical-dose fold-error **n=0** and
PET-anchored-dose fold-error **n=0**, both searched-and-empty. This is a
deliberate negative result, not a registry or gate. The task can be reopened
when the missing same-entity oral exposure and reference-weight records exist
and the non-N05A endpoint thresholds have been pre-specified.

## Phase 29, part four: panel occupancy-time at clinical dose (P29.4)

P29.4 was stopped at the same load-bearing assumption that P29.3 exposed, but
with the panel/PET denominator checked explicitly. The frozen benchmark has
exactly eight held-out drugs with PET dose/occupancy observations:
amisulpride, asenapine, escitalopram, lurasidone, milnacipran, paroxetine,
quetiapine and venlafaxine. All eight have a P28.2 human Ki panel. Thus the
observation side is large enough for the brief's ``>=8 drugs`` condition.

The prediction side is not. P29.2 predicts human IV CL and Vss per kilogram;
it does not provide oral F, oral AUC, oral CL/F or a source-defined reference
weight. The benchmark therefore cannot turn a clinical mg/day dose into the
plasma concentration-time curve required by occupancy. The equation
``AUC_po = F * dose / CL`` still has an unmeasured F, and the per-kg P29.2
clearance cannot be multiplied by an invented 70 kg. The held-out P29.2 CL
error (n=5, GMFE 6.774746573244732) is an IV translation result, not a licence
to attach a band to an unidentified oral curve.

The target-exposure assumption was checked separately. Among these eight,
P28.3 contains a usable rat Kp,uu for quetiapine and venlafaxine only. The
tagged P29.1 transfer method can carry those two values as translated inputs,
but it does not create values for the other six. P23.2's earlier comparison
also remains binding: applying an in-vitro Ki as if it were an in-vivo PET
constant is a weaker quantity, and the measured haloperidol discrepancy
reaches 0.368 occupancy units. No Ki-to-PET correction was fitted here.

Venlafaxine is the closest apparent case because it has a P29.2 CL prediction
and rat Kp,uu. It still fails the same-entity check: its human SERT exposure
includes active O-desmethylvenlafaxine, while the benchmark panel is the
parent's panel. Klamerus et al. 1992 (PMID 1487561) is the primary human
parent/metabolite PK source. Dropping the metabolite would make the apparent
success a parent-only substitution.

The full census, external search trail and reopening conditions are in
`docs/p29-4-occupancy-time.md`. The external pass searched primary or
first-party sources for oral population PK and Kp,uu for all eight drugs,
including Søgaard et al. 2005 (PMID 16291715), Bartlett & van der Voort
Maarschalk 2012 (PMID 22936407), Zhang et al. 2023 (PMID 37731733), Zhou et
al. 2015 (PMID 25975812), Li et al. 2022 (PMID 36172189), Li et al. 2012
(PMID 22653299), Fridén et al. 2009 (PMID 19764786), and Loryan et al. 2022
(PMCID PMC9246790). The candidates either supplied direct human PK rather than
a preclinical translation, lacked brain exposure, used a different route, or
left the active metabolite unresolved. None closes the requested chain.

The result is deliberately **searched-and-empty, n=0 predictions**: no
occupancy registry, panel container, or always-failing gate was added. A
future run may report receptor-wise MAE and signed bias only after the
preclinical oral exposure path is complete and frozen before comparison with
the already recorded PET observations.

## Phase 29, part five: oral exposure and PET plasma-pair evidence (P29.5)

P29.5 checked the load-bearing data assumption before extending P29.2/P29.3
into an oral exposure prediction. The source search found same-entity human
oral exposure records for all eight held-out PET drugs, but it did not find
enough numerical PET dose/plasma pairs or enough train-side preclinical
oral/clearance inputs to meet the brief. The task therefore adds evidence
records and an explicit negative coverage result, not an oral fitter.

The oral truth layer has 8/8 records: AUC/dose for amisulpride and quetiapine,
CL/F for escitalopram, lurasidone, paroxetine and venlafaxine, and F or an
explicit source-defined range for asenapine, lurasidone, milnacipran,
paroxetine and venlafaxine. The values remain route- and qualifier-specific.
In particular, sublingual and swallowed asenapine are not merged, lurasidone's
9--19% label value remains an absorbed-fraction range, and no unreferenced
body weight or F midpoint is introduced.

Only five PET drugs have defensible dose/plasma records: amisulpride,
asenapine, paroxetine, quetiapine and venlafaxine. Asenapine is explicitly a
regulatory target-concentration model point, paroxetine is a plateau boundary,
and venlafaxine is a NET/active-moiety PET series, so these qualifiers are
machine-readable rather than silently treated as homogeneous parent-SERT
measurements. Escitalopram, lurasidone and milnacipran remain
searched-and-empty because the reachable sources print model or
dose/occupancy summaries without numerical paired plasma values.

The preclinical input census is 36/130 train drugs (27.7%) and 5/8 of the
held-out PET drugs. Asenapine's rat F range and lurasidone's rat oral F,
clearance, Vss and binding were added with their regulatory/primary citations;
amisulpride, paroxetine and quetiapine have explicit searched-and-empty rows.
Existing P28.3 ADME fields are counted only when a cited record already
contains CLint, in-vivo clearance/Vss, or an explicit oral-absorption field.
Fraction-unbound and brain-exposure fields alone are not oral inputs.

The records live in
`src/neurocascade/benchmark/p29_5/{oral_exposure,pet_plasma_pairs,preclinical_oral_inputs}.json`,
with the coverage loader in `p29_5.py` and tests in
`tests/test_p29_5_data.py`. P29.5 loaders are evidence readers only: no
fitting module imports them, and the held-out truth records remain outside the
fit path. The full source trail and per-drug search outcomes are in
`docs/p29-5-oral-exposure-pet-data.md`.

The acceptance result is deliberately incomplete: oral truth is 8/8, but PET
pairs are 5/8 (required >=6) and train preclinical coverage is 36/130
(required >=60%). No prediction or calibration is reported from these records.

## Phase 29, part seven: PDSP Link digits repaired as citations (P29.7)

### What was wrong, read off the PDSP CSV rather than the brief

The brief described 19 nonexistent PMIDs that "look like PDSP Ki-database
record IDs". Re-reading the PDSP CSV the panels were built from (sha256
`45c9a18a…`, the same file recorded in every panel's provenance) showed the
cause was different. P28.2's `_pmid_from_link` took the first 6-9 digit run of
PDSP's free-text `Link` column as a PMID, whatever the URL was. When the link
was a publisher URL, the digits were a publisher identifier:

| Stored "PMID" | Where the digits came from | PDSP Reference(s) in the panels |
|---|---|---|
| 001429990 | Elsevier pii S0014-2999(01)… (Eur J Pharmacol ISSN) | Schmidt 2001 |
| 022352341 | Elsevier pii S0223-5234(18)… (Eur J Med Chem ISSN) | Zajdel 2018 |
| 0960894 | Elsevier pii S0960-894X(…) (Bioorg Med Chem Lett ISSN) | Ablordeppey 2006, Panczyk 2018, Yarravarapu 2018 |
| 096808960 | Elsevier pii S0968-0896(06)… (Bioorg Med Chem ISSN) | Van der Mey 2006 |
| 13543784 | Taylor & Francis DOI 10.1517/13543784… | Keck 2003 |
| 4119213, 5313063 | PMC ids PMC4119213, PMC5313063 | Gassaway 2014, Song 2017 |
| 430248 | Hindawi article number | Clayton 2015 |
| 6500342 | Nature DOI sj.tpj.6500342 | Davies 2005 |
| 908643 | Prous `p_RefId` | Silvestre 2005 |
| 93617739 | ScienceDirect `_alid` search id | Seeman 2001 |

So these are not PDSP record ids either (a PDSP row's own id is its `Number`,
already kept in every measurement's `record` as "PDSP Ki ID n"). Only 93617739
and 096808960 fail esummary outright; the other nine strings resolve to
unrelated papers (908643 is a 1977 corneal-cell paper, 430248 a 1979 zinc
paper), which is worse, because a PubMed existence check passes them. One
stored key, `PMID:0960894`, also stood for three different papers. The
brief's count of 19 could not be reproduced from this tree; what the sweep of
all 702 distinct PMIDs in benchmark JSON found is the table above: 11 strings,
13 papers, 684 PDSP measurements in 32 binding panels. Every other PDSP-sourced
PMID came from a PubMed URL, and its first author and year were checked against
esummary.

### What changed

- `_pmid_from_link` now reads a PMID only from an `ncbi.nlm.nih.gov` link that
  is not a PMC link. Any other link gives no PMID.
- `PDSP_PAPERS` maps each of the 13 PDSP Reference strings to its paper. Each
  was found from its DOI or pii (PubMed esearch, Crossref for Seeman) and then
  verified by title and authors in PubMed esummary on 2026-10-15. Twelve have a
  PMID. Seeman P (2001) *Antipsychotic drugs, dopamine receptors, and
  schizophrenia*, Clin Neurosci Res 1:53-60, doi 10.1016/S1566-2772(00)00007-4,
  is not in PubMed: esearch on the DOI and on the title returned nothing, so it
  stays a `PDSP_REF:` reference with its DOI and no PMID. That is a
  searched-and-empty PMID, not a guessed one.
- The former digits are kept in each reference record as `pdsp_id`, next to
  `pdsp_link` and `pdsp_reference`. They are not deleted, so the old key can be
  traced to the new one.
- `pmid_note` is added wherever a drug is not named in the paper's PubMed
  title or abstract. The test is the abstract, not the host guard's looser
  title + abstract + MeSH test. The first review of this task rejected
  Schmidt 2001 and Ablordeppey 2006 for clozapine etc.: MeSH lists them, the
  abstract does not. The note states the paper's scope. Two scopes matter for
  later users of these numbers. Silvestre & Prous 2005 is a **compilation**: its
  25 antipsychotics' pKi come from Prous Science Integrity, not a measurement.
  Keck 2003 is a review.
- `add_ref` now merges instead of first-wins. The first source still sets the
  citation, but a later PDSP row adds `pdsp_id`/`pmid_note` to an existing
  ChEMBL record of the same paper.
- `relink` is a new offline stage. It needs only the cached PDSP CSV and
  re-derives every committed PDSP measurement's reference from its PDSP row
  number. The committed panels were repaired with it, not by hand. A second run
  changes nothing.

### Values

No measurement value, relation, record or target changed (checked
measurement-by-measurement against the previous commit). Spot checks of
measurement values against the real source agree. Clayton 2015's full text
(PMC4657098) prints alprazolam 0.8/0.59/1.43/1.54/10000 nM and diazepam
14/20/15/11 nM at α1/α2/α3/α5(/α6)β3γ2, the PDSP values. Gassaway 2014's
abstract prints tianeptine MOR Ki 383 nM. Yarravarapu 2018's prints
(S)-citalopram hSERT 1.77 nM. No source was found reporting a different value.

Summaries did change, and this is the P28.2 rule working, not a new choice.
Three of the papers were already cited under their real PMID by ChEMBL for the
same drug: Zajdel 2018, Panczyk 2018 and Yarravarapu 2018. The bogus key had
made one paper's table count as two references in the median-over-references.
Re-keyed, they merge as P28.2 intends ("keeps one paper's table … from
counting three times"). The changes:

| Drug | Target | ki_nM before → after | n_references |
|---|---|---|---|
| aripiprazole | HTR1A | 6.45 → 5.94 | 18 → 17 |
| aripiprazole | HTR2A | 10.78 → 9.60 | 24 → 23 |
| aripiprazole | HTR7 | 22.51 → 19.49 | 14 → 13 |
| escitalopram | SLC6A4 | 1.77 → 1.71 | 7 → 6 |
| haloperidol | HTR1A | 1931 → 1950 | 20 → 19 |
| haloperidol | HTR6 | 5742 → 6000 | 10 → 9 |
| haloperidol | HTR7 | 408 → 403 | 13 → 12 |
| mianserin | HTR2A | 3.20 → 2.99 | 17 → 16 |
| olanzapine | HTR7 | 207.5 → 208.9 | 12 → 11 |
| risperidone | DRD2 | 2.91 → 2.95 | 31 → 30 |
| risperidone | HTR1A | 363 → 355 | 20 → 19 |
| risperidone | HTR6 | 1329 → 1397 | 15 → 14 |
| risperidone | HTR7 | 3.16 → 3.69 | 13 → 12 |
| ziprasidone | DRD2 | 3.60 → 3.80 | 19 → 18 |
| ziprasidone | HTR1A | 2.51 → 3.16 | 13 → 12 |
| ziprasidone | HTR6 | 60.9 → 62.0 | 9 → 8 |

On clozapine HTR2A, haloperidol DRD2 and HTR2A, olanzapine DRD2 and
ziprasidone HTR2A, only `n_references` fell by one. The haloperidol D2 anchor
stays 2.0 nM.

### Not done, and why

- Hydroxyzine cites Panczyk 2018 (PMID 29730027) through ChEMBL, not PDSP,
  and the paper's title, abstract and MeSH do not name hydroxyzine. The rule
  this task applies is per citation of the twelve repaired PMIDs, not per
  source, so `_note_unnamed_papers` runs after `build` and `relink` assemble a
  panel's references and notes any citation of a `PDSP_PAPERS` paper by a
  drug outside its `named` list, whichever database supplied it. It changed
  only hydroxyzine's record. A `pmid_note` sweep of every other genuine
  ChEMBL/GtoPdb citation is a larger task than this brief's and is not done.
- No validation-ledger row. This task makes no prediction and scores no drug.
  It repairs the provenance of inputs that later rows score against.

## Phase 30, part one: occupancy profile to clinical-effect probabilities (P30.1)

P30.1 is implemented in `neurocascade.benchmark.effects`. The first design
decision was made against the data, not the brief: P28.4's committed truth has
130 training records but the conductor checkout intentionally removes all 55
held-out truth records. The held-out evaluator therefore returns an explicit
`searched-and-empty` result and never interprets a missing record as a
negative. The host can run the same function when it supplies the frozen
held-out truth.

### Exposure is a pluggable, two-tier input

`clinical_exposure(drug)` is the one exposure seam. It uses a source-printed
WHO oral DDD when one exists. If a drug has no DDD, a single printed label dose
is used; for a printed range, the lower endpoint is retained and labelled as a
lower-bound exposure. No range midpoint is invented.

- **Tier 1** uses an observed human oral CL/F in P28.4, where the label prints
  an absolute L/h value. The dose/CL/F result is retained as an exposure index.
  Per-kg CL/F is refused because the benchmark has no source-defined weight.
  The current train data have two usable absolute CL/F records: olanzapine and
  zuranolone.
- **Tier 2** uses the pre-registered dose-proportional fallback, with the
  training median of the observed absolute CL/F values. It is explicitly a
  dose/Ki ranking proxy, not P29.2 predicted PK. The current train fit has 33
  tier-2 and 2 tier-1 exposure records among drugs with usable binding, dose
  and effect truth.
- P29.1's drug-specific Kp,uu is multiplied in only where a repository record
  exists. A missing Kp,uu or human unbound fraction is not filled from another
  drug. Because P28.1 does not carry molecular weights and P28.4 does not carry
  human fu for this task, the feature is named an `occupancy index`, not a
  molar brain occupancy. This is the load-bearing limitation to resolve before
  calling the model a clinical occupancy predictor.

### Labels are auditable and placebo subtraction is not hidden

`effect_labels(drug)` emits one row per effect with drug percentage, a
placebo percentage, source, evidence terms, and the rule applied. P28.4 stores
drug-arm percentages and SIDER frequency bounds, but not a paired placebo
percentage for those rows. A table caption saying “greater than placebo” is not
itself a placebo number. Therefore `placebo_percent` remains `null` and the
row is marked `absolute-fallback-unpaired-placebo-percentage-not-printed` (or
`absolute-fallback-no-placebo-arm-published` where no placebo is present). This
is a flagged fallback, not silent placebo subtraction. A future label source
with paired arms can replace the adapter without changing the model.

### Model, split, and result

The model is one additive L2-regularised logistic regression per effect. The
intercept and one coefficient per human Ki-panel target are returned by
`EffectModel.coefficient_table()`, so receptor drivers remain inspectable. The
coefficients are per one standard deviation of the train-split occupancy
index: every fit standardises its own rows (the leave-one-out fold's training
drugs, never the left-out drug) before applying the penalty. The L2 strength is
`1.0`, explicitly an illustrative analysis hyperparameter, not a literature or
biological constant. It is fixed before fitting and is reported in `report()`.

**Why standardisation is load-bearing, not cosmetic.** The first fit of this
task applied the L2 penalty to raw occupancy indices, which span roughly 1e-4
to 4e-1. At that scale the penalty dominates the likelihood, every coefficient
shrinks to at most 0.024, and each prediction is essentially the fold's
intercept. Because a leave-one-out fold that omits a positive drug has a lower
class prevalence, that drug receives the *lower* intercept: the model ranked
every positive below every negative and produced a leave-one-out AUROC of
exactly 0.000 for all seven effects while the in-sample AUROC was 0.755. Two
facts identify that as a collapsed fit rather than a real inversion: the exact
0.000 for every effect, and the near-constant predicted probabilities (about
0.312 versus 0.346, spread under 0.04). The zero table this task first
committed is withdrawn; the fit was repaired by standardising each fold's
features, and a regression test now fails if leave-one-out predictions collapse
to their fold intercept again. No tolerance, label, class weight, feature set
or split was changed.

The primary internal estimate is leave-one-drug-out over every train drug with
that effect labelled:

| effect | n scored | positive / negative | AUROC | headline status |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EPS | 30 | 10 / 20 | 0.565 | scored |
| sedation | 31 | 25 / 6 | 0.500 | scored |
| weight gain | 28 | 11 / 17 | 0.497 | scored |
| anticholinergic | 29 | 26 / 3 | 0.077 | underpowered; excluded |
| orthostasis | 32 | 3 / 29 | 0.069 | underpowered; excluded |
| sexual dysfunction | 29 | 8 / 21 | 0.542 | scored |
| seizure | 31 | 0 / 31 | not estimable | underpowered; excluded |

**Read the corrected table as a mostly negative result.** On the train split
the model is at or near chance for every well-populated effect (0.497–0.565),
and the two effects it ranks below chance are the two the class-count rule
already excludes. With 35 fitted drugs and 57 target features an L2 logistic at
this penalty does not learn a transportable occupancy-to-effect map. Any effect
with fewer than five examples of either class is excluded from headline
metrics, which excludes anticholinergic, orthostasis and seizure in this data,
not just seizure.

The tier-1-only sensitivity analysis has n=2 for every effect, with at most one
positive and one negative and therefore every effect underpowered. It is
reported beside the headline by `report()` and is not promoted to a clinical
claim.

### Held-out result (run on a host that holds the frozen truth)

The conductor's checkout removes all 55 frozen held-out effect records, so
there `heldout_evaluation()` returns `searched-and-empty` with every drug named
and no drug counted as a negative. `n_scored` counts only drugs with at least
one known binary label, so the number is a scored-drug count, not a
drugs-with-a-profile count. On a host with the full tree the same
function scores the held-out drugs that have both a known label and a unique
exact oral clinical dose. The denominator is easy to overstate: of the 55
held-out drugs, **18 carry at least one known binary effect label, 39 have a
unique exact oral clinical dose, and 17 have both** — that 17 is the held-out
scoring set. The other 38 split into two disjoint reported buckets: 22 have a
dose but no known label for any effect (`unlabelled`; 37 held-out drugs in all
have all-unknown labels, and 15 of those also lack a dose), and 16 have no
unique exact oral clinical dose (`missing_input`; asenapine is the one of those
16 that does carry labels — its label gap is a dosing gap). Neither bucket is
ever scored as a negative:
amineptine, asenapine, bifemelane, bitopertin, bradanicline, chlorproethazine,
droperidol, fluanisone, gedocarnil, mosapramine, navacaprant, oxitriptan,
pinazepam, pipotiazine, tofisopam, verucerfont (no unique exact oral clinical
dose). Nothing in the fit or the feature set is chosen on held-out data.

| effect | n scored | positive / negative | AUROC | underpowered |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EPS | 14 | 5 / 9 | 0.956 | no |
| sedation | 17 | 12 / 5 | 0.542 | no |
| weight gain | 15 | 4 / 11 | 0.705 | yes (4 positives) |
| anticholinergic | 16 | 15 / 1 | 0.333 | yes |
| orthostasis | 15 | 3 / 12 | 0.306 | yes |
| sexual dysfunction | 12 | 6 / 6 | 0.806 | no |
| seizure | 14 | 0 / 14 | not estimable | yes |

**These held-out point estimates are not evidence of a working map.** They
contradict the train-split estimate: EPS is 0.565 in leave-one-out and 0.956 on
held-out, on 14 drugs with 5 positives, and sedation is 0.500 versus 0.542.
A model at chance on its own train drugs that scores 0.96 on 14 held-out drugs
is describing the noise in a 14-point sample, not a mechanism; the comparison
that would separate the two is a baseline, which is P30.2's job and is
deliberately not done here. The held-out numbers are reported as measured and
no headline claim is made from them.

The choice of a regularised logistic model follows the interpretability goal:
regularised logistic models are used specifically to expose a compact set of
non-zero, comprehensible predictors in clinical prediction (Liu et al. 2016,
PMID 26921029). The paper is methodological support for the model family, not
a source for any neurocascade parameter.

## Phase 30, part two: effect baselines and uncertainty (P30.2)

P30.2 is implemented in `neurocascade.benchmark.effect_scoring` and its artifact
is generated, never hand-written: `python scripts/score_p30_2.py` writes
`results/P30.2.json` from `score_p30_2()` on a checkout that holds the frozen
truth. It compares the frozen P30.1 train-only occupancy model with two
baselines on the *same* eligible rows, reporting AUROC, AUPRC with a prevalence
baseline, and calibration (Brier score) with a drug-level percentile bootstrap
(2,000 replicates, seed `20261018`, Efron 1979, doi:10.1214/aos/1176344552 —
illustrative analysis settings, not biological parameters).

* `strongest_target_ki`: negative log10 of the smallest reported human Ki. Its
  score is not a probability, so its Brier score is reported as null with a
  reason rather than as a number that would only measure the score's scale.
* `nearest_neighbor`: 1-nearest binding fingerprint over shared log10(Ki)
  targets, returning that neighbour's binary label. Because its scores tie
  heavily, AUPRC resolves ties by averaging over every ordering inside a tied
  block; the first version broke ties by row index, so its AUPRC and CI
  depended on drug order (found in acceptance review of PR #31 and fixed here,
  with a permutation test).

On a host holding the frozen truth the held-out split, as in P30.1, is small:
**17 of the 55 held-out drugs are scorable** (18 carry at least one known
binary label, 39 have a unique exact oral clinical dose, 17 have both; the
other 22 have a dose but no label and the remaining 16 have no dose, and none of
them is ever scored as a negative). A three-way comparison needs all three
methods on the same drug, which drops four more: clobazam has no human Ki panel
for the strongest-Ki baseline, and clobazam, alprazolam, diazepam and aprepitant
have no nearest neighbour with a shared target and that label. Those exclusions
are reported per effect in `results/P30.2.json` (`excluded_for_baseline`, with
its reason) and counted in the table's `excluded` column, so per-effect n
compared is 9–13 out of the 17:

| effect | n compared | excluded | +/– | model AUROC (95% CI) | strongest-Ki AUROC | 1-NN AUROC | model AUPRC (95% CI) | prevalence | 1-NN AUPRC | model Brier (95% CI) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| EPS | 11 | 3 | 4 / 7 | 1.00 [1.00, 1.00] | 0.61 | 0.62 | 1.00 [1.00, 1.00] | 0.36 | 0.65 | 0.10 [0.05, 0.18] |
| sedation | 13 | 4 | 9 / 4 | 0.61 [0.20, 1.00] | 0.78 | 0.39 | 0.81 [0.55, 1.00] | 0.69 | 0.70 | 0.23 [0.07, 0.42] |
| weight gain | 12 | 3 | 3 / 9 | 0.74 [0.43, 1.00] | 0.33 | 0.61 | 0.44 [0.20, 1.00] | 0.25 | 0.50 | 0.24 [0.13, 0.37] |
| anticholinergic | 13 | 3 | 12 / 1 | 0.42 [0.17, 0.73] | 0.67 | 0.42 | 0.94 [0.78, 1.00] | 0.92 | 0.93 | 0.07 [0.01, 0.20] |
| orthostasis | 12 | 3 | 3 / 9 | 0.30 [0.00, 0.82] | 0.52 | 0.67 | 0.26 [0.08, 0.73] | 0.25 | 0.63 | 0.22 [0.01, 0.44] |
| sexual dysfunction | 9 | 3 | 5 / 4 | 0.85 [0.44, 1.00] | 0.50 | 0.90 | 0.88 [0.52, 1.00] | 0.56 | 0.95 | 0.25 [0.12, 0.38] |
| seizure | 11 | 3 | 0 / 11 | NA | NA | NA | NA | 0.00 | NA | 0.00 [0.00, 0.00] |

**Every held-out effect is underpowered** (fewer than five positives or
negatives), so the headline fields are empty by the pre-declared rule and no
clinical claim is made. Read as descriptives, the occupancy model beats *both*
baselines on AUROC for EPS and weight gain, but on AUPRC only for EPS. The
perfect EPS row is four positives and seven negatives, and its `[1.00, 1.00]`
interval is what a degenerate bootstrap looks like, not evidence. The
strongest-Ki baseline wins sedation and anticholinergic on AUROC;
nearest-neighbour wins orthostasis and sexual dysfunction. A different winner
per effect on 9–13 drugs is what a set of noise-sized estimates looks like.
No number in this paragraph is restated from the tables above on purpose:
prose that repeats the artifact is how the previous draft drifted.

The all-available LODO diagnostic (52 drugs, leave-one-drug-out over frozen
inputs, not held-out evidence) is harsher:

| effect | n | model AUROC / AUPRC / Brier | strongest-Ki AUROC / AUPRC | 1-NN AUROC / AUPRC |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| EPS | 37 | 0.68 / 0.55 / 0.24 | 0.63 / 0.53 | 0.56 / 0.48 |
| sedation | 42 | 0.39 / 0.81 / 0.16 | 0.73 / 0.92 | 0.35 / 0.78 |
| weight gain | 36 | 0.47 / 0.44 / 0.28 | 0.54 / 0.45 | 0.78 / 0.74 |
| anticholinergic | 39 | 0.06 / 0.84 / 0.08 | 0.35 / 0.91 | 0.44 / 0.92 |
| orthostasis | 39 | 0.36 / 0.17 / 0.18 | 0.59 / 0.24 | 0.64 / 0.39 |
| sexual dysfunction | 34 | 0.80 / 0.65 / 0.20 | 0.48 / 0.37 | 0.57 / 0.46 |
| seizure | 38 | NA / NA / 0.00 | NA / NA | NA / NA |

In LODO the occupancy model beats both baselines on both metrics for EPS and
sexual dysfunction, and for no other effect; on held-out it does so for EPS on
both metrics and for weight gain on AUROC alone. **The failure analysis this
task's acceptance asks for is explicit: outside those effects the occupancy map
is not shown to predict any effect better than a one-feature or
nearest-neighbour baseline.** Seizure cannot be separated by the committed
label rule at all (no positive in 38 or 39 drugs). These qualitative claims are
read straight off the two tables above, which are rendered from
`results/P30.2.json`; the prose does not restate their numbers, because
restating them is exactly how the previous draft drifted (acceptance review of
PR #35 found an EPS LODO 1-NN AUPRC of 0.43 here against 0.48 in the
artifact).

Why this is expected: with 35 fitted train drugs and 57 target features, the
frozen P30.1 model is already at or below chance on its own train drugs (train
LOO 0.497–0.565), so there was no transportable signal for P30.2 to recover.
The result that must not be over-read is EPS held-out 1.00 — four positives, a
degenerate interval, and a 0.68 LODO estimate beside it.

Two data gaps are now explicit and separate from the model. First, no paired
placebo incidence exists anywhere in the repository, so the label rule remains
the flagged absolute fallback and no label is placebo-subtracted. Second, 37 of
the 55 held-out drugs have all-unknown P28.4 effect labels — 22 of them have a
dose and are reported as `unlabelled`, the other 15 also lack a dose and are
reported under `missing_input` (asenapine is the single labelled drug among the
16 without a dose) — which caps the held-out scorable set at 17 regardless of
the model. The classifier is identical in `effects.heldout_evaluation` and
`effect_scoring._heldout_coverage`.
